detail.title: Exploring The Influence of Salesperson Lone Wolf Tendencies on Customer Value Co-Creation: A Social Exchange Perspective
detail.abstract: Purpose-As business-to-business (B2B) sales organizations increasingly adopt collaborative and solution-oriented selling approaches, the lone wolf tendencies (LWTs) in salespeople require further examination due to their potential to impact salesperson-customer relationships. With shifts toward cooperative paradigms favoring value co-creation between salespeople and their customers, LWTs may act as a deterrent to building successful and mutually collaborative salesperson-customer relationships. Although the potential link between salesperson personality traits and customer reactions in B2B sales has been suggested, it is unclear how the impact of salesperson's LWTs on customer value co-creation is. Design/methodology/approach-A multi-method, multi-study approach was used to explore the link between salesperson LWTs and customer responses by analyzing data from B2B salespeople, customers, and company sales figures, using a social exchange framework that emphasizes trust and conflict levels. Findings-The results from the quantitative study indicate that salesperson LWTs reduce customer value co-creation, which can, in turn, boost sales performance while decreasing customer propensity to leave. The findings suggest that salespeople with higher LWTs are more likely to undermine customer trust and escalate conflicts with customers. A qualitative study confirms earlier quantitative results and shows how LWTs are deeply embedded in sales culture, especially in high-autonomy, high-pressure environments. While LWTs can promote short-term individual success, they also pose risks to team cohesion and long-term value-highlighting the importance of strategic management that balances independence with collaboration. Originality/value-The study's insights offer a theoretical contribution to the sales literature by revealing the mechanisms through which salesperson LWTs influence customer relationships and ultimately impact sales performance. The study offers a clearer understanding of how LWTs impact sales and behavioral performance. By advancing the knowledge of these complex dynamics, this research provides valuable insights for both academicians and practitioners.

title: Factors Affecting Executive Level Employees’ Retention at Hayleys Travel & Aviation

detail.title: Factors Affecting Executive Level Employees’ Retention at Hayleys Travel & Aviation

keywords: Career Development Employee Retention; Executive-Level Employees; Performance Appraisal System; Reward System

detail.abstract: Employee retention is now one of the greatest challenges in the rapidly evolving and highly competitive travel and aviation sectors, particularly at the executive ranks whose turnover threatens continuity of operations and affects quality of services. This study examines the determinants of executive-level employee retention at Hayleys Travel & Aviation through three main human resource factors: career development, performance management systems, and reward systems. Based on Expectancy Theory and Social Exchange Theory, the study used a quantitative approach with a standard questionnaire to obtain responses from a stratified random sample of 140 executives out of which responses of 126 valid cases were analyzed using SPSS (Version 26). Descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and multiple regression analysis were used to test hypotheses. Findings show that all three variables play a significant and positive role in retention, with reward system having the highest prediction rate (R² = 0.680), followed by performance appraisal (R² = 0.629) and career development (R² = 0.614). The findings highlight the importance of competitive and fair rewards, open and developmental appraisal processes, and formal career progression possibilities in improving retention. The study offers practical recommendations for enhancing human resource practices at Hayleys Travel & Aviation and contributes to the bigger body of knowledge on employee retention practices in service industries.

title: The Role of Salespeople in Value Co-creation and its Impact on Sales Performance

detail.title: The Role of Salespeople in Value Co-creation and its Impact on Sales Performance
detail.abstract:
Purpose: This paper aims to examine salesperson skills, including listening, communication, and adaptive selling, that can enable value co-creation with customers and increase sales performance, while taking into consideration the contingent role of salesperson relationship-enhancing activities. 

Methodology: Survey and objective sales performance data were collected from 201 B2B salespeople in the industrial goods industry. The hypotheses were tested using PLS-SEM. 

Findings: The results show adaptive selling, listening, and communication of salespeople positively impact the behaviors of salespeople to co-create value with customers. The results show that when salespeople co-create value with customers, they will have a positive effect on sales performance. Results show how value co-creation mediates the effects of listening and adaptive selling on sales performance. 

Research Implications: Salespeople need to effectively listen to their customers to provide needed solutions by jointly working with them to co-create value. Similarly, a salesperson's communication and adaptive selling skills have collective impacts that positively contribute to the value co-creation process. Results supplement previous findings in the literature by showing value co-creation holds a positive effect on sales performance at the micro salesperson level. The results offer additional support to the ongoing dialog on the role of a salesperson as a value co-creator. 

Practical Implications: This study has identified several variables that engender successful cocreation by salespeople in B2B sales contexts. Findings demonstrate that salespeople who can adapt their selling approach, are good listeners, and can effectively communicate with customers can engender the value co-creation process with customers. The findings serve as a base to create professional guidelines about the skills and capabilities salespeople need to successfully execute a value co-creation process. 

Originality/Value: The study adds to the literature on value co-creation by highlighting three factors that can enhance the value co-creation process at the level of salespeople leading to better sales outcomes. This research adds the existing literature on the role of value co-creation in sales by empirically examining the relationship between value co-creation and sales performance at the salesperson level.

title: Sustainability and Professional Sales: A Review and Future Research Agenda

detail.title: Sustainability and Professional Sales: A Review and Future Research Agenda
detail.abstract: Sustainability has become a consideration for every firm operating in today’s business landscape. Scholars are tasked with uncovering bridges and barriers to successfully implement sustainability strategies, and the academic community has largely responded. However, while sustainability research has proliferated across business disciplines, it is conspicuously missing from professional selling and sales management. This is partly due to conceptual ambiguity, but also because sustainability generally involves firm-level policies and programs, and therefore domains like consumer behavior, marketing strategy, and supply chain management have occupied the space. This is problematic because while executives develop sustainability strategies, the sales force is responsible for conveying those priorities to external stakeholders. Therefore, the goals of our manuscript are to: 1) organize and refine the definition of sustainability in a professional selling context, 2) review relevant literature that examines sustainability in that context, 3) explore emergent themes from this review that 4) reveal gaps in our understanding, and 5) present a research agenda for sales scholars to bridge these gaps and advance our understanding of the role of sustainability in sales and vice versa.

detail.title: The Interplay of Morality, Emotional Labor, and Customer Injustice: How Salesperson Experiences Shape Job Satisfaction
detail.abstract: Despite the significant role emotions play in business-to-business (B2B) sales transactions, the impact of salesperson emotional labor on well-being, specifically job satisfaction, has garnered limited attention. To address this gap, the present study examines the relationships among salesperson moral identity, emotional labor strategies, customer injustice, and job satisfaction. An analysis of responses from B2B salespeople reveals that moral identity internalization is positively related to deep acting and negatively to surface acting, whereas moral identity symbolization is positively related to both deep and surface acting. Furthermore, surface acting has a stronger unfavorable effect on customer injustice compared to deep acting, which in turn negatively influences job satisfaction. The paper concludes with theoretical contributions and managerial implications.

keywords: Service Performance Paper Type Research Paper the Negative Effects of Role Conflict

detail.abstract: Purpose-This study examines the contextual variables that can curb the negative effects of role conflict on job satisfaction and enhance the positive effect of job satisfaction on creativity and service performance. More specifically, adopting the job demands-resources theory, the authors explore the interactive effect of frontline employee (FLE) self-monitoring and FLE-manager trust on the relationship between role conflict and job satisfaction. Extending this line of inquiry, the authors adopt social identity theory and analyze the moderating effect of FLE-manager identification on the relationship between job satisfaction and creativity and between job satisfaction and service performance. Design/methodology/approach-Dyadic data utilizing 122 responses from FLEs and their managers were obtained from FLEs working with a major financial services firm in India. Structural equation modeling and PLS were used to assess the hypothesized relationships. Findings-The negative relationship between role conflict and job satisfaction is reduced at higher levels of FLE self-monitoring and FLE-manager trust. Furthermore, FLE manager identification accentuates the effect of job satisfaction on creativity and service performance. Practical implications-Organizations should invest in developing FLEs' personal and job-related resources to reduce the deleterious effects of role conflicts on FLEs' job outcomes. Specifically, managers should hire FLEs who are high in self-monitoring while enhancing FLE-manager trust and FLE-manager identification. Originality/value-Role conflict is inevitable in a service job and can have serious negative downstream consequences. Hence, the study explores the important contextual factors that can help an organization develop policies to reduce the negative effects of role conflict.

title: Value Get, Value Give: The Relationships Among Perceived Value, Relationship Quality, Customer Engagement, and Value Consciousness

detail.title: Value Get, Value Give: The Relationships Among Perceived Value, Relationship Quality, Customer Engagement, and Value Consciousness
detail.abstract: In today's market, firms expect customers to not only consume their offerings, but also to market these offerings indirectly through different engagement behaviors. This study is conducted to examine factors that may drive customers to engage with restaurants. The research builds on the theory of engagement and relationship marketing literature to propose that customer perceived value (CPV) and relationship quality (RQ) are antecedents of CE. In addition, a mediated relationship between CPV and CE through RQ is examined to better understand the effects of CPV on CE. Customer value consciousness (CVC) is incorporated into the model as a boundary condition of the hypothesized positive impacts of CPV on CE and RQ. Findings demonstrate support to the relationships hypothesized. Further, the study develops the 'value get, value' framework to extend research on customer relationship and engagement. Findings are discussed in detail with implications for theory and practice.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the resale prices of fashion brands can act as a signal of the brand equity of those fashion brands. Using the resale price ratio (RPR), which is the average resale price of branded products divided by the original retail price of those products, this paper analyzes 842 resale listings from fifteen different fashion brands classified as either heritage, premium streetwear, or youth-indie brands. Results indicate that the premium streetwear brands have the highest average RPR of 1.15, followed by heritage brands with an average RPR of 0.71, and youth-indie brands, which range between an average RPR of 0.66 and 0.93. Additionally, a survey of young Indian consumers was conducted to determine their perceptions of different fashion brand categories and their willingness to pay for branded resale products. The results of both surveys provide insights into the relationship between brand equity and resale prices, as well as implications for emerging fashion brands.

detail.title: Which Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) Approach Optimizes Customer Engagement Behavior? The Role of Customer-brand Identification, Brand Love, and Social Communication
detail.abstract: While the CSR literature proliferates, understanding the effects of chiefly proactive (vs. chiefly reactive) CSR activities on customers’ brand identification and brand love lags, leaving managers in the dark. To illuminate these issues, three studies were conducted. First, study 1 deployed an experimental design to test the effect of chiefly proactive/reactive social CSR activities on customer-brand relationships, as measured by brand identification and -love, and their respective impact on customer engagement. To ensure the validity and generalizability of the results, a second study was conducted, which replicated the previous study’s design, albeit focusing on environmental CSR activities. Using survey data, study 3 tested the moderating role of social CSR communication on the association of chiefly proactive/reactive CSR activities on customer-brand identification and brand love. The findings suggest chiefly proactive (vs. reactive) CSR’s particular effectiveness in driving customer-brand identification, -love, and engagement. The study uncovered social CSR communication’s key role in building customer brand relationships, particularly for chiefly proactive CSR activities. Moreover, it shows that the effectiveness of CSR activities improves when social CSR communication is used to communicate the firm’s CSR efforts on social media. This study offers theoretical insights and practical suggestions.

title: Designing Trust-aware Benchmark Measurements: Reliability and Fragility as Purpose-built Scores for Marketing Channels
affiliations: and Università di Milano Cattolica

detail.title: Designing Trust-aware Benchmark Measurements: Reliability and Fragility as Purpose-built Scores for Marketing Channels
detail.abstract: A benchmark must answer two questions that a measure of central tendency cannot: what constitutes a normal result, and whether that result can be trusted to guide a decision. We argue that the second question decomposes into two logically independent properties, temporal stability and compositional concentration, and we present a derivation procedure that turns a stated decision, the fields already collected, and elementary statistics into a purpose-built measurement of each. The procedure yields two bounded and scale-invariant scores: Reliability, a monotone transform of the coefficient of variation of a series of period totals, and Fragility, a size-normalized Herfindahl concentration index over the contributing brands. We instantiate both for three marketing channels with different natural units of aggregation, coupon click-through, direct email, and push notifications, and show that a single measurement design renders heterogeneous benchmarks comparable and interpretable at a glance. We further argue that measurement design is inseparable from data-regime validity: a score computed over an untrustworthy period does not merely carry noise, it estimates an artifact, and we describe a diagnostic that fixes the effective window before any benchmark is published. All data are reported in anonymized or illustrative form. The contribution is methodological: a repeatable way to construct the measure a decision requires, rather than adopting a convenient one.

title: The Usage of Classic Matrix Marketing Instruments for Bank Strategy Formation
affiliations: Kyiv National Economic University (KNEU)

detail.title: The Usage of Classic Matrix Marketing Instruments for Bank Strategy Formation
detail.abstract: The relevance of classic matrix usage for the creation and implementation of bank marketing strategies is examined. The SWOT analysis matrix has been analyzed. Variations of PEST analysis, such as PESTLE, STEPLE, and STEEPLED, have been briefly analyzed. The Ansoff matrix and its capacity to account for new banking markets and new technologies have been analyzed. The disadvantages of the Boston Consulting Group matrix, which make it difficult to apply to the banking market, have been described. The relevance of the improved General Electric-McKinsey matrix has been examined. The difficulties of strategy selection and the impact of subjective factors on the General Electric-McKinsey matrix have been described. The advantages and disadvantages of different approaches to choosing the most effective instrument for bank marketing strategy development have been compared.

title: FMCG 4.0 and Signal-to-Shelf Analytics ML Framework for Integrated Automation in Fast Moving Consumer Goods

detail.title: FMCG 4.0 and Signal-to-Shelf Analytics ML Framework for Integrated Automation in Fast Moving Consumer Goods

declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted as part of a PhD programme at University College London, Department of Computer Science.

detail.abstract: Fast-Moving Consumer Goods (FMCG) markets are characterised by rapid consumption, high turnover, short product lifecycles, and narrow margins. Translating emerging consumer preferences into scalable products is therefore a cross-functional optimisation problem spanning consumer analytics, product discovery, manufacturing, and commercial execution. FMCG 4.0 is a framework that extends Industry 4.0 by integrating consumer signal detection, trending product discovery, manufacturing optimisation, go-to-market strategy, and sales analytics within a single continuously optimising system. The framework extends Industry 4.0 beyond smart manufacturing to the full FMCG innovation and commercialisation lifecycle through a closed-loop Signal-to-Shelf process. Signal-to-Shelf measures the time-normalised efficiency with which consumer and market signals are detected, interpreted, converted into product and commercial decisions, and translated into shelf-ready offerings within the available market opportunity window. Time-to-Market measures execution speed, while the Coupling Benefit Ratio measures the performance gain achieved through integrated rather than sequential decision-making. The paper presents FMCG 4.0 and iCOMP (Intelligent Companywide Machine Learning Optimizer for Manufactured Products), as a computational implementation of FMCG 4.0. iCOMP combines federated data and learning, natural language processing (NLP), dynamic-action-space reinforcement learning (Ref), and multi-objective optimisation. Its four coupled services perform: a) consumer signal identification, b) product discovery, c) manufacturing optimisation, and d) explainable go-to-market modelling. iCOMP establishes a continuously updating control architecture for integrated the FMCG 4.0 framework.

detail.abstract: The Saudi Pro League (SPL) is a site where a rapidly internationalising football project meets a bilingual public. This article reads the SPL as a case of sport-and-society intersection in a postcolonial and pan-Arab context. Drawing on a bilingual close-reading corpus of 441 items (275 X posts and 166 YouTube comments, balanced across Arabic and English) sampled between Ronaldo's Al-Nassr signing in December 2022 and May 2026, the analysis identifies three patterns. The Anglophone label sportswashing travels unevenly across languages, largely absent from the Arabic sample where critique moves through institutional-fairness grievance, religious-moral economy, and ironic rights-idiom appropriation. Pan-Arab regional attachment appears as a distinct scale of football belonging on Arabic YouTube. Player-centred attention is analytically distinguishable from league-system evaluation. The study contributes a bilingual, platform-sensitive account of Global South football legitimacy that English-only analysis misses.

detail.abstract:
Early-stage founders, students, and innovators often rely on weak validation signals—such as verbal encouragement, stated willingness to pay, clicks, signups, or positive feedback on a prototype—to justify advancing an idea to the next stage. This paper does not argue that such signals are useless. Rather, it argues that validation evidence is sufficient only when the strength of the customer-choice signal is appropriate to the size, irreversibility, and strategic consequence of the next investment.

This paper introduces the term signal-investment fit: the principle that the evidentiary threshold for advancing an entrepreneurial idea should rise with the cost, irreversibility, and consequence of the next step. A weak signal may justify a small, cheap, fast, and reversible learning step. That same signal may be dangerously insufficient when the next step requires a large financial commitment, significant founder time, inventory, hiring, reputational exposure, relational capital, or opportunity cost.

Based on that principle, the paper introduces the $50,000 Test, a named own-risk thought experiment and practical validation process. The name is fixed, but the operational amount should be comparable in scale to the actual quantified investment required for the next step, including material financial and nonfinancial commitments. The test asks founders to determine, before testing, what customer-choice evidence would justify making that investment if they personally had to bear the loss. The framework shifts the validation question from “Will customers say they are willing to pay?” to “Will enough target customers choose this product over their Best Current Alternative with enough behavioral or economic commitment to justify the next investment?”

The paper distinguishes between B2C validation, where confidence often comes from behavioral volume across the purchase funnel, and B2B validation, especially in large-deal environments, where confidence often comes from fewer but stronger commitment signals such as paid pilots, purchase orders, non-cancellable commitments, and letters of credit. The contribution is a practitioner-oriented framework for founders, students, educators, and innovation leaders seeking to align validation evidence with investment risk.

title: Does ESG Risk Matter for Corporate Bond Returns?
affiliations: University of Groningen - Faculty of Economics and Business, University of Groningen and University of Groningen, Faculty of Economics and Business, Department of Economics, Econometrics and Finance

detail.title: Does ESG Risk Matter for Corporate Bond Returns?
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether ESG risk is priced in the cross-section of corporate bond returns. Using an international sample of bonds, we find that bonds issued by firms with better ESG profiles earn lower excess returns. A one-standard-deviation increase in the ESG score implies an ESG premium of approximately 2.21% per year. Decomposing the overall rating reveals that the premium is driven by the Environmental and Social dimensions, whereas Governance emerges as a significant pricing factor only among investment-grade bonds. These results are robust to alternative ESG data providers and different lag specifications, with the magnitude of the premium declining for longer horizons.

title: Consumer AI and Exploitation of Information-processing Frictions

detail.title: Consumer AI and Exploitation of Information-processing Frictions
detail.abstract: We study whether LLMs, as increasingly accessible consumer-side AI tools, would eliminate consumer exploitation targeting information-processing frictions or merely relocate it. LLM adoption does not improve products on its own: firms keep exploiting maximally until a rising share of expert consumers tips them into competition over product value. Even then, firms counter with adversarial investment that corrupts capability enhancement by LLMs. This arms race arises in equilibrium, persists as adoption broadens, peaks then fades as LLMs improve, and can neutralize consumer gains when adversarial investment is cheap. Consumer-side AI thus reshapes cognitive exploitation rather than eliminating it.

title: FX Hedging, Currency Choice, and Dollar Dominance
affiliations: University of Luxembourg, Banque de France and IESE Business School

detail.title: FX Hedging, Currency Choice, and Dollar Dominance
detail.abstract: Exporters pricing their goods in a foreign currency are exposed to foreign exchange (FX) risk, but they can hedge it by underwriting FX derivative contracts. This paper provides firm-level evidence on how the cost of FX hedging affects exporters' currency choice. We formalize the channel in a model in which a firm jointly chooses its invoicing currency and its optimal hedging ratio, predicting that cheaper hedging makes foreign currency pricing more attractive. Consistent with our model, we empirically find that hedging firms price their exports more in foreign currency, and especially in US dollars. We then exploit an unexpected increase in the cost of hedging and find that it leads hedging firms to reduce both dollar and local currency pricing, with larger effects for smaller firms. Finally, we show that hedging is associated with stickier export prices. Our findings indicate that cheaper FX derivatives markets nurture dollar dominance while weakening the link between prices and exchange-rate movements.

detail.abstract: Luxury firms burn unsold inventory rather than discount it; the EU forbids this from July 2026. The ban's premise-destruction the harm, prohibition the remedy-can run the other way. I model ex-post destruction as commitment for a Veblen monopolist, credible when internalized brand value exceeds the liquidation margin. The ban forces an ex-ante quantity commitment: output weakly falls and the off-price share conditionally rises. At a full-extraction benchmark, absent external destruction costs, the option weakly dominates the ban; a decomposition prices reversals. Predictions are recorded before the EU's disclosure data exist; France's 2022-24 record leans their way.

title: Market Physics Research Series • Paper V State Dynamics

detail.title: Market Physics Research Series • Paper V State Dynamics
detail.abstract: Electronic markets are commonly analyzed through prices, returns, trades, spreads, depth, and order flow. These variables are indispensable, but they do not by themselves identify the higherorder object that is changing: the market's evolving structural state. This paper introduces Market State Dynamics (MSD), a unified framework in which the electronic market is represented as a time-varying configuration of liquidity commitment, queue topology, passive-liquidity flux, aggressive execution pressure, information arrival, matching-engine response, and recovery capacity. The central proposition is that price formation is not adequately described as a sequence of isolated trades or quote updates. It is an observable consequence of transitions among market states with different levels of stability, susceptibility, and resilience. The framework extends the Market Physics research program by integrating Microstructural Pulse Dislocation (MPD), Event-Driven Microstructure Collapse (EMC), the Matching Engine Response Window (MERW), and Liquidity Commitment Theory (LCT) within a single transition architecture. MPD is treated as a price-path manifestation; EMC as a disruption in absorptive capacity; MERW as a bounded process window in which event ordering becomes economically decisive; and LCT as the measurement layer governing the reliability, persistence, withdrawal, and replenishment of executable interest. The paper distinguishes four broad state familiesstable, transitional, disrupted, and recovery states-and introduces preliminary constructs for state momentum, state fragility, transition intensity, and recovery distance. Market State Dynamics is not offered as a literal mechanical law, a deterministic trading rule, or a claim that the full market state is observable. It is a falsifiable research architecture. Its empirical validity depends on whether state-transition variables improve explanation, hazard estimation, and out-of-sample prediction beyond conventional measures such as returns, volatility, depth imbalance, order-flow imbalance, and trade intensity. The intended contribution is therefore both conceptual and operational: to make the evolving market state a measurable object of inquiry and to establish a disciplined foundation for studying how liquidity, execution, information, and adaptation jointly produce electronic price formation.

title: Financial Interpretation Gaps and Operational Sustainability Risks in Owner-Operated Café and Restaurant Businesses: A Preventive Operational awareness Framework

detail.title: Financial Interpretation Gaps and Operational Sustainability Risks in Owner-Operated Café and Restaurant Businesses: A Preventive Operational awareness Framework
detail.abstract:
Independent cafés and small food‑service businesses frequently operate under persistent financial
pressure within highly constrained pricing environments. Rising labor costs, occupancy burdens,
ingredient inflation, delivery‑platform commissions, and intensified competition have become
structural realities for owner‑operated cafés and restaurants. Yet financial deterioration often
develops gradually beneath outwardly stable operations. Customer traffic may remain strong,
sales volume may appear consistent, and daily activity may seem normal, even as liquidity
weakens, margins compress, and operational flexibility declines.

Prior hospitality and small‑business research identifies weak financial management,
limited financial literacy, and inadequate planning as recurring contributors to business
instability. Building on this literature, the present study argues that the central challenge facing
many owner‑operated cafés is not the absence of financial information but the limited ability to
interpret financially connected operational pressures before they evolve into severe structural
problems. The study proposes a preventive operational awareness framework that emphasizes
pattern recognition, early interpretation of emerging risks, and the integration of financial
literacy with practical managerial judgment.

Using a conceptual synthesis methodology, the paper examines how margin compression,
cash‑flow pressure, delayed financial interpretation, weakening reserve capacity, and diminishing
operational flexibility interact cumulatively to increase long‑term vulnerability. The framework
positions financial literacy as a sustainability capability rather than a compliance function,
suggesting that improved financial‑operational interpretation can enhance decision‑making
resilience and long‑term sustainability in owner‑operated café and restaurant businesses.

title: Optimal Execution with Passive Market Impact

detail.title: Optimal Execution with Passive Market Impact
detail.abstract: We derive a mesoscopic model for optimal execution with limit orders that incorporates microstructural features of passive price impact. Our framework is based on two empirical observables: the approximately exponential decay of limit-order fill probabilities with distance from the midprice, and the short-term linear response of price changes to order flow imbalance. Combining these ingredients, we obtain a reduced-form passive impact rate that decays exponentially with quote distance. The model describes passive execution at a tactical level, where fills arise from a sequence of quote adjustments that balance execution probability, adverse selection, and opportunity cost. We formulate and solve an optimal liquidation problem in which the trader controls the aggressiveness of passive sell quotes. This generates a trade-off between higher fill intensity and larger accumulated impact on the one hand, and lower impact but greater non-execution risk on the other. Empirical calibration using NASDAQ equities and public FX supports the empirical foundations of the model. We also analyse extensions with heterogeneous decay rates, transient impact, and target execution schedules.

detail.abstract: Language models now produce earnings forecasts. Do they behave like the analysts and firms whose text appears in their training data? I ask three frontier models to forecast quarterly EPS for fictional firms. The rational forecast is computable, and its final digits are uniform. The firms do not exist, so memorization cannot drive the results. I test two classic patterns. Human analysts round forecasts to nickels at 2.75 times the expected rate (Herrmann and Thomas 2005). Firms meet or narrowly beat salient thresholds (Burgstahler and Dichev 1997; Degeorge, Patel and Zeckhauser 1999). The models barely round. Their full-sample heaping ratios are 1.05 for GPT-5.4, 1.57 for Grok-4.3, and 1.15 for Claude Sonnet 5. Yet they reproduce meet-or-beat beliefs. Shown a consensus estimate, they place most predicted surprises a penny or two above it. With no consensus, this upward placement disappears. When I move the consensus, predictions follow. The slopes are 0.361 for Grok-4.3, 0.472 for Claude Sonnet 5, and 0.609 for GPT-5.4. These slopes estimate how much weight each model puts on consensus relative to its own signal. The rationales state the belief directly: consensus estimates are conservative, and firms beat them. The results separate a forecaster's own heuristic from its belief about strategic firms. The models largely discard the first and reproduce the second.

title: Freshwater Scarcity and the Physical Limits of State Stability

detail.title: Freshwater Scarcity and the Physical Limits of State Stability

detail.abstract: Twentieth-century fears of overpopulation focused on food scarcity. Those predictions failed as agricultural output scaled with energy, technology, irrigation, and trade. The more persistent constraint on long-term population sustainability and state stability is freshwater availability: a locally bounded, inelastic flux governed by the hydrological cycle. A framework of dimensionless ratios linking population, renewable freshwater supply, usable water, firm supply, and energy is proposed. Specifically, a hydrological sufficiency ratio distinguishes gross freshwater abundance from regional and operational scarcity, identifying regimes in which demand exceeds sustainable supply and is temporarily buffered through groundwater depletion, desalination, reuse, and virtual water trade. Aggregate freshwater supply remains large relative to observed global withdrawals, but many basins, subregions, and operating systems - including those in the Middle East, North Africa, South Asia, and parts of North America and Europe - already operate near or below hydrological sufficiency once geography, infrastructure, energy, and reliability constraints are considered. Freshwater scarcity is therefore a first-order constraint on political order. Where demand persistently exceeds firm usable supply, societies face rising pressure toward rationing, migration, depopulation, or chronic instability. As water and energy systems become increasingly coupled, hydrological sufficiency becomes a key variable for development, demographic forecasting, and security strategy in the twenty-first century.

title: Pound-for-Pound Productivity: Opponent-Adjusted Benchmarking and Era-Specific Technical Efficiency in the UFC

detail.title: Pound-for-Pound Productivity: Opponent-Adjusted Benchmarking and Era-Specific Technical Efficiency in the UFC

declarations.funderStatement: There are no funding interests to disclose.

detail.abstract: This study provides, to our knowledge, the first frontier-based benchmarking of professional mixed martial artists, applying data envelopment analysis (DEA) to 2,674 Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) athletes across 8,612 bouts contested between 1994 and 2026. Two structural features of combat sports are addressed methodologically. First, standard DEA assumes independent decision making units, yet combat KPIs are bilateral: every strike landed by one athlete is absorbed by another athlete in the same sample. We introduce an opponent-pool normalization that rescales each bilateral KPI to a common reference opponent; the correction re-ranks athletes substantially (Spearman ρ = 0.67 versus raw scores) and reduces the share of frontier athletes from 28.6% to 9.2%. Second, because three decades of rule and regulatory change preclude a common technology, we estimate era-specific, sequential, sex-specific, and weight-class frontiers alongside a metafrontier, using metatechnology ratios to adjudicate among partitions. Second-stage inference uses the Simar-Wilson double-bootstrap truncated regression on era-specific scores-for which the separability condition holds by construction-on the full covariate sample: wins, losses, and verified championship status are associated with efficiency, while age at UFC debut is not, a null that survives four independent design changes. An out-of-sample validation exercise shows that efficiency differentials add significant predictive information to a tuned Elo baseline (clustered 95% CI on the AUC gain excludes zero), while the opponent adjustment's case rests on measurement validity rather than forecasting gains. Sex-specific frontiers prove mandatory (women's metatechnology ratio: 0.81), and an apparent age-cohort decline in efficiency is shown to be an artifact of fixed-date age measurement in a pooled multi-era frontier.

title: Regret-Robust Newsvendor Model for a Trade Agent
affiliations: Dalian University of Technology, Department of Decisions, Operations and Technology, CUHK Business School, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Dalian University of Technology, Dongbei University of Finance and Economics and Dalian University of Technology

detail.title: Regret-Robust Newsvendor Model for a Trade Agent
detail.abstract: In a newsvendor-type procurement problem, a trade agent bids for upstream supply under an all-or-nothing allocation mechanism to satisfy known downstream demand. The agent must determine the bid before observing the seller's private ask price and the realized supply yield. Because only limited historical data on ask prices and yields are available, their joint distribution cannot be reliably estimated. We develop a data-driven minimax regret model to determine the bid that performs best against the worst plausible misspecification of the observed data. We derive finite-sample regret bounds and show that, under a uniqueness condition, the regret-optimal bid approaches the true optimum as more data become available. By exploiting the structure of the regret function, we obtain an exact, tractable reformulation and develop a finite-search algorithm to compute the optimal bid. Numerical experiments show that the proposed minimax regret model delivers stable out-of-sample performance and strong average profits, particularly with small sample sizes and under ask-price shifts. This advantage diminishes under adverse yield shifts when the agent bears a larger share of supply risk. A regret-based policy supports more aggressive bidding when lost sales are costly and data are scarce, but recommends tempering that aggressiveness when the agent bears a large share of supply risk or expects yields to worsen.

detail.abstract: This study examines the relationship between exchange rate movements and Nigeria's trade balance over the period 1990-2023, using annual time-series data sourced from the World Bank's World Development Indicators. Adapting the elasticity-approach framework and the empirical model of Anning, Riti, and Yapatake (2015), the study estimates an Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression of trade balance on the real exchange rate, domestic GDP, foreign (US) GDP, and the inflation rate, and complements this with pairwise Granger causality tests. The results show that inflation is the only statistically significant determinant of Nigeria's trade balance in the sample, exerting a significant negative effect, while the real exchange rate, domestic GDP, and foreign GDP are not statistically significant. Granger causality tests indicate that trade balance Grangercauses both domestic and foreign GDP, but no significant causal relationship runs from the real exchange rate to the trade balance in either direction. The Durbin-Watson statistic (0.76) points to positive autocorrelation in the residuals, and the study discusses this as a limitation warranting further investigation using cointegration-based methods such as ARDL or VECM. The findings suggest that exchange rate depreciation alone is unlikely to be a reliable lever for improving Nigeria's trade balance, and that inflation control should feature more prominently in tradebalance-oriented policy.

title: Business Dynamism and Innovation: Evidence from Novel 19th-Century Microdata
affiliations: HEC Paris, Cardiff University - Cardiff Business School and University of Bristol

detail.title: Business Dynamism and Innovation: Evidence from Novel 19th-Century Microdata
detail.abstract: We construct a novel establishment-level dataset combining the nineteenth-century U.S. Census of Manufactures (1850-1880) with patent records from CUSP to examine how innovation shaped firm performance in early industrial America. Patenting establishments were substantially larger than comparable non-patenters across all dimensions (employment, capital, output, and output per worker) with premia further amplified among firms that produced breakthrough inventions. Estimating establishment-level production functions using Levinsohn-Petrin approach, we find that patenting is associated with higher revenue total factor productivity (TFPR) while leaving markups unchanged on average. Breakthrough innovations, however, are associated with gains on both margins, with a size decomposition revealing the strongest amplification among the largest establishments, consistent with superstar dynamics, yet small breakthrough innovators also capture meaningful gains, suggesting the returns to invention were not exclusive to large firms.

title: Quantified Cognitive Readiness: An Assessment for the Enablement of Organizational Readiness in Strategic Management

detail.title: Quantified Cognitive Readiness: An Assessment for the Enablement of Organizational Readiness in Strategic Management
detail.abstract:
The following paper deals with the quantification of strategic management based on its implications on business psychology and organizational behaviour. The result is a framework that enables the appreciation of cognitive readiness in strategic management under the application of quantum mechanical analogies.

The following paper serves as a theoretic ground for the quantification of business psychological factors with a focus on customer behaviour for strategic alliances and market entry. Never has evidence-based management been so crucial as today. Many organizations use mathematical implications in KPI Engineering in order to set up suitable KPIs. The analogical application of this approach as an assessment of client strategy can bring in an analytical ground for strategic adjustment in other fields of management sciences. While evidence-based management becomes subject of controversy in regards to its inflationary application and a too gap-analytic mindset, the customer-oriented analysis in this paper can provide a strategically valuable ground for anticipative risk management for successful customer relations. 4 Formulas are used first of which is the psychological superposition function, secondly the Product Assimilation Entanglement, third the PESTEL Observer Effect and last but not least the Cognitive load Index. The audit combining all equations can also be referred to as the quantified cognitive readiness assessment (QCRA), a framework that translates qualitative corporate and consumer-oriented psychological states into mathematical formulations.

detail.title: Regulating Autonomous and Agentic AI

declarations.funderStatement: Microsoft Inc via its funding of the Queen Mary Cloud Legal Project

detail.abstract: Regulating activities where regulatees use autonomous and agentic AI is challenging. Regulatory assumptions about regulatee knowledge and control no longer hold true; much of that lies elsewhere in the AI supply chain which thus needs to be brought within the scope of regulation. Governance systems for autonomous AI cannot replicate existing governance models, but need a fresh approach. Retrospective supervisory oversight becomes ineffective as a risk management tool, and AI autonomy generates new systemic risks which require new solutions. This paper investigate four regulatory systems: UK regulation of content platforms, data protection, UK financial services, and the EU AI Act's cross-sectoral regime. It analyses the challenges posed by autonomous and agentic AI and proposes potential solutions which regulators might adopt. These will transform regulation from a reactive process to an active one, and assist it in adapting to the challenges of AI autonomy.

title: Documenting Transit Delay between Central Asia and Europe

detail.title: Documenting Transit Delay between Central Asia and Europe
detail.abstract: This article examines the evidentiary consequences of undocumented delay along the Trans-Caspian route between Central Asia and Europe. The route links national railway systems to the ports of the Caspian and Black Seas before entering the CIM environment from SMGS territory. Because operational control changes repeatedly, an interruption created by one participant may generate charges under another contract after the cargo has entered a different jurisdiction. The article treats the commercial act as one expression of a broader problem of documentary control. It argues that a participant able to create, preserve, or disclose a record of a legally material event should not benefit from uncertainty caused by the unexplained absence of that record. The proposed response is evidentiary rather than automatic liability. It relies on a continuous record of each transfer and a rebuttable evidentiary response to missing data, while leaving the governing railway and maritime rules intact. This model allows downstream charges to be traced to their factual origin without collapsing several contracts into a single liability regime.

title: After the Designation: A Counter-TCO Due Diligence Framework for U.S. Contractors with Brazilian Supply-Chain and Capital Exposure

detail.title: After the Designation: A Counter-TCO Due Diligence Framework for U.S. Contractors with Brazilian Supply-Chain and Capital Exposure
detail.abstract: Two federal actions, thirteen months apart, have changed what it means to vet a Brazilian counterparty. In June 2025 the Department of Justice restarted enforcement of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act under guidelines that treat a counterparty's link to a cartel or transnational criminal organization as a primary charging consideration. In May and June 2026 the State Department designated Comando Vermelho and the Primeiro Comando da Capital as Foreign Terrorist Organizations and Specially Designated Global Terrorists. A Brazilian supplier that used to present a bribery question now presents a sanctions and material-support question as well, and the second question is the harder of the two, because the organizations involved operate through licensed distributors, payment institutions, and investment funds that look entirely ordinary on paper. This article is written for the mid-sized U.S. contractor that has an FCPA program and no financialintelligence unit. Drawing on the author's decade building third-party compliance programs on the Brazilian side of these relationships, and on the closest available precedent-Chiquita's 2007 conviction for payments to a designated Colombian organization-it maps where the exposure actually sits, including the coerced payment that no ownership screen will ever surface. Its central claim is uncomfortable: list screening, which is where most programs stop, is the part of the exercise least likely to catch anything.

title: Challenges and Opportunities in Achieving Universal Energy Access: A Pathway to Sustainable Development Goal 7 and Net-Zero Emissions by 2050 Adhvay Jagadeesh
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Challenges and Opportunities in Achieving Universal Energy Access: A Pathway to Sustainable Development Goal 7 and Net-Zero Emissions by 2050 Adhvay Jagadeesh
detail.abstract: Transitioning to renewable energy is essential to realizing Sustainable Development Goal 7 (SDG 7), which calls for universal access to affordable, reliable, and sustainable energy by 2030, and to reaching net-zero emissions by 2050 under the Paris Agreement and the finance commitments negotiated at COP30 in Belém. Despite measurable progress, an estimated 666 million people still lack electricity access and approximately 2.1 billion rely on polluting cooking fuels, with the majority of this deficit concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa (International Renewable Energy Agency [IRENA] et al., 2025). Elevated public debt, high energy prices, and constrained international financial flows continue to slow momentum toward SDG 7 (International Energy Agency [IEA], 2025a). Countries such as Ghana possess substantial solar, wind, and hydropower potential but remain constrained by technological, financial, and regulatory barriers. This paper argues that low-income countries must accelerate the adoption of decentralized renewable energy technologies, including solar mini-grids, hybrid power systems, and off-grid solar, supported by expanded international finance. Beyond synthesizing existing evidence on technological, financial, and policy barriers, this paper contributes an original integrated Technology-Finance-Policy-Community (TFPC) framework for analyzing decentralized energy interventions, a comparative matrix scoring four documented energy-access programs, and a quantitative pace-gap analysis benchmarking current global progress against the trajectories required to meet 2030 targets. As of 2025, global renewable capacity had reached approximately 5,149 gigawatts, supporting an estimated 16.6 million jobs worldwide (IRENA, 2026; IRENA & International Labour Organization [ILO], 2026), even as Africa received only about 2% of global clean energy investment despite housing roughly 20% of the world's population (IEA, 2025b). The pace-gap analysis finds that current trajectories would need to accelerate roughly five-fold for electricity access, seven-fold for clean cooking access, and 1.7-fold for renewable capacity additions to meet their respective 2030 targets. Achieving SDG 7 also depends on engaging youth through skills training and entrepreneurship, alongside transformational policy architecture, targeted financial investment, and strong public– private partnerships throughout this Decade of Action (2020–2030). Coordinated action between energy-intensive and energy-vulnerable nations, using their natural resource endowments and cross-sectoral partnerships, is necessary to accelerate progress toward SDG 7 and global net-zero targets, driving improvements in health, education, and socioeconomic development worldwide.

title: Reinforcement Learning-based Dynamic Right-sizing for Apache Spark Workloads across Multi-cloud Environments A Conceptual Framework and Literature Synthesis

detail.title: Reinforcement Learning-based Dynamic Right-sizing for Apache Spark Workloads across Multi-cloud Environments A Conceptual Framework and Literature Synthesis
detail.abstract: Apache Spark remains the dominant engine for large-scale batch and streaming analytics, yet the provisioning of Spark clusters, the choice of executor count, executor memory, executor cores, and driver resources is still governed largely by static configuration heuristics or narrowly reactive mechanisms such as Spark's built-in Dynamic Resource Allocation. These mechanisms respond to queued and running tasks but do not learn from historical workload patterns, do not reason jointly across memory and compute dimensions, and do not account for the heterogeneous and timevarying pricing structures of multiple cloud providers. This paper synthesizes the literature on reinforcement learning (RL) for cloud resource management, Spark-specific dynamic allocation, cost-aware and spot-instance-aware scheduling, and multi-cloud resource portability, and proposes an integrated conceptual framework for RL-based dynamic right-sizing of Spark workloads across multi-cloud environments. Building on the cost-aware, single-cloud right-sizing approach recently proposed for Azure Databricks (Mohammed, Bohra, & Soni, 2026), the framework extends the right-sizing problem to a multi-cloud Markov Decision Process in which an RL agent observes workload and pricing signals across providers and learns a joint policy for executor scaling and workload placement. The paper formalizes the state, action, and reward spaces of this problem; proposes a layered system architecture; and discusses the governance, safety, and portability considerations that a production deployment would require. No empirical claims of performance improvement are made; the contribution is a structured, literaturegrounded framework intended to guide subsequent empirical validation. Theoretical, practical, and policy implications are discussed, and a research agenda for empirical follow-up work is proposed.

title: Rarely hyperbolic: bias and the `Russell' graph measure of technical efficiency; Theory and Evidence from the UFC

detail.title: Rarely hyperbolic: bias and the `Russell' graph measure of technical efficiency; Theory and Evidence from the UFC

declarations.funderStatement: There are no funding interests to disclose.

detail.abstract: Two graph-space measures of technical efficiency, the single-factor hyperbolic index and the coordinate-wise Russell graph (FGL) index, measure inefficiency of input-output systems through different lenses. We make explicit an ordering implicit in the classical literature: the FGL index never exceeds the hyperbolic index, so the hyperbolic score carries a one-signed downward bias in measured inefficiency, and we give an exact decomposition identity for that bias as a dimension-averaged sum of coordinate deviations. The bias vanishes along sequences approaching full (Pareto-Koopmans) efficiency, but because the hyperbolic index fails the indication property not along sequences approaching hyperbolic efficiency: in our data the largest single bias occurs at a hyperbolic score of exactly one. Dispersion of slack across coordinates, not the level of inefficiency, governs the bias; the conjecture that the gap widens as efficiency falls holds under fixed-direction inefficiency and fails otherwise. Estimating both indexes on D = 1,593 UFC athletes on a pooled CRS frontier, we find a mean bias of 0.159, positive for every fighter; 40 of 130 hyperbolic-efficient fighters carry strictly positive bias (up to 0.369), the empirical face of the indication failure. The ordering, the decomposition, and the indication failure survive under variable returns, and Simar-Wilson bootstrap correction shifts score levels (mean hyperbolic 0.861 → 0.822) without disturbing the wedge.

title: Hidden Global Risk in Domestic Supply Chains: Evidence from Port Congestion
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, , Zhejiang University and Fudan University - School of Management

detail.title: Hidden Global Risk in Domestic Supply Chains: Evidence from Port Congestion
detail.abstract: Using high-frequency shipping data, we construct a novel port-level congestion measure and examine how port congestion propagates through domestic supply chains and affects U.S. manufacturers. The central empirical finding is an asymmetry: a manufacturer's own port-congestion exposure has little effect on its sales, whereas congestion faced by its domestic suppliers leads to economically meaningful sales losses. This pattern is robust to an instrumental-variable strategy that uses unexpected port-level wind shocks to isolate exogenous variation in congestion. We then trace the propagation mechanism. First, distributor suppliers play a critical role in shocks transmission, consistent with their role as non-producing intermediaries with limited production flexibility and thin per-SKU inventory buffers; larger focal firms are more resilient, consistent with buyer market power, priority allocation, and more robust supplier relationships. Second, supplier congestion depletes focal firms' inventories, especially raw materials and work-in-process, and preshock inventory buffers attenuate the resulting sales decline. Third, the effect is stronger when focal firms operate at high capacity utilization, indicating that limited production slack converts upstream delays into lost sales. Finally, propagation is pronounced when inputs are more relationship-specific and when focal firms belong to time-sensitive industries. The findings challenge the view that domestic sourcing insulates firms from global logistics risk and show that local supply relationships can embed substantial exposure to upstream maritime bottlenecks. This suggests that firms should also watch closely their domestic suppliers, especially distributors, and conduct better inventory management for domestic sourcing.

title: Democratic Legitimacy in an Era of Digitised Globalisation: A Novel Model for e-governance and Participatory Democracy

contentType.other: A LLM thesis that has not been published

detail.abstract: Contemporary representative democracies exhibit a persistent gap between declining institutional trust and the rigid, election-cycle-bound mechanisms available to citizens for expressing dissent. Existing participatory e-democracy initiatives have failed to close this gap, constrained by limited citizen awareness, weak cause-effect linkage between input and policy outcome, and insufficient political commitment to binding implementation. This paper introduces Digital Polity (D-Polity), a blockchain-based Digital Public Infrastructure that reifies public trust as a continuous, measurable, and binding metric. Under this model, public offices are tokenised as non-transferable credentials bound to citizens' state-verified digital identities, with each office governed by a smart contract encoding its constitutional conditions of acquisition, tenure, and revocation. Sustained collective dissent exceeding a codified threshold triggers self-execution of the office's revocation clause, without discretionary human intermediary, reverting the office to the appointing body for reassignment under identical rules. Critically, this mechanism directs the collective right to dissent solely toward the Head of State, preserving separation from substantive policy contestation. Grounded in the constitutional principle that sovereign authority is non-transferable, and the liberal state's dependence on unmanufacturable civic preconditions, D-Polity is presented as a structural offering of a coercion-resistant, tamper-resistant, and continuously auditable alternative to episodic electoral accountability. With advancements in digital and information technologies, Digital Polity enables a modular form of direct e-participatory democracy that supplements, rather than replaces, the normative legitimisation of traditional representative models.

title: Reframing the ISO 9001:2026 Revision as a Management Effectiveness System: An Integrated Interpretation of Quality Culture, Opportunities and Risks, Resource Allocation, and Certification Auditing

detail.title: Reframing the ISO 9001:2026 Revision as a Management Effectiveness System: An Integrated Interpretation of Quality Culture, Opportunities and Risks, Resource Allocation, and Certification Auditing

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This conceptual study did not involve human participants, personal data, or animal subjects; therefore, ethics approval was not required.

detail.abstract:
Purpose: This paper develops an integrated management interpretation of the ISO 9001:2026 revision. It examines quality culture, the clearer distinction between opportunities and risks, resource allocation, process operation, and management-system effectiveness as a single decision-and-learning process rather than as isolated compliance requirements.

Design/methodology/approach: The study applies normative and interpretive document analysis to ISO 9000:2026, ISO/FDIS 9001:2026, ISO 10010:2022, ISO 19011:2026, ISO/IEC 17021-1:2015, and official ISO revision materials. It distinguishes propositions directly supported by standards from the author’s original conceptual interpretation and derives implications for organizations, auditors, certification bodies, and accreditation-related transition arrangements.

Findings: Quality culture can be interpreted as a decision infrastructure that shapes which opportunities an organization recognizes, which uncertainties it treats as material risks, and where it allocates limited resources. Opportunity-based thinking begins with a desired beneficial result and the organizational capability required to pursue it. Risk-based thinking considers how uncertainty may affect the conversion of committed resources into intended results. Effectiveness is therefore not demonstrated by the existence of procedures or favourable indicators alone; it is demonstrated by a credible connection between planned activities, implementation, and intended results.

Originality/value: The paper proposes four linked contributions: a value-creation/value-protection interpretation of quality management; a temporal opportunity-risk-resource sequence for managerial decisions; a point-line-surface model for auditing effectiveness across clauses and processes; and a purpose-based approach to evaluating the significance of audit findings without converting certification auditing into consultancy.

Practical implications: Organizations should use transition planning to reconnect quality policy, objectives, culture, opportunities, risks, resources, operations, results, and management review. Certification bodies should calibrate auditors not only on textual differences but also on clause-to-clause audit trails, while preserving impartiality and evidence-based conformity assessment.

Limitations: This is a conceptual and standards-based paper. It does not empirically establish causal effects, prescribe a single quality culture, or propose that the author’s managerial interpretation is itself an additional ISO requirement.

detail.abstract: A constellation of new digital technologies has been triggering the Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR). This study examines the firm-level process of digital technological diversification, primarily driven by two complementary forces: path-dependence and path-breaking. Using a unique dataset combining firm-level and patent information of Chinese companies between 2000 and 2020, we document a remarkable increase in 4IR invention activities over the last decade. Our findings reveal a high degree of path-dependence in the development of 4IR technologies within firms, particularly in the creation of enabling technologies, a category of 4IR technologies enabling data-driven value creation. These insights provide a nuanced understanding of the heterogenous patterns of firm-level capability accumulation in the 4IR era.

title: Broad Reach, Uneven Depth? Reconciling Philippine Generative-AI Diffusion across Three Telemetry Systems

detail.title: Broad Reach, Uneven Depth? Reconciling Philippine Generative-AI Diffusion across Three Telemetry Systems
detail.abstract: Claims about national artificial-intelligence adoption increasingly rely on corporate telemetry, even though the available systems count different phenomena. This paper compares the Philippines across Microsoft AI Diffusion, OpenAI Signals, and the Anthropic Economic Index. Microsoft estimates the share of working-age people reaching any of 19 covered generative-AI products; OpenAI reports a population-normalized rank based on consumer ChatGPT messages; Anthropic reports Claude conversation activity and composition. We align early-2026 observations, hold the Philippines out of crosscountry regressions, and express its prediction error as a leave-one-country-out residual percentile under common development, access, services, education, and service-export covariates. The three systems strongly agree on the international ordering of countries, with pairwise Spearman correlations of 0.83-0.88 in the harmonized sample. They do not agree that the Philippines is an outlier. Microsoft's modeled AI User Share is 20.1 percent, compared with a structurally predicted 15.2 percent in the core model, placing the Philippine residual at the 82nd percentile. OpenAI places it at the 65th residual percentile, while populationnormalized Claude activity is near the middle of the residual distribution. Growth in Microsoft's estimate is also close to the crosscountry median. The evidence therefore does not establish a robust national "adoption premium." It instead shows that Philippine standing changes materially with the telemetry construct, motivating direct household, worker, and firm measurement.

title: Whose Work Counts as Meaningful? A Bibliometric Analysis of Meaningful Work and the Gig Economy, and What it does not Contain (2021-2025)

detail.title: Whose Work Counts as Meaningful? A Bibliometric Analysis of Meaningful Work and the Gig Economy, and What it does not Contain (2021-2025)
detail.abstract: This chapter maps the scholarly field at the intersection of meaningful work and the gig economy between 2021 and 2025, and asks what that field's structure reveals about whose experience of platform labour is available to be theorised. Using Scopus records for 150 peer-reviewed articles and reviews, and VOSviewer for keyword co-occurrence, co-citation and co-authorship analysis, the chapter identifies a field organised into distinct and weakly connected traditions. The psychological literature on meaningfulness and the institutional literature on decent work occupy separate positions in both the conceptual and the intellectual structure of the field: meaningful work does not co-occur with any of the five principal normative and structural terms in the map, a joint pattern that would arise by chance with a probability of approximately 0.0002, and the foundational works of meaningfulness theory record the lowest external connectivity in the co-citation network. The chapter then reads the same data for its absences. No South East European country meets the minimum threshold for inclusion in the collaboration network, and none appears in any title, keyword or abstract in the corpus; the feminist social reproduction canon is almost entirely unrepresented in the field's reference base; and gender-focused scholarship forms the newest and least-cited thematic cluster. These are not gaps in the analysis but findings about the field. For a volume concerned with feminist futures in a region largely absent from the evidence base, they carry a direct implication: the Gold Economy vision cannot be built on imported evidence, because the evidence does not extend to the region it would govern.

title: Distributionally Robust Template-Based Chemotherapy Scheduling with Override Policies under Patient-Mix Mismatch and Duration Uncertainty
affiliations: , University of Minnesota - Twin Cities - Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering and Mayo Clinic - Robert D. and Patricia E. Kern Center for the Science of Health Care Delivery

detail.title: Distributionally Robust Template-Based Chemotherapy Scheduling with Override Policies under Patient-Mix Mismatch and Duration Uncertainty
detail.abstract: Outpatient chemotherapy units commonly employ fixed scheduling templates that partition the operating day into appointment slots with predefined treatment durations. While templates facilitate operational standardization and workforce planning, they face two major sources of uncertainty: mismatches between daily patient mix and template slots, and variability in treatment durations. To address patient-mix mismatches, infusion centers often employ override policies such as combining consecutive slots, splitting longer slots, or assigning shorter treatments to longer slots. However, these decisions are typically based on nominal durations and do not explicitly account for treatment time uncertainty, which can lead to undesirable operational costs, including patient waiting, chair idle time, and overtime. We propose a two-step distributionally robust optimization (DRO) framework for templatebased chemotherapy scheduling under uncertain treatment durations. The first step assigns appointments to chairs, while the second step jointly determines override decisions, appointment sequencing, and time allocation. Both models use moment-based ambiguity sets for uncertain treatment durations and admit tractable 0-1 second-order cone programming (SOCP) reformulation. Using real-world data from a Mayo Clinic infusion center, we show that accounting for uncertainty reduces total operational costs by up to 39% compared with deterministic scheduling.

title: Contamination-Aware Sorting Thresholds for Material Recovery

detail.title: Contamination-Aware Sorting Thresholds for Material Recovery
detail.abstract: Material-recovery facilities must choose how aggressively to accept a scored material stream when contamination changes between calibration and operation. A permissive rule preserves volume but can violate an accepted-stream purity specification; a conservative rule can discard useful material or starve downstream processing. This paper studies that trade-off with a fully reproducible synthetic experiment. We compare a quality-ignoring rule, a nominal expected-value threshold, and a lower-quantile threshold that maximizes nominal value subject to a bootstrap purity constraint. All policies are evaluated with common random numbers under baseline, contamination-surge, class-overlap, optimistic-score-shift, and small-lot conditions. The lower-quantile rule selects a threshold of 0.650, compared with 0.450 for the nominal rule. In the baseline, it raises mean purity from 0.815 to 0.842 and specification compliance from 31.7% to 95.7%, while reducing useful-material recovery from 0.929 to 0.848. Its net value is lower by-28.5 units per 1,000 inputs. Under class overlap, every evaluated rule misses the specification, and a score-inversion stress test identifies both acceptance starvation and reversed score orientation. The results support a governance approach in which purity protection is paired with recovery, accepted-yield, value, and score-validity monitoring. Transfer to a facility requires local score calibration, locked validation thresholds, and route-specific economic coefficients.

title: Efficiency and Cost Alignment in Batched LLM Serving via Resource-Fair Scheduling
affiliations: and HKUST

detail.title: Efficiency and Cost Alignment in Batched LLM Serving via Resource-Fair Scheduling
detail.abstract: This paper studies a resource-allocation inefficiency in batched large language model (LLM) serving: heterogeneous requests that share a decode batch impose max-driven computational costs on one another. Because the wall-clock cost of a batch step is largely governed by the largest active KV-cache footprint, a short request co-batched with a long request can experience latency and GPU-resource consumption disproportionate to its own token workload. We formalize this phenomenon as a resource-fair scheduling problem. We develop a mathematical scheduling model that connects within-batch resource fairness to system throughput. The proposed fairness constraint bounds the disparity in decode progress, equivalently KV-cache footprint, among co-batched requests. Based on this model, we design the Insert-Short-Jobs-with-Limit (ISJL) algorithm, a parameterized hybrid batching policy. We prove that ISJL achieves a global competitive-ratio lower bound of 3/4 and further characterize how the worstcase guarantee varies with the fairness budget. Empirical evaluations show that ISJL improves throughput and end-to-end latency relative to standard scheduling baselines. We further examine the profit implications of resource-fair scheduling under the token-metered pricing convention used by commercial LLM APIs. In this environment, for a fixed accepted workload, revenue is additive in token counts and is independent of the scheduling policy; scheduling affects profit through inference cost. We prove a cost decomposition showing that inference cost consists of an intrinsic workload term, a time/overhead term, and a schedule-induced batching externality term. The fairness constraint bounds the batching externality, while the ISJL throughput guarantee controls the time/overhead component. Numerical experiments show that ISJL occupies a favorable middle ground between FCFS, which has large batching externalities, and LJF, which is cost-aligned but sacrifices batching flexibility. Thus, ISJL provides a bi-criterion scheduling policy: it maintains high throughput while aligning max-driven batch cost with token-metered revenue.

title: The Growing Significance of Cryptocurrency Acceptance Research: A Systematic Review and Bibliometric Analysis
affiliations: Corvinus University of Budapest

detail.title: The Growing Significance of Cryptocurrency Acceptance Research: A Systematic Review and Bibliometric Analysis
detail.abstract: The adoption of cryptocurrencies has accelerated rapidly over the past decade-particularly in recent years-yet consumer acceptance remains one of the least explored and understood dimensions in the field. This study conducts a comprehensive bibliometric analysis and systematic literature review to assess the development of consumer-focused cryptocurrency research up to 2024. Drawing from 152 peer-reviewed articles and conference proceedings indexed in Scopus and Web of Science, the paper identifies dominant research trends, methodological patterns, and theoretical frameworks. Findings indicate a rise in publication activity beginning in 2019, with a marked peak in 2023, signaling the emergence of cryptocurrency acceptance as a standalone research field. Despite this growth, the review uncovers substantial gaps in regional coverage, conceptual diversity, and empirical focus, underlining the need for targeted future research. There is a clear shift from Bitcoin-centric research to broader cryptocurrency applications, including alternative coins, hypothetical systems, and practical use cases like tourism or payment solutions. In addition to mapping thematic trends, the study synthesizes methodological practices related to sampling strategies, data collection techniques, analytical tools, and software use, offering a holistic overview of how this topic is researched. By synthesizing these insights, the study offers strategic implications primarily for researchers by outlining concrete directions for future investigations and suggesting how the field could be shaped moving forward. At the same time, the findings also provide valuable insights for regulators and businesses aiming to better understand the broader adoption of cryptocurrency technologies.

detail.abstract:
Background: Women leaders in health across low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) navigate compounding stressors that threaten their mental health and leadership sustainability. Despite growing global attention to leadership diversity, the mental health experiences of women in health leadership remain under-researched in LMIC contexts, and no named psychological framework set has previously been derived from this population's lived experience.

Methods: This study employed a Human-Centered Design (HCD) co-research methodology with 23 women leaders in health across 14 countries (South Sudan, Uganda, Zambia, Zimbabwe, South Africa, Lesotho, Malawi, Angola, Rwanda, India, Botswana, Mozambique, Kenya, and the United States) representing roles from nursing officers and heads of department to country directors and CEOs. Data were collected through individual in-depth interviews and a focus group discussion, analyzed using thematic analysis, and synthesized into psychological framework development.

Findings: The analysis produced six original psychological frameworks representing the first named, evidence-based psychological framework set derived from the lived experiences of women leaders in health in LMIC contexts. The six frameworks are the Strength Invisibility Gap, the Isolation Paradox, the Internalization Default, the Double Burden Tax, the Representational Weight, and the Performative Support Trap. Each framework was grounded in participant testimony and existing leadership psychology literature, and developed into an evidence-based intervention point. The frameworks interact as an integrated system highlighting six expressions of one structural failure: the failure of professional and institutional environments to design systems around the full reality of what women leaders in health are managing.

Conclusions: Mental health stressors for women leaders in health are systemic, relational, cultural, and structural not individual failings. The six frameworks presented provide the conceptual tools for understanding the mechanisms that produce these stressors and the intervention points at which they can be addressed. Solutions require both organizational policy reform and the creation of trusted peer support ecosystems grounded in women-led co-design.
