detail.abstract: The growth of integrated statistical software environments has led to a pressing requirement of independent numerical validation to verify that new platforms give correct results. AnalyVa is an Electron-based desktop application; offline, locally installed, that integrates structural equation modelling, general statistical analysis, and qualitative text analysis into one program. The current paper presents a nine-study validation programme for its general statistical analysis module. Studies 1-8 compare AnalyVa to R 4.4.x across descriptive statistics, t-tests, one-way ANOVA, correlation, multiple regression, exploratory factor analysis, reliability analysis, and chi-square tests using three canonical datasets (iris, mtcars, and a simulated survey; combined N = 782), showing numerical consistency (mean absolute difference ≤ .005) with remaining differences attributable to documented algorithmic conventions. Study 9 benchmarks descriptive statistics, ANOVA, and regression against the certified values of the 31 NIST Statistical Reference Datasets using the log relative error (LRE). The initial run exposed three numerical defects-catastrophic cancellation in ANOVA sums of squares, an additive guard corrupting F ratios, and normal-equations regression failing on ill-conditioned data-which were corrected by compensated summation, grand-mean centring, and Householder QR least squares. The corrected engine attains certified accuracy at or above reference-implementation levels on all 31 datasets, including the numerically hostile Longley, Filip, and Wampler problems. The programme illustrates that certified benchmarking can serve not only to validate statistical software but to drive measurable improvement of it.

detail.abstract:
The integration of AI has been a gamechanger for enterprises in the fight against various forms of fraud. Retailers, banks, insurance companies, government and public institutions, and educational entities, among others, have adopted AI models both to help evaluate suspicious users or transactions in realtime and to distinguish between legitimate and fraudulent events. However, like many emerging technologies, algorithmic fraud detection is not without its growing pains. Some can be relatively minor annoyances, such as having to respond to an alert before a large purchase is approved. However, others may be more serious, such as potentially disparate outcomes for different groups of users. As with many emerging technologies, legislative and regulatory efforts aimed at safeguarding consumers have tried to keep up with technological progress but remain in their early stages. This article explores real-world applications of AI based
fraud detection mechanisms and discusses how these technologies have evolved to help safeguard institutions and businesses from the ever-evolving threat of fraudulent activities. Next, it identifies issues around “false positive” identification, or the possibility that legitimate users and transactions are incorrectly identified as fraudulent, potentially leading to limitations or delays in accessing services, products, or assets. It concludes by outlining the legislative efforts in this space as well as the need for further collaboration between policymakers and system developers.

title: Accounting for Cliff Risk: A Dynamic Framework for Horizontal Merger Analysis
affiliations: , ,  and

detail.title: Accounting for Cliff Risk: A Dynamic Framework for Horizontal Merger Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper develops a novel framework to incorporate dynamic incentives into the antitrust analysis of horizontal mergers, specifically for industries facing the risk of permanent demand disruption. We motivate our analysis through the proposed 2020 Arch/Peabody thermal coal joint venture, where the threat of coal-fired power plant retirement-driven by competition from natural gas-created a powerful incentive for coal producers to maintain low prices to preserve future demand. We derive a dynamic Lerner condition for oligopoly that endogenizes this risk of demand transition, demonstrating that post-merger upward pricing pressure is significantly attenuated when forward-looking firms internalize the link between current pricing and long-term demand. Finally, we propose a tractable approach to calibrate this risk and simulate post-merger price effects using limited data typically available to regulators. Our results demonstrate that traditional static models likely overestimate competitive harm in industries facing stochastic, irreversible demand transitions: what we refer to as "cliff risk." 1.

title: Asymmetric Effects of Economic Diversification on GDP Growth Volatility in GCC Countries: Evidence from a Composite Diversification Index and a Panel NARDL Model
affiliations: Beirut Arab University, Economics Department, Lebanon, Beirut Arab University and Beirut Arab University

detail.title: Asymmetric Effects of Economic Diversification on GDP Growth Volatility in GCC Countries: Evidence from a Composite Diversification Index and a Panel NARDL Model
detail.abstract: This paper examines the asymmetric association between economic diversification and gross domestic product (GDP) growth volatility in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries during the period 2000-2022. GDP growth volatility is measured using the rolling five-year standard deviation of real GDP growth. Economic diversification is measured using a Composite Economic Diversification Index (CEDIX), which is constructed through principal component analysis (PCA) and comprises export, fiscal revenue, and sectoral diversification. The index is rescaled to the unit interval and is decomposed into cumulative positive and negative partial sums in order to distinguish between diversification gains and diversification deteriorations. The empirical methodology includes cross-sectional dependence, panel unit-root and cointegration tests, and then the estimation of a pooled mean group nonlinear autoregressive distributed lag (PMG-NARDL) model. The results indicate a long-run relationship between growth volatility and its determinants, with significant long-run asymmetry between diversification gains and diversification deteriorations. Diversification gains are linked to lower volatility of GDP growth, whereas diversification deteriorations are linked to higher volatility. This suggests that deteriorations in diversification may be more strongly associated with macroeconomic instability than diversification gains are associated with stabilization. Short-run diversification effects are statistically insignificant, and the Wald test does not support short-run asymmetry. These results are consistent with the notion that diversification is more strongly associated with long-run resilience than with short-term stabilization.

title: The Unexpected Case for Public School Opt-Outs
affiliations: University of Southern California Gould School of Law

detail.title: The Unexpected Case for Public School Opt-Outs
detail.abstract:
In the Supreme Court's 2025 decision, Mahmoud v. Taylor, religious parents won a landmark victory: the right to opt their elementary school children out of reading books featuring gay and trans characters. Reactions were divided. Conservatives praised the case as a victory for parental rights and religious freedom, while progressives condemned it as an attack on LGBTQ equality. 

This debate, however, has obscured another perspective. Contrary to conventional assumptions, opt-outs may strengthen public education. They might reduce inequality between wealthy and poor dissenting parents, encourage curricular compromise, preserve students' exposure to publicly shaped curricula, and combat affective polarization. These effects could make public education more legitimate and durable. 

The equality value of public school opt-outs is generally overlooked. Wealthy parents can shelter their children from unwanted lessons by relocating or enrolling them in private schools, and they can use the threat of flight to pressure schools into changing policies. Opt-outs offer parents who lack the means to fully exit the public school system a similar power, partially equalizing parental influence over public education. That same equality goal counsels extending opt-outs to secular parents: a system that accommodates only religious dissenters leaves non-religious low-income parents without recourse. 

Beyond the equality benefit, opt-outs might strengthen public education. Critics contend that opt-outs undermine public education by prompting students to leave classes or schools to avoid instruction on controversial material. These worries are understandable, but evidence from states with opt-outs suggests that they need not have these effects. Opt-outs create incentives for schools to adopt moderate curricula that most parents can accept. Once curricula become sufficiently moderate, many parents may choose not to exercise their opt-out rights, leaving students enrolled and exposed to curricula reflecting public values.

 If we extend opt-outs to secular parents, they may also reduce affective polarization and depoliticize education. Properly understood, opt-outs may be an unexpected tool for preserving public education in a polarized democracy.

title: Recursive Self Learning
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, George Mason University and

detail.title: Recursive Self Learning
detail.abstract: A system that trains on its own output is performing repeated relative entropy projection. We show that the round operator is the exponential tilt  which is simultaneously the Gibbs conditional of Sanov's theorem, the reweighting step of AdaBoost, and the closed form optimum of Kullback-Leibler regularised policy improvement. This identification yields an exact gain identity in which the boosting edge is a variance, so that weakness is a property of the current posterior rather than of the base learner. Three consequences follow. First, unverified recursion collapses for structural reasons: in any regular exponential family the sufficient statistic is a martingale, so its conditional variance must vanish, and the recursion converges almost surely to a degenerate law with total expended dispersion at most nD 2. The Gaussian case gives the rate, almost sure geometric decay at κ n =-2/n + O(n-2) per round, twice the annealed rate, so expected dispersion is sustained only by rare non-collapsing trajectories. Second, the total gain of a verified Gaussian recursion is a Vervaat perpetuity with mean exactly nσ 2 0 /β, and after normalisation it converges to an inverse gamma law, βG/(nσ 2 0) ⇒ IG(2, 1), by Dufresne's identity. The mean therefore exceeds the median by 68 percent, the tenth and ninetieth percentiles differ sevenfold, and the variance is infinite, so averages of realised self improvement across pipelines estimate nothing stable. Third, a data processing inequality caps information gain by the capacity of the verifier channel, and when all feedback derives from one fixed external object the bound is free of the horizon, so self improvement is exactly as unbounded as its external referee and a fixed referee is depletable. We situate the argument in the evidence framework of MacKay and the Bayesian reading of deep learners of Polson and Sokolov, arguing that complexity control is automatic once the marginal likelihood is the criterion, and that double descent is prior collapse rather than paradox. We then critique the position of Sutton, whose bitter lesson we read not as an argument against priors but as an argument about where priors should live, and whose era of experience we bound quantitatively. The paper closes with the full Bayesian viewpoint: scale is the marginalisation operator, architecture is the prior, and the verifier is the likelihood.

title: Urban Climate Resilience and Sustainable Development: A Comparative Analysis of Global Smart Cities
affiliations: and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Urban Climate Resilience and Sustainable Development: A Comparative Analysis of Global Smart Cities
detail.abstract: Rapid urbanization and intensifying climate disruptions pose profound challenges to sustainable development, compelling cities worldwide to integrate resilience-building strategies into their governance and infrastructural frameworks. This study presents a comparative analysis of urban climate resilience and sustainable development across a selected cohort of global smart cities, examining how technological innovation, institutional capacity, and ecological stewardship converge to shape adaptive outcomes. Drawing on insights from geographic information systems, ecological risk assessment, and socio-technical transitions, the research evaluates the extent to which smart city initiatives advance—or inadvertently undermine—long-term sustainability and resilience to climate shocks. The analysis focuses on cities recognized for leadership in smart urbanism, including Singapore, Copenhagen, Amsterdam, and Barcelona, among others. Each city’s approach is assessed through a multidimensional lens that encompasses climate mitigation (emissions reduction, renewable energy adoption), adaptation (flood defense, heat island mitigation, green infrastructure), and socio-economic equity (affordable housing, inclusive digital access, food system resilience). A mixed-methods design combines quantitative indicators from global urban databases with qualitative case study material derived from policy documents and expert interviews. Geographic information systems are employed to map spatial patterns of climate vulnerability and resilience infrastructure, revealing significant disparities between affluent and marginalized districts within the same urban agglomeration. Results indicate that smart city technologies—such as real-time environmental monitoring networks, intelligent traffic systems, and automated waste management—can enhance operational efficiency and reduce resource consumption. For instance, Copenhagen’s extensive district heating system and cloud-based flood warning infrastructure demonstrate measurable gains in energy efficiency and disaster preparedness. However, the study also uncovers critical tensions: the deployment of sensor networks and algorithmic governance often privileges datarich, high-capacity zones, exacerbating digital divides and leaving informal settlements and peri-urban communities exposed to climate risks. Moreover, a heavy reliance on technological fixes can divert attention from structural reforms in land use planning, social protection, and ecological restoration that are essential for genuine resilience. A key finding concerns the relationship between automation, labor displacement, and sustainable urban economies. Adopting automation and artificial intelligence in sectors such as logistics, construction, and retail can boost productivity and facilitate circular economy practices—for example, through robotic sorting of recyclables or drone-based supply chain optimization. Yet these same technologies threaten to displace low-skilled workers without adequate social safety nets, potentially increasing inequality and social fragility. Cities that embed reskilling programs, universal basic services, and participatory governance mechanisms into their smart city strategies exhibit stronger resilience outcomes, as social cohesion and trust buffer communities against shocks. The research also explores the interplay between climate resilience and food system stability. Urban food supply chains in the studied cities revealed pronounced vulnerabilities during recent extreme weather events and pandemics. Smart cities that invest in local food networks, peri-urban agriculture, and blockchain-enabled traceability systems demonstrate superior capacity to maintain nutritional security during disruptions. This aligns with evidence that diversified, short-supply-chain food systems enhance resilience to global commodity price volatility and transportation failures. Conversely, over-reliance on just-in-time logistics and centralized distribution hubs magnifies fragility.

title: The Hyperbolic Secant Family, Salem's Criterion, and the Reciprocal Zeta and Ξ Functions in the Critical Strip

detail.title: The Hyperbolic Secant Family, Salem's Criterion, and the Reciprocal Zeta and Ξ Functions in the Critical Strip
detail.abstract: Lai and Vere-Jones (1979) list, as the rst of two open problems for the hyperbolic secant distribution, the completeness of the scale family {sech θx, θ ≥ 0}. This is a statistical restatement of a WienerTauberian non-vanishing condition, and Salem's 1953 criterion for the Riemann Hypothesis is the same condition for an exponentially tilted secant kernel, the bridge being (e x + 1)-1 = 1 2 e-x/2 sech(x/2). Three results are new. First we determine the completeness set exactly. Writing S for the set of weights σ > 0 at which the tilted family is complete, we prove (1, ∞) ⊂ S, and unconditionally 1 / ∈ S and 1 2 / ∈ S, with explicit obstructions in both cases, so that RH is precisely the statement S = (0, ∞) \ { 1 2 , 1}. Second, interpolating the tilt produces symbols 2Γ(s)Λ(s, θ) with Λ(s, θ) a dierence of Hurwitz zeta functions running from β at θ = 0 to 2-s η at θ = 1; we exhibit simple zeros of Λ(•, 1 2) and Λ(•, 2) o the critical line and to the right of σ = 1, located by root-nding and conrmed by the argument principle, so non-vanishing cannot be transported along the path. Third, a single Dirichlet inversion lemma subsumes the Möbius identities recovering e-x from dilated secants, with generating series 1/ζ, 1/β, 1/η, whose convergence in the critical strip is Littlewood's criterion. We close with the reciprocal Ξ function: s → ξ(1 2 + √ s) is entire of order 1 2 , RH is equivalent to its reciprocal being a generalized gamma convolution transform, and sech √ 2s realises every step of that equivalence unconditionally.

detail.abstract: The study sought to assess the relationship between digital financial inclusion, economic growth, inclusive business participation, income inequality and social protection expenditure on poverty reduction in Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, Ethiopia and Rwanda between 1990 and 2025. The study used the Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) estimator and was based on the Inclusive Growth Theory and the Growth-Inequality-Poverty (GIP) framework. title: Quadrature-order Requirements for G2++ Swaption Pricing: A Reproducible Validation Study
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Quadrature-order Requirements for G2++ Swaption Pricing: A Reproducible Validation Study
detail.abstract: Tensor Gauss-Hermite quadrature is attractive for low-dimensional Gaussian short-rate models, but the positive-part swaption payoff introduces a kink that can make a seemingly plausible fixed order materially inaccurate. This paper measures the quadrature order required for European payer swaptions under G2++. Orders 8, 16, and 32 are tested on a predeclared 135-cell grid covering five parameter regimes, three expiries, three tenors, and three moneyness levels, with QuantLib and an independently time-stepped Monte Carlo engine as references. For the 123 cells worth at least one basis point of notional, increasing the order from 8 to 32 reduces the median absolute relative difference against QuantLib from 0.184% to 0.005% and the 95th percentile from 2.486% to 0.131%, with a maximum material-cell relative difference of 1.228%; the full-grid maximum absolute gap at order 32 is 0.320 basis points of notional. On the 2Y-by-5Y ATM anchor, the price moves from 0.013527738 at order 8 to 0.013432825 at order 32, versus 0.013430989 in QuantLib. Secondary experiments propagate the converged price into finite-difference risk, bound Monte Carlo discount-integration error, report multi-start calibration outcomes, and compare Longstaff-Schwartz values with independent QuantLib tree and finite-difference engines. The accompanying C++20 artifact regenerates the tests, CSV evidence, tables, and figures. The contribution is a reproducible quadrature-convergence and error-budget study, not a new short-rate model.

title: Assessing State-Level Energy Transition Readiness in India: A Systems Approach to Reducing Regional Disparities in Renewable Energy Deployment
affiliations: Tyche Investments - Climate Consulting Group and University of Oxford - Smith School of Enterprise and the Environment

detail.title: Assessing State-Level Energy Transition Readiness in India: A Systems Approach to Reducing Regional Disparities in Renewable Energy Deployment
detail.abstract: India's transition toward a low-carbon energy system is constrained by significant disparities in renewable energy deployment across states despite a common national policy framework. Existing studies primarily evaluate energy transition using static indicators, offering limited understanding of the dynamic interactions among institutional, financial, infrastructural, technological, governance, and stakeholder factors that influence state-level readiness. This study addresses this gap by developing a State-Level Energy Transition Readiness Framework (SETRF) using a systems-based approach. The research employs secondary data synthesized from peer-reviewed literature and integrates System Thinking (ST), System Dynamics Modelling (SDM), and Agent-Based Modelling (ABM) to examine the structural, dynamic, and behavioural determinants of energy transition readiness. System Thinking identifies the causal relationships and leverage points among key readiness dimensions, SDM explains how reinforcing and balancing feedback loops influence transition dynamics over time, and ABM captures the adaptive behaviour of governments, regulators, investors, developers, distribution companies, and consumers. The integrated findings demonstrate that institutional readiness is the principal leverage point, influencing financial mobilization, infrastructure development, technological adoption, governance effectiveness, and stakeholder coordination. The study further shows that regional disparities emerge from cumulative interactions among these dimensions rather than from resource availability alone. Based on these findings, a State-Level Energy Transition Readiness Framework (SETRF) is proposed to guide the assessment and improvement of renewable energy transition readiness across Indian states. The framework provides a comprehensive systems-based approach for identifying policy priorities, strengthening multi-level governance, mobilizing green finance, modernizing grid infrastructure, and enhancing stakeholder collaboration. The study contributes to the literature by integrating ST, SDM, and ABM within a unified analytical framework and offers a practical decision-support tool for reducing regional disparities and accelerating India's renewable energy transition.

detail.abstract: Collective bargaining law has a neglected but morally essential role to play in employment. Each person possesses fundamental and equal moral authority over what to do with their bodies, how to think, and what kind of projects and life to pursue, and that authority is directly implicated by employment. Collective bargaining law has the potential to safeguard that authority by displacing the brute power dynamics of common law bargaining with a form of common reason that respects the basic rights and interests of all involved parties. But for collective bargaining law to realize this potential, it cannot be agnostic about the outcome of collective bargaining and must apply broadly to all workplace matters, including traditional managerial prerogatives. Good faith bargaining should thus evince a willingness to share authority not just over determining the terms of work but over the workplace itself.

detail.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) are transforming not only production technologies but also the financial architecture supporting technological innovation. This paper argues that the growing reliance on private credit and structured finance has created a new channel through which technological shocks may propagate across the financial system. Unlike previous technology booms financed predominantly through equity markets, the current AI ecosystem increasingly relies on debt secured by technological assets whose value is highly sensitive to successive waves of innovation. More generally, economies characterized by rapid capital-embodied technological change continuously reshape the collateral base of the financial system, making Schumpeterian creative destruction an increasingly important source of macro-financial vulnerability. Using the financing of frontier AI infrastructure as an illustrative case, the paper shows how asset-based lending, shadow banking and structured credit can amplify technological shocks through declining collateral values, fire-sale dynamics and institutional interconnectedness. The analysis argues that preserving financial stability increasingly requires preserving the information-insensitive character of debt. This objective calls for a macroprudential framework combining enhanced supervisory capabilities, technology-aware risk assessment and coordinated industrial policy. Beyond the case of AI, the paper highlights the need to integrate innovation economics, financial intermediation and macroprudential policy in the study of economies undergoing rapid capital-embodied technological change.

detail.abstract: This comprehensive academic paper examines the phenomenon of "voluntary return" among Sudanese internally displaced persons (IDPs) and refugees against the backdrop of a devastating civil war that has entered its fourth year. Drawing on empirical data from the International Organization for Migration (IOM), the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the World Bank, the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), and other international agencies, this study argues that the narrative of voluntary return masks a complex reality of coerced displacement decisions driven by unbearable conditions in host countries and areas of asylum rather than genuine improvements in security or living conditions in areas of origin. The paper develops an integrated theoretical framework combining forced migration decision-making theory (including the Theory of Reasoned Action and the Aspiration-Capability Framework), the political economy of post-conflict reconstruction (with specific attention to Sudan's militarized political economy and colonial legacies), and the Three-Gap Model of foreign aid effectiveness (savings gap, foreign exchange gap, and fiscal gap) to analyze the sustainability of current return patterns. Through extensive scenario analysis using the UNDP's three-scenario framework (Protracted Conflict, Current Path, and Ambitious Recovery) and comparative historical assessment with the Marshall Plan (1948-1951), the paper evaluates the feasibility of a large-scale international reconstruction program for Sudan. The analysis reveals that without a comprehensive "Sudanese Marshall Plan" addressing all three gaps simultaneously-and without fundamental political resolution addressing the root causes of Sudan's recurrent conflicts-current return movements represent not sustainable solutions but a prelude to repeated displacement and deepening humanitarian crisis. The paper concludes with detailed policy recommendations for a coordinated international reconstruction framework, including specific financing mechanisms, institutional reforms, and sectoral investment priorities.

title:
When the Machine is Watching: 
Making Sense of the AI Observer Effect at Work
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title:
When the Machine is Watching: 
Making Sense of the AI Observer Effect at Work
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming workplace management by enabling continuous monitoring of employee activities, performance, and decision-making. While these technologies promise improvements in productivity and organizational efficiency, they also alter employee behavior simply through the awareness of being monitored. This paper introduces the concept of the AI Observer Effect, defined as the behavioral, performance, and psychological changes that occur when employees know that AI systems are observing and evaluating their work. Drawing on interdisciplinary literature from organizational psychology, surveillance studies, algorithmic management, and AI ethics, the paper synthesizes contemporary evidence on the opportunities and risks associated with AI-enabled workplace monitoring. The review indicates that AI monitoring can improve task performance and support productivity when implemented transparently, developmentally and within high-trust organizational environments. However, opaque or excessively intrusive monitoring practices are associated with reduced trust, diminished perceptions of fairness, increased psychological strain, and concerns over employee autonomy and privacy, particularly among knowledge workers with high levels of job discretion. Based on these findings, the paper develops a three-dimensional conceptual framework encompassing productivity, employee well-being, and ethical governance to explain how awareness of AI monitoring shapes workplace outcomes. The framework provides practical guidance for organizations seeking to balance the operational benefits of AI-driven performance management with the need to preserve trust, fairness, and employee dignity. The paper concludes by identifying limitations in the current evidence and outlining future research directions to strengthen understanding of the long-term organizational and human implications of AI-enabled workplace surveillance.

title: Consistent Pricing of Bivariate Interest Rate Exotics Via Constrained Schrödinger Optimal Transport
affiliations: Imperial College London - Department of Mathematics

detail.title: Consistent Pricing of Bivariate Interest Rate Exotics Via Constrained Schrödinger Optimal Transport
detail.abstract: We develop a modeling framework for pricing bivariate interest rate exotic derivatives that maintains consistency across three interconnected markets: CMS spread options and the two underlying CMS option markets that define the spread. Our approach also enables the computation of no-arbitrage bounds for exotic derivatives given observable market prices in the spread option and underlying CMS option markets. The method relies on solving the dual Lagrangian of a constrained version of the Schrödinger optimal transport problem and we demonstrate the practical applicability of our framework through concrete numerical examples that illustrate both the pricing methodology and the computation of no-arbitrage bounds.  The approach offers a robust tool for pricing complex interest rate derivatives while ensuring consistency with liquid market instruments.

title: Capped Base-Stock Policies: A 2.33-Approximation
affiliations: Cornell University - School of Operations Research and Information Engineering

detail.title: Capped Base-Stock Policies: A 2.33-Approximation
detail.abstract: We study the classical periodic-review lost-sales inventory model with lead times. Since its introduction in Xin (2021), the class of capped base-stock policies has emerged as a state-of-the-art baseline for evaluating both traditional inventory policies and more recent AI-driven approaches. In particular, capped base-stock policies have served as a strong baseline in studies of deep reinforcement learning and, more recently, LLM-based inventory control. Despite extensive numerical evidence suggesting that these policies perform near optimally, their theoretical guarantees remain an open question. In this paper, we prove that the best capped base-stock policy achieves an approximation ratio of 7/3 ≈ 2.33. Our analysis introduces two novel ideas. First, in contrast to the existing literature that predominantly derives lower bounds from single-variable optimization problems, we formulate a two-variable optimization problem that provides a lower bound on the optimal cost. This richer formulation allows a direct policy comparison because each capped base-stock policy is characterized by exactly two parameters. Second, unlike the common approach of bounding the best capped base-stock policy through single-parameter base-stock or constant-order policies, we use each feasible solution pair of the lower-bound problem to construct two policies in the capped base-stock class. We then use a coupling argument to show that the better of the two satisfies the desired approximation guarantee. Although the ratio 2.33 is numerically larger than the long-standing 2-approximation guarantee for the dual-balancing policy established by Levi et al. (2008), the two guarantees concern different policy classes and therefore do not directly reflect their practical performance. Extensive numerical evidence indicates that capped base-stock policies generally outperform the dual-balancing policy, sometimes by a significant margin. Our result therefore closes an important part of the gap between empirical performance and theoretical understanding. It also suggests that the main obstacle to breaking the 2-approximation barrier may lie in current analytical techniques rather than in the capped base-stock policy class itself. The analytical framework developed in this paper provides a foundation for further refinements that may ultimately yield an approximation ratio strictly below 2.

title: Ecolabel Persuasion Effect Across Cultures: A Comprehensive Meta-Analysis

detail.title: Ecolabel Persuasion Effect Across Cultures: A Comprehensive Meta-Analysis
detail.abstract: Purpose: Companies around the world have included ecolabels as a marketing strategy to convince consumers to choose products with lower environmental impact. However, the literature lacks a consensus on the effectiveness of ecolabels in persuading consumers to choose green products. The present meta-analysis addresses this gap by, first, evaluating the net persuasion effect of using ecolabels and, second, investigating the role of cultural orientations, operationalized at the country level, in this effect. Methodology: This cross-cultural meta-analysis analyzed data from 26,116 consumers across 18 countries, encompassing 75 papers published between 1995 and 2023. Univariate and meta-regression analyses were utilized. Findings: The results demonstrate that the presence (vs. absence) of ecolabels has a medium positive persuasion effect. Findings show cultural orientations moderate the persuasion effect of ecolabels in that the effect is stronger in countries with high power distance, individualism, masculinity (motivation towards achievement and success), and uncertainty avoidance orientation, which create contingent conditions to ecolabels' persuasion. In addition, results show other methodological factors that affect ecolabel persuasion. Contributions and implications of the findings are discussed. Originality: This meta-analysis is distinctive for its global scope, including diverse countries and cultures. It addresses a crucial gap in ecolabel persuasion research, providing insights that reconcile discrepancies in existing studies. It offers practical implications for businesses and policymakers while laying the groundwork for future cross-cultural research in this field.

title: Regulating Yield in Digital Money: Stablecoins, Tokenized Treasury Funds, and the Economics of Competing Regulatory Frameworks
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: Regulating Yield in Digital Money: Stablecoins, Tokenized Treasury Funds, and the Economics of Competing Regulatory Frameworks
detail.abstract: The European Union's Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) and the United States' GENIUS Act of 2025 both prohibit stablecoins from offering interest. However, this restriction has failed to curb the demand for yield on digital dollars. Instead, capital has migrated to functional alternatives, including decentralized finance lending protocols, offshore stablecoin issuers, and tokenized Treasury funds. This paper analyzes the economic impact of restricting yield in digital currency markets. It focuses specifically on tokenized Treasury funds, which are SEC-registered money market funds that now manage over $15 billion in assets. Because these funds offer blockchain-based yields, they compete directly with non-interest-bearing stablecoins for the same investors. This regulatory inconsistency creates a significant opportunity for regulatory arbitrage, raising significant questions about the coherence of current digital asset frameworks. Furthermore, data from the Council of Economic Advisers indicates that the macroeconomic benefits of banning stablecoin yield are modest compared to the associated welfare costs. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these findings for future financial stability and policy design.

title: The University Is Not a Parliament
affiliations: Columbia Law School

detail.title: The University Is Not a Parliament
detail.abstract: Daniel Hemel and David Pozen's In Search of University Democracy asks why no American university lets faculty, students, staff, or alumni elect a majority of its governing board, and argues that shared governance should give way to stakeholder governance. Drawing on my experience as Special Advisor to the Acting President of Columbia University during the 2025 to 2026 academic year, I contend that the university's real governance problem is not a shortage of constituencies but the allocation of authority among a board, a president, and academic professionals so as to control both agency costs and the principal costs that arise when well intentioned decision-makers make honest mistakes, lack relevant information, or cannot coordinate. Drawing on Henry Hansmann's account of the costs of heterogeneous ownership and Albert Hirschman's theory of exit and voice, the essay argues that stakeholder governance would import precisely the heterogeneity costs that explain why so few enterprises are jointly controlled by different patron classes, while doing little for constituencies, particularly faculty and students, who can already discipline the institution through exit. It further shows how electorally mandated trustees risk turning the presidency into an exercise in permanent coalition management, eroding the accountability that presidential leadership exists to secure. In place of stakeholder democracy, the essay proposes mission-centered fiduciary governance through layered delegation: an independent board selects and monitors the president, faculty exercise genuine primacy over academic judgments, and relevant expertise informs oversight without collapsing the line between oversight and management. On this account, the university is not a parliament, and its future depends on preserving, rather than dissolving, that division of labor.

title: AI Development Cost Attribution and Automated Structural Remediation in Software Engineering Workflows
affiliations: and

detail.title: AI Development Cost Attribution and Automated Structural Remediation in Software Engineering Workflows
detail.abstract:
Background: The widespread adoption of AI-assisted code generation has created a new category of operational expenditure that most software organisations cannot explain or control. Token-level billing data from AI provider APIs is available, but no established mechanism connects those costs to the engineering conditionsrequirement instability, architectural debt, or prompting quality-that drive them. 

Objective: This paper proposes a systems-oriented architecture for (a) attributing AI-assisted development expenditure to concrete software engineering activities recorded in version control and issue-tracking systems, and (b) automatically identifying and remediating the recurring structural patterns that generate disproportionate cost.

 Method: The architecture combines four components: IDE-level session instrumentation with commit-embedded trace propagation; semantic-similaritybased alignment of session traces to issue artefacts; Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) divergence analysis and prompt-embedding distance to classify friction sources; and FP-Growth frequent-pattern mining to rank high-cost structural patterns by cumulative financial impact. An event-driven remediation loop generates humanreviewed pull-request fixes when projected continuation cost exceeds estimated remediation cost. 

Results: The architecture is presented as a validated conceptual and technical design. Feasibility arguments are grounded in the known properties of constituent algorithms and tooling. Empirical evaluation of attribution accuracy, friction classification precision, and remediation effectiveness is identified as necessary future work. 

Conclusions: Treating AI expenditure as an observable engineering signal-rather than an undifferentiated overhead-enables organisations to causally explain cost variation and prioritise refactoring investment by its measurable downstream effect. The proposed architecture provides a technically coherent foundation for industrial case-study evaluation.

title: Closing the First Mile: From Passive Visibility to Active Orchestration and Governance
affiliations: Jagiellonian University

detail.title: Closing the First Mile: From Passive Visibility to Active Orchestration and Governance
detail.abstract:
Supply chains spent the past decade learning to see. Visibility platforms now track containers across oceans and milestones across networks. In 2025, 95 percent of companies reported visibility into at least their tier-one supplier risks. Yet response has not kept pace with observation. Disruption response still takes an average of two weeks against a weekly operating cycle. In a recent survey, 44 percent of supply chain leaders described their response as firefighting. The industry bought instruments. It did not buy reflexes.

This paper argues that the gap between seeing and acting is structural, and that it originates in the first mile: the origin leg between purchase order confirmation and cargo departure. This leg is the least instrumented and most multi-party segment of the international supply chain. It is where records fork, where accountability dissolves across company boundaries, and where the data behind every downstream decision either propagates or quietly dies. Closing the gap requires a shift from passive visibility to active orchestration and governance. The shift runs through three layers. Visibility answers what is happening. Orchestration answers what happens next. Governance answers who is accountable for it. The paper sets out a first-mile governance operating model, a four-stage maturity model, a 90-day agenda, and a ten-question diagnostic any operator can run without a transformation programme.

The timing matters. Gartner predicts that by 2031, 60 percent of supply chain disruptions will be resolved without human intervention. An agent working from a governed first mile resolves disruptions at machine speed. An agent working from today's forked records automates the confusion. Govern the first mile first. Then automate it.

title: Strategic Human Capital Leadership toward 2030: Digital Fragmentation, Socio-organizational Cohesion, and Dynamic Capabilities
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and

detail.title: Strategic Human Capital Leadership toward 2030: Digital Fragmentation, Socio-organizational Cohesion, and Dynamic Capabilities
detail.abstract: Digital transformation, artificial intelligence, algorithmic management, platform-mediated work, and the declining half-life of skills are fundamentally reshaping the nature of human capital in contemporary organizations. Under these conditions, human capital can no longer be understood merely as a resource for implementing strategy; rather, it increasingly constitutes a strategic foundation for capability formation, innovation, resilience, and sustainable advantage. Although the literatures on human capital, strategic human resource management, the future of work, and dynamic capabilities have expanded significantly, they still provide limited theoretical explanation of how organizations can strategically lead human capital under conditions of digitally induced fragmentation. This conceptual theory-building paper develops a multilevel framework of strategic human capital leadership toward 2030. The paper makes three main contributions. First, it introduces the construct of digital fragmentation to explain how digital technologies disaggregate and reconfigure traditional linkages among jobs, tasks, work locations, time, employment relationships, professional identity, and decision-making. Second, it conceptualizes socio-organizational cohesion as the organizational capacity to rebuild trust, shared meaning, learning culture, empowerment, psychological safety, ethical governance, and coordination under conditions of digital dispersion. Third, it theorizes how strategic human capital leadership converts human capital into dynamic capabilities-sensing, learning, integrating, and reconfiguring-through socioorganizational cohesion. The proposed framework suggests that organizations approaching 2030 will require not only advanced technologies but also leadership architectures capable of transforming fragmented work into sustainable human capital, innovation, agility, public value, and long-term strategic advantage.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is becoming a practical concern for telecommunications operations, where
service assurance, customer operations, network intelligence, predictive support, and process
automation increasingly depend on data-driven decision support. Nevertheless, the central
challenge is not simply whether an AI model, platform, or vendor tool can be introduced. The
more difficult question is whether the surrounding operation is ready to use AI-supported outputs
in a controlled, explainable, and useful way.
This paper proposes the Telecommunications AI Operations Readiness Framework (TAORF), a
practice-informed conceptual framework for assessing readiness before deploying AI-enabled
capabilities in telecommunications service operations. TAORF is organized around six
interdependent readiness layers: use-case and risk framing; process ownership and decision
rights; data readiness and traceability; systems integration and operational observability; human
oversight and decision governance; and governance, dual-metric feedback, and continuous
learning.
The paper argues that AI readiness is an operational and managerial discipline before it is a
technical deployment activity. It also positions business analysis as a translation capability that
connects AI ambition with operational problems, data requirements, decision controls,
stakeholder expectations, and measurable outcomes. TAORF is not presented as a technical
architecture, regulatory compliance instrument, or validated maturity model. Its contribution is to
provide a structured readiness lens for responsible AI planning, pre-pilot review, and cross-
functional alignment in telecommunications operations.

title: FTC V. Meta: The Importance of Quantitative Evidence in Antitrust
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, University of Chicago - Department of Economics, Compass Lexecon,  and University of Chicago - Department of Economics

detail.title: FTC V. Meta: The Importance of Quantitative Evidence in Antitrust
detail.abstract: The Federal Trade Commission ("FTC") brought an antitrust lawsuit against Meta in 2021, claiming that Meta's acquisitions of Instagram and WhatsApp had allowed it to monopolize a relevant market for apps providing "Personal Social Network Services" and that consumers had been harmed because the acquisitions allowed Meta to increase ad loads imposed on Facebook and Instagram app users. However, the FTC's market definition was not based on quantitative evidence and its assertion of harm ignored the two-sided nature of the Meta platforms, which makes it impossible to determine whether a merger would increase ad loads based on theory alone. In contrast, Meta's economic experts used modern theoretical and quantitative tools of economic analysis to address market definition and competition issues. This paper summarizes the field experiment, natural experiments, and related quantitative analyses presented by Meta's economic experts that demonstrated the FTC's market definition excluded apps that were closer substitutes to Meta's apps than the included apps. The paper also summarizes the results of a de-merger simulation that accounted for the two-sided nature of apps and was based in part on the results of the field experiment. That analysis demonstrated that the FTC's claim that the acquisitions had led to increased ad load was not supported by the data.

detail.abstract: A pepper sauce of three ingredients, made on one island in Louisiana, sits on restaurant tables in more than a hundred and sixty countries, and the company behind it employs about two hundred and fifty people. Strategy says global reach is bought with organizational scale, subsidiaries and country managers and local plants, so the maker of Tabasco should look like a multinational. It does not. I argue that the theory is missing a mechanism, and that the mechanism is physical. There are three routes to global coverage: decouple the product and pay in organization, as Coca-Cola does; ship it whole and pay in margin, as wine and perfume do; or shrink the serving until freight per serving vanishes, and pay in neither. I name the third route dosage and give it a construct, serving density, that predicts how much organization a firm must build. Two firms, Tabasco and Angostura bitters, reached the world this way in the nineteenth century by riding shipping networks they never owned. The physics is copyable; the head start is not.

detail.abstract: Kelly allocation is growth-optimal under known parameters but fragile under estimated moments. Regime conditioning is standard, but where the label enters is open—a choice between two costs, which we price. Data-side conditioning—keeping only same-regime observations—pays in sample: it reverts to the unconditional estimator on 30 to 43 per cent of decision dates and, when it operates on the single-name panels, its median retained sample is no larger than the asset count. Sizing-side conditioning—RegimeDial, which scales long-only Kelly weights by a pre-specified fraction from a Bayesian online changepoint state—spends nothing from the estimator and pays in timing, acting on a label formed a week before the returns it sizes. Dimensional burden predicts which cost is likely to bind: at p/n of roughly 0.48, median realized same-regime samples are at or below the asset count; at 0.09 they remain ample despite similar fallback rates. RegimeDial posts the highest Calmar in the headline six-strategy lineup in all three universes, with drawdowns 11 to 33 percentage points shallower than the filter’s, a gap whose bootstrap interval excludes zero on two of three panels. The Calmar margins are narrow, so the ordering rests on specification robustness, not sampling certification. A long-only shrinkage identity, exact on interior windows, reads the dial as state-conditional mean shrinkage. Full-window p/n is known before any backtest and flags where data-side conditioning risks an inadequate retained sample; sizing preserves all observations.

detail.abstract: Token projects face a financing deadlock: a professional security audit is the single strongest pre-launch signal of contract safety, but audits cost tens of thousands of dollars and must be paid for before a token exists to sell, while contributors who could fund the audit have no way to verify what they are funding. Existing launchpads resolve this deadlock by inserting trusted parties (the platform, a review council, the founder's promises), which relocates the trust problem rather than removing it. We formalize the verifiable launch: a deposit-and-deployment protocol in which an escrow contract accepts exactly four kinds of input (money, clock time, cryptographic proofs, and per-user choices affecting only that user) and in which no actor ever attests, approves, or decides anything on behalf of another actor. A founder commits on-chain to a fixed-schema claims manifest describing the token's properties, together with a zkVM receipt proving that a complete implementation satisfying those claims existed before any money moved, without revealing the code. Contributions sit in a non-custodial escrow; on success, an audit fee derived deterministically from the proven code size is escrowed for a pre-named auditor; the audit report is bound on-chain either by the auditor's own typed-data signature or by a permissionless web proof of the report on the auditor's domain; machine-evaluated launch conditions over the report's finding counts gate deployment; a second receipt binds the post-remediation code to the same manifest; and the escrow itself deploys the token by CREATE2 and doubles as the distribution ledger. Every failure path degrades automatically to pull-based refunds. We give the mechanism as a formal state machine with exact verification predicates, analyze its security against adversarial founders, contributors, auditors, platforms, and proof-layer attacks, treat the incentives game-theoretically (including why paying the auditor independent of findings dominates outcome-contingent payment), and cost the hard engineering: compiling Solidity inside a zkVM, for which we define a tiered deployment path that upgrades from attested to fully proven verification by verifier substitution alone. We are precise about what the mechanism cannot do: it proves process, never quality; it removes discretionary trust, never market or legal risk; and a clean audit of an honest manifest does not make a good project. Section 8 records the seven design revisions the analysis forced on earlier iterations of the protocol.

detail.abstract: Crosscountry decompositions of labor-productivity growth in the Kumar-Russell/Henderson-Russell tradition rest on an intensive-form technology whose structure has not been fully exploited. We establish two exact results for this setting: the frontier admits a closed form (the nondecreasing concave envelope of the country points through the origin), and the slacks-based efficiency measure factors exactly into the radial score times a slack term with a clean average-productivity interpretation. The closed form makes computationally feasible what the Simar-Wilson critique demands but applied macro work rarely delivers: a country-cluster bootstrap that re-estimates the world frontier within every draw. A Monte Carlo calibration puts the empirical size of the conventional nominal-5% test at 17% under a true null, versus 7% for the bootstrap. Applying the toolkit to a 200-country fiscal-policy panel, we show the choices matter: a sovereignty interaction that is significant at 1% under conventional panel inference is statistically indistinguishable from zero under design-based inference and under an order-m robust frontier, while the slack factorization reveals that radial and slack components of the same SBM change load with opposite signs on the same regressor. Finally, we document a domain-dependence result for bad-output decompositions: a by-production-style separation of the bad-generating set, appropriate for emissions, degenerates when the bad's minimum is attained at every input level-as it is for fiscal deficits-so attribution there requires the joint technology. A companion paper (Levkoff, 2026) develops the substantive fiscal-policy economics on the same panel.

title: The Underutilization of Mediation in Pakistan's Justice System: Structural Challenges, Comparative Analysis, and Practical Implementations

detail.title: The Underutilization of Mediation in Pakistan's Justice System: Structural Challenges, Comparative Analysis, and Practical Implementations
detail.abstract: The underutilization of mediation within Pakistan's civil justice system, despite its recognition in procedural and statutory frameworks. The study identifies the key structural, institutional, and cultural barriers that hinder the effective implementation of mediation, including the lack of awareness, resistance within the legal profession, and insufficient institutional capacity. A comparative analysis of mediation frameworks has been provided in contrast with the UK, USA, and Malaysia; the paper highlights best practices that can be adapted within the Pakistani context. It further incorporates a Sharia perspective by analyzing the concept of Sulh as a culturally relevant foundation for mediation. The study concludes by proposing legal, institutional, and policy reforms aimed at enhancing the utilization of mediation and improving access to justice in Pakistan.

title: The Algorithm of Decarbonization: Ip Ownership and Liability in AI-Driven Ccus Technologies
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Algorithm of Decarbonization: Ip Ownership and Liability in AI-Driven Ccus Technologies
detail.abstract: The intersection of artificial intelligence (AI) and Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage (CCUS) technologies presents one of the most consequential and underexplored frontiers in contemporary energy and intellectual property (IP) law. As AI systems increasingly drive the design, optimization, and real-time operation of CCUS infrastructure, generating novel algorithmic outputs, process innovations, and predictive models, fundamental legal questions arise regarding who owns the resulting inventions, who bears liability when AI-driven systems fail, and how existing Nigerian and international IP frameworks can accommodate these challenges. This article examines the ownership puzzle at the core of AI-generated CCUS innovations, analysing the doctrinal inadequacy of current patent and copyright regimes to accommodate machine-generated inventive output. It interrogates the liability gap that emerges when autonomous algorithmic decision-making causes environmental harm, and the extent to which existing Nigerian tort, regulatory, and statutory frameworks can be applied or must be reformed. The article further explores the access-to-technology dimension, arguing that monopolistic IP control over AI-CCUS systems risks undermining the public interest in accelerating decarbonization. Proposing a sui generis regulatory and licensing framework, the article argues that Nigeria must act proactively to shape a legal architecture that promotes innovation, ensures accountability, and advances the Just Transition imperative.

title: Estimating the Timing of Large-scale Humanoid Robot Adoption: An Analytical Simulation Framework
affiliations: Universidad Complutense de Madrid (UCM)

detail.title: Estimating the Timing of Large-scale Humanoid Robot Adoption: An Analytical Simulation Framework
detail.abstract: The rapid development of humanoid robotics has intensified interest in when these technologies will become economically viable on a large scale. Existing research has primarily examined technological capabilities and labour-market impacts, while providing limited analytical guidance on the timing of widespread adoption. This paper proposes an analytical simulation framework that estimates adoption timing by combining economically viable acquisition-cost thresholds with alternative trajectories of future robot prices. Rather than forecasting technological progress, the framework translates externally specified economic and technological assumptions into conditional adoption dates. An illustrative application considers alternative cost-reduction scenarios and previously estimated break-even prices for firms and households. The results indicate that commercial adoption is likely to precede household adoption under all scenarios, although the timing depends critically on assumptions regarding future price declines. The proposed framework provides a transparent, modular and readily updateable tool for analysing the economic diffusion of humanoid robots and other emerging automation technologies under uncertainty.

detail.abstract: Article 18 of the EU Taxonomy Regulation is a small provision with an unusually large jurisprudential burden. It makes minimum safeguards a cumulative condition of taxonomy alignment, but describes those safeguards through procedures intended to secure alignment with responsible-business standards produced outside the Union legislative process. The difficulty is not simply that the standards are non-binding in their original setting. It is that they change over time, speak in evaluative terms, and operate at the level of an undertaking while the Taxonomy ultimately classifies economic activities. This article argues that Article 18 is best understood as bounded operative incorporation. Union law supplies the source of authority and fixes the legal consequence; selected external standards supply content that the legal inquiry cannot ignore; and Union institutions retain control over scope, temporal reach and authoritative meaning. The temporal dimension of that relationship is a bounded ambulatory reference. A later revision should affect taxonomy classification only after a staged continuity-and-control inquiry asks whether the enacted form of reference permits updating, whether the revision remains continuous with the selected subject matter and legislative settlement, whether it was accessible and fairly applicable to the reporting period, and whether its Union-law effect remains publicly reviewable. This account supports qualified use of the 2023 OECD Guidelines, creates a strong presumption against automatically replacing Article 18's eight fundamental ILO Conventions with ten, and exposes the fragility of Article 18(2) if the pending SFDR revision removes the provision to which it refers. The article also develops a functional-nexus doctrine that connects undertaking-level procedures to activity-level claims. On that basis, compliance with the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive is powerful but rebuttable evidence, not a statutory safe harbour. The result is a source-based account of law that takes evaluative content seriously without surrendering legal authority to the institutions that drafted it.

title: Local Competitive Advantage in Location-bound Platforms: Market Density, Resource Appropriability, and the Temporal Horizon of Competition

detail.title: Local Competitive Advantage in Location-bound Platforms: Market Density, Resource Appropriability, and the Temporal Horizon of Competition
detail.abstract: Platform competition research has long predicted convergence toward a single winner. Yet for platforms whose transactions require physical movement and are completed within a local market-food delivery, ride-hailing, and spot-work matching, which we call locationbound platforms-outcomes depart from this prediction: hundreds of independent platforms persist alongside the leaders, market leadership has changed hands, and withincity duopolies endure. More strikingly, the same firm's competitive position often differs across local markets. This integrative review asks why competitive advantage in locationbound platforms forms locally, and under what conditions local advantages aggregate into firm-level performance and persist. Drawing on recent spatial analyses in economics, we organize the underlying mechanisms into three layers-spatial market structure, the appropriability structure of competitive resources, and competitive dynamics-and integrate them along two axes: local market density and the stage of market development. The synthesis yields two baseline propositions and six propositions. The central claim extends the resource-based view: local advantage aggregates into firm-level rents when local resources are inimitable by rivals and the routines that form them are replicable within the firm across local markets. To the classic question "can rivals take this resource?" we add the paired question "can we replicate it in another local market?" We close with a measurement strategy and a research agenda, highlighting the institutional variation of the Japanese market as a testing ground.

title: Transitory Energy, Persistent Core: Asymmetric Energy Pass-through in Greek Sectoral Inflation, 1996-2026

detail.title: Transitory Energy, Persistent Core: Asymmetric Energy Pass-through in Greek Sectoral Inflation, 1996-2026
detail.abstract: In June 2026 Greek headline inflation stood at 3.9%, more than a percentage point above the euro-area average, with energy prices falling and service prices remaining firm (Eurostat, 2026). Using monthly Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices data for 1996-2026, I examine inflation persistence, long memory, and asymmetric energy pass-through across thirteen COICOP divisions, the main special aggregates, and a hierarchy-robust set of mutually exclusive elementary categories. Three findings emerge. First, persistence falls for the large majority of categories once regime mean shifts are removed, while apparent long memory largely disappears after break adjustment and false-discovery control, surviving in at most 4% of elementary categories and mainly in the non-energy core at the aggregate level. Second, energy is among the least persistent components, although differences from the core are not statistically decisive under a block bootstrap. Third, energy passes through asymmetrically into the non-energy core: a one-percentage-point positive innovation in monthly energy inflation raises cumulative core inflation by about 0.34 percentage points at the twelve-month horizon, whereas an equally sized negative innovation lowers it by only about 0.08, yielding a ratchet gap of 0.26 points (p = 0.03). The evidence is consistent with asymmetric downstream transmission as one channel through which energy disturbances leave a more persistent imprint outside the energy component.

detail.abstract: We examine the effect of the staggered implementation of mandatory environmental, social, and governance (ESG) disclosure regulations on stock price crash risk worldwide using a difference-in-differences framework. We find that mandatory ESG disclosure significantly reduces future stock price crash risk. This result is robust to a stacked-cohort difference-in-differences design, placebo tests, alternative fixed-effects and crash-risk measures, and the exclusion of U.S. firms. Mandatory ESG adoption reduces tax avoidance and improves ESG performance, consistent with enhanced transparency and stronger monitoring as mechanisms through which mandatory disclosure mitigates crash risk. Cross-sectional analyses indicate that the crash-risk-reducing effect is stronger for firms operating outside the IFRS reporting regime, in countries with weaker government effectiveness but stronger public enforcement, and in countries that adopted mandatory ESG disclosure after a prior voluntary ESG disclosure phase. We also find that mandatory ESG disclosure is more effective under full-compliance regimes, all-at-once implementation, and when implemented by stock exchanges rather than government agencies. Overall, our findings suggest that the effectiveness of mandatory ESG disclosure depends on both the institutional environment and regulatory design, highlighting the complementary roles of disclosure mandates and credible enforcement in reducing the risk of future stock price crashes across diverse institutional settings.

title: "Factors Affecting People’s Climate-Induced Migration from the Rural to Urban Areas: A Socioeconomic Case Study in Bangladesh”

detail.title: "Factors Affecting People’s Climate-Induced Migration from the Rural to Urban Areas: A Socioeconomic Case Study in Bangladesh”

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest, financial or personal, that could have influenced this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study was conducted with informed consent from all participants. Ethics approval was granted by Dr. Mohammad Ali Ashraf, Department of Economics, United International University.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently as part of the author's undergraduate thesis requirement at United International University.

detail.abstract: Purpose – This paper aims to analyze the both direct and indirect effects of climate-related, economic, social, and political factors on the decision to migrate among those living in Bangladesh who are affected by the climate. In particular, how do these drivers interact to influence rural-to-urban migration, especially to Dhaka? Besides being a theoretical one, the research framework designed for this project was based on integrating the Push-Pull Model, Sustainable Livelihoods Framework, Multi-Pathway Approach, and Social Vulnerability Approaches. Design/methodology/approach – Migrants (n = 130) utilizing a structured questionnaire to survey residents of Dhaka's urban slums. The data was processed using multiple regression analysis, which included stepwise regression. Research limitations/implications – Possibly, the limitation of this work could be the size of the sample and the concentration on the migrants of Dhaka obtained from private surveys, with no inclusion of crossborder or public data sources. Sampling here consists of 130 respondents selected in urban slums only. Consequently, if more extensive, longitudinal data from various cities and rural areas were considered, the findings would probably have more generalizability. Therefore, the caution in extrapolating the results strictly beyond this sample population still holds here. Deepening the understanding of these phenomena in future research could be achieved through the inclusion of long-term tracking of migrants. Practical implications – The research on climate migration constitutes a major part of the cumulative body of work, which, from a practical point of view, will allow us to offer better guidance to the policymakers and urban planners in their decision-making processes. This study gives the policymakers a piece of very helpful information from the area of findings that mainly concern the improvement of adaptation measures for the rural areas, such as cyclone shelters and drought-resistant crops, with the objective of lessening the volume of forced migration, in particular. Social implications – The social implication may be that the decision-makers who are in charge can give priority to justice and equity in the demographic vulnerabilities (e.g., gender, low-income groups) and integrated support packages for job satisfaction, urban integration, and resilience as immediate measures to address the issues of slum growth and human insecurity. Originality/value – The results of this study serve as turning points, guiding policymakers in climatevulnerable regions, highlighting the infrequency of all-factor alignment in migration drivers, and reaffirming the reliance on compounded environmental stressors. Thus, it is a study that fills gaps in multihazard research entirely.

title: Global Financial Markets and Multinational Company Investment
affiliations: , University of Notre Dame - Department of Finance and School of Business, University of Kansas

detail.title: Global Financial Markets and Multinational Company Investment
detail.abstract: Using detailed data on the foreign subsidiary networks of U.S. multinational companies (MNCs), we find that U.S. MNCs are more likely to operate subsidiaries in countries with more developed financial markets. This relation is strongest where host-country labor markets are more complementary to an MNC's activities, consistent with financial market development supporting the local production ecosystem on which foreign subsidiaries rely. Examining credit and stock markets separately, we also find that credit market development plays a more prominent role in this relation. We further show that MNCs with subsidiaries in countries with more developed financial markets have higher parent firm-level capital investment, especially when they depend more heavily on external finance, an effect corroborated by within-country reforms that improve access to credit. Overall, our findings show that host-country financial markets are an important determinant of multinational activity and investment.

title: De-Indexing the Guarantee: Fiscal Substitution and Pension Retrenchment in Kazakhstan's 2027 Social Code Reform

detail.title: De-Indexing the Guarantee: Fiscal Substitution and Pension Retrenchment in Kazakhstan's 2027 Social Code Reform
