title: Wealth Transfer in Practice: Client Retention Across Generations at Boutique Registered Investment Advisers

detail.title: Wealth Transfer in Practice: Client Retention Across Generations at Boutique Registered Investment Advisers
detail.abstract: The United States is in the middle of what researchers are calling the largest intergenerational wealth transfer in history, with an estimated $84 trillion expected to change hands over the next two decades. This paper examines what that actually looks like from the inside of boutique wealth management firms. From October 2025 to February 2026, I worked as a wealth management intern, where I had a front-row seat to the operational, relational, and educational dimensions of serving clients whose estates will eventually pass to the next generation. Since February 2026, I have continued in the wealth management space at another registered investment advisory firm where the question of multigenerational wealth retention sits even closer to the center of day-to-day operations. Through a combination of hands-on internship experience across both firms and an extensive review of academic and industry literature, this paper explores why so much inherited wealth disappears within a generation, what the regulatory environment looks like for the RIAs navigating this moment, and what boutique advisory firms can realistically do to serve families across generational lines rather than just individual clients. The paper concludes with a set of concrete recommendations grounded in both the research and in direct practitioner observation. Together, these two internship experiences have given me a fuller picture of how the wealth transfer conversation actually unfolds inside small advisory firms and why the firms that treat it as a relationship challenge rather than a financial planning problem are the ones most likely to survive it.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that the trajectory of the U.S.–Iran war is constrained less by battlefield capability than by political time: elections, media-defined frames, and the durability of public consent. The central variable is defining power—the ability to fix the meaning of the war in a fragmented information environment. The paper develops three linked claims. First, a structural conflict between the administration and established media institutions weakens coordinated agenda-setting in wartime. Second, the reversal of diplomatic normalisation after 7 October 2023 illustrates how quickly regional predictability can be undone when proxy architectures reintroduce high-intensity conflict. Third, the U.S. midterm cycle exerts a gravitational pull towards short-term stabilisation over strategic completion, making definitional power and public support decisive constraints on strategic resolve. In developing this claim, the paper also argues that procedural framing, curated voices, and conclusion-first framing can narrow interpretive openness and pre-empt longer-horizon arguments about order, while linked patterns of technology transfer, capital flow, and uneven security responsibility complicate contemporary claims to regional and wider leadership. Throughout, the paper separates factual claims from scenario-level inference and treats projections with caution.

detail.abstract: The deepest quarters of the Great Recession exhibited below-expected inflation and real GDP growth, indicating they were driven by shocks to aggregate demand (AD). To gauge the severity of these shocks, I calculate unexpected inflation and GDP growth as differences from the quarterly forecasts by the Federal Reserve Board staff from 1982 through 2019. Using regression analysis, I estimate the effects of ADdriven inflation shocks on real GDP growth. I find that AD shocks account for approximately 75% of the cumulative GDP shortfall in Great Recession. I discuss the implications of these results for improving monetary policy.

title: Skill Measurement in Thermal Soaring: Exploitation, Selection, and a Research Agenda for Instructional Assistance that Withdraws
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Skill Measurement in Thermal Soaring: Exploitation, Selection, and a Research Agenda for Instructional Assistance that Withdraws
detail.abstract:
Autonomous systems can now find and exploit thermal updrafts without human input. Separately, guidance indexed to a learner's estimated latent skill has been shown to outperform both no guidance and guidance indexed to performance error. Neither literature has been applied to teaching a human pilot to exploit rising air, and no validated measure of soaring skill exists. 

This paper argues that thermal soaring is an unusually informative domain for skill-state-aware assistance, because it has no reference trajectory: the correct action depends on an invisible and shifting airflow field, so assistance cannot be defined as error correction and must instead be indexed to an estimate of how well the learner is extracting information from the air. 

We propose that soaring skill consists of two measurable families. Exploitation concerns the quality of a pilot's response to the mechanosensory cues that a successful autonomous controller was shown to require. Selection concerns which available lift a pilot chooses to use. Selection has been treated as unmeasurable from an individual pilot's flight log because a thermal the pilot declines leaves no trace in that record. We show how pooling logs across pilots can overcome this limitation, and we report a preliminary demonstration: one day of publicly available data yielded 20,171 segmented thermal climbs from 933 flights across latitudes from 37 degrees south to 61 degrees north. 

We describe an assistance architecture indexed to a latent skill estimate derived from these measures, set out a three-study programme with explicit falsification conditions, and state the specific limits of each data source.

detail.title: Revisiting the Rules-versus-Discretion Debate: Forecasting Evidence from the Bank of England, 1870-1913
detail.abstract: Under the classical gold standard, historians have long debated what guided the Bank of England's adjustments to Bank Rate: whether policy followed a mechanical goldstandard rule or discretion when City or exchange conditions required it, and whether domestic money-market stability or external convertibility carried greater weight. This paper revisits those questions with a London-specific monthly panel, 1870-1913, jointly testing ten domestic and external indicators the Court watched when setting the published minimum rate. The findings fit neither a single frozen channel nor unstructured ad hoc policy. Instead, the Bank appears to have drawn repeatedly on a multivariate information settrade settlement, gold movements, City asset prices, billmarket conditions, and episodic convertibility pressurewith state-dependent weights across subperiods. In the confirmatory specification, exports, gold flow, and industrial share prices carry the clearest joint forecasting content for changes in Bank Rate. Gold flow forecasts rate changes even when reserve stock does not, separating bullion settlement from balance-sheet position. Bill-market and convertibility pressures also carry incremental forecasting content in the multivariate specification, though their prominence depends on how domestic and external indicators are modeled together. The overall pattern is most consistent with systematic discretion under the classical gold standard.

detail.title: Objective on the Outside, Presumptive on The Inside: Qualifying The Habitual Tax Debtor between Patrimonial Fictions, Burden-of-Proof Reversal, and The Requirement of Clear and Convincing Evidence (Brazilian Complementary Law No. 225/2026)
detail.abstract:
Brazil's federal regime for the habitual tax debtor (devedor contumaz), created by
Complementary Law No. 225/2026 and implemented by Joint Ordinance RFB/PGFN/MF No. 6/2026,
presents itself as a set of objective, cumulative criteria. This article addresses a question logically prior to
the prevailing debate over criteria and consequences: how each element of habitual default is proven,
who bears the burden of proving it, and under what degree of conviction the authority decides. The
analysis shows that all three statutory elements rest on normatively constructed inputs: substantiality
takes total assets as its denominator — a magnitude that measures balance-sheet size rather than
solvency, and one that missing bookkeeping reduces to zero through a regulatory fiction lacking
statutory basis; on a literal reading, credits whose enforceability is suspended under article 151, III, of
the National Tax Code may be counted as irregular for recurrence purposes; and lack of justification,
framed as an absence, shifts onto the taxpayer the proof of negative facts. The qualification procedure
stacks an automatic reversal of the burden of proof and deemed confession by default within proceedings
of a punitive nature, while the regime itself demands a final administrative or judicial decision merely to
remove an ancillary procedural effect — an asymmetry that reveals the appropriate measure. The article
concludes that qualification requires clear and convincing evidence of each element, forbidding the
combination of fiction, reversal and default as a substitute for evidentiary instruction, and proposes four
operational parameters: reading 'irregular status' consistently with the Tax Code; construing known
assets in light of ability to pay; replacing the zero-asset fiction with duly reasoned indirect assessment
modeled on the Tax Code's arbitramento; and adopting the intermediate standard of proof.

title: Digital Trade Commitments for a WTO Accession Candidate: Uzbekistan after the 2026 E-Commerce Moratorium Lapse

detail.title: Digital Trade Commitments for a WTO Accession Candidate: Uzbekistan after the 2026 E-Commerce Moratorium Lapse
detail.abstract: Uzbekistan is seeking to complete a WTO accession process that has remained open since 1994 at a moment of significant change in the governance of digital trade. The WTO moratorium on customs duties on electronic transmissions lapsed in March 2026, while a plurilateral Agreement on Electronic Commerce is moving forward through interim arrangements among members representing roughly 70 percent of global trade. This creates a problem that existing scholarship on WTO plurilateralism has not squarely addressed: how should an acceding country structure its terms of entry when digital trade rules are being made partly outside the multilateral consensus? This article argues that Uzbekistan should adopt a calibrated strategy of selective alignment. It should align early with the Agreement's relatively settled baseline provisions, including electronic signatures and authentication, electronic contracts, paperless trading, open government data, and the customs treatment of electronic transmissions, because these commitments support market access, administrative modernization, and predictability for digital services. At the same time, Uzbekistan should expressly reserve its position on less settled and more sovereignty-sensitive issues, including cross-border data flows, data localization, and source code disclosure. The paper concludes that Uzbekistan should bind digital openness only where legal and regulatory benefits are clear, while preserving policy space over data governance, cybersecurity, and digital industrial policy.

detail.abstract: We extend research on relative performance information (RPI) by examining how individuals respond to recent performance signals when they receive contradictory RPI in highstakes settings. Drawing on recency theory, we predict that the latest signal carries greater weight in shaping motivation and behaviour. We test this prediction using professional bestof-three-set tennis matches that reach a deciding third set. We find that a recent positive signal is associated with better subsequent performance than a recent negative signal, even when both occur close in time. We further document substantial heterogeneity in this relationship, with RPI informativeness moderating the recency effect. Responses also differ by gender. The recency effect is attenuated among male players classified as Top Players-our proxy for higher self-efficacy-but persists among other male players and among female players. Responses also differ depending on whether recent RPI is positive or negative: women tend to underperform following unexpected positive signals, consistent with choking under pressure, whereas men respond more negatively to recent setbacks, consistent with the Golem effect. Overall, our findings highlight the importance of recency as a motivational dimension of performance information and show how individual characteristics and signal properties shape responses to and interpretations of recent performance signals.

title: Testing Nationesis: A Comparative Assessment of Regenerative Political Development in Finland, South Korea, Costa Rica, and Nigeria

detail.title: Testing Nationesis: A Comparative Assessment of Regenerative Political Development in Finland, South Korea, Costa Rica, and Nigeria
detail.abstract: The study of political development has traditionally been dominated by theories of state capacity, institutional quality, governance effectiveness, and resilience. These approaches have significantly improved scholarly understanding of why some countries achieve sustained economic growth, political stability, and institutional performance while others experience persistent fragility. However, the accelerating complexity of the twenty-first centuryincluding climate change, digital transformation, artificial intelligence, demographic transitions, geopolitical competition, and ecological disruption-has exposed important limitations in conventional governance paradigms. Effective institutions alone do not fully explain why certain political communities continuously adapt, innovate, and regenerate whereas others remain trapped in cycles of institutional stagnation despite repeated reforms. This article provides the first empirical assessment of the Theory of Nationesis through a comparative analysis of Finland, South Korea, Costa Rica, and Nigeria. These four countries represent contrasting trajectories of political evolution, ranging from highly regenerative governance systems to persistent developmental constraints. Using the Nationesis framework, the article examines eight interrelated dimensions of national regeneration: institutional regeneration, national political intelligence, innovation capacity, adaptive governance, social cohesion, economic transformation, ecological resilience, and symbolic legitimacy. Rather than treating political development as the accumulation of bureaucratic capacity, the study conceptualizes nations as complex adaptive systems whose long-term performance depends upon their ability to regenerate institutional, cognitive, social, and ecological capacities. The article argues that regenerative capacity provides a broader explanatory framework than state capacity alone and offers a new analytical perspective for comparative politics, governance studies, and development research. By empirically examining contrasting national trajectories, the study contributes to the emerging science of regenerative political development and establishes the empirical foundations of the Nationesis research programme.

title: When the Law Meets the Wage Grid: Minimum Wages under Weak Enforcement in India
affiliations: Madras School of Economics, International Labour Organization (ILO) and The University of Manchester

detail.title: When the Law Meets the Wage Grid: Minimum Wages under Weak Enforcement in India
detail.abstract:
Reported pay for low-educated male casual workers in India concentrates on a grid of
round rupee values, while several hundred statutory minimum wages, revised annually
in small steps, mostly sit between grid points. We study how the legal line and the
wage grid interact, using a statutory panel of authority-industry-year minimum wages
matched to six Periodic Labour Force Survey rounds, with treatment the annual change
between consecutive 31 December snapshots, predating the survey window. Four results
follow. First, sixty per cent of casual wages sit within one per cent of multiples of
fifty; where the floor sits just below a round value, seventeen per cent are paid at the
round value and one per cent at the statute, replicated in the redesigned 2025 survey.
Second, floor increases raise measured sub-floor incidence by 0.57 to 0.84 per log point
while median and lower-tail wages do not respond; a first above-median increase raises
it by 16 points. Third, revisions that carry the floor across a round value raise strict
violation by nine points, nineteen near the crossed point, while parked mass and deeper
violation do not move. Fourth, among own-account workers, with no employer and no
minimum wage entitlement, the same increases raise sub-floor incidence by 6.5 points
while reported earnings and work intensity do not move. Statutory increases move
measured legal status more than wages; compliance statistics partly reflect where the
legal line sits on the grid, and our mechanical adjustment separates threshold reclassification
from change in the reported-pay distribution.

title: Stablecoins, Sovereignty, and Currency Competition

detail.abstract: This paper studies how fiat-pegged stablecoins reshape currency competition, seigniorage, and welfare in a Lagos-Wright economy. Stablecoin entry is modeled through the joint determination of sellers' currency acceptance and households' portfolio choices in decentralized trade, with buyers paying a per-transaction gas fee on stablecoin payments. The model yields three results. First, stablecoin acceptance lowers the valuation threshold of the domestic currency and narrows the inflation range over which domestic money circulates, with stronger displacement when the gas fee is low. The same logic extends to the anchor currency: for sufficiently small gas fees, the stablecoin can displace domestic residents' holdings of the pegged currency from valued equilibria. Second, stablecoin adoption shifts the domestic seigniorage Laffer curve downward by shrinking the domestic inflation-tax base. This erosion is mitigated by higher rival-currency inflation, larger gas fees, or greater local-currency exclusivity among sellers. Third, stablecoin entry can raise red-country welfare by integrating previously segmented trading opportunities, but red-country gains must be netted against both payment-fee outflows and stablecoin inflation-tax outflows. Numerical results reveal a trade-off between expanded market access and seigniorage loss, implying that inflation discipline and transaction-cost regulation both matter for preserving monetary sovereignty under stablecoin competition. A final extension endogenizes the gas fee as the payment infrastructure's average cost, creating a zero-adoption trap that eases as domestic inflation rises.

title: A Heterogeneous Graph Transformer with Dose-Aware Cross-Layer Attention for Joint lncRNA-miRNA-Drug Resistance Association Prediction in Cancer

detail.title: A Heterogeneous Graph Transformer with Dose-Aware Cross-Layer Attention for Joint lncRNA-miRNA-Drug Resistance Association Prediction in Cancer
detail.abstract: Cancer drug resistance is increasingly understood to be mediated by long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) and microRNA (miRNA) regulatory networks, yet computational models typically treat lncRNA-drug and miRNA-drug resistance as separate, static prediction tasks. This paper proposes a Dose-Aware Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT) that jointly models lncRNA, miRNA, and drug entities as a single heterogeneous graph, extending meta-relation-typed attention with a dose-conditioned gating mechanism and a cross-layer attention pooling module for interpretability. Because no real dataset was available in this working environment, the architecture is validated as a proof-of-concept (PoC) on a synthetic heterogeneous graph, implemented and trained from scratch in numpy (no GPU deep-learning framework was available), with manual backpropagation verified against numerical gradients. Two implementations are compared: a fixed-projection encoder with a trained prediction head, and a fully end-to-end trainable encoder. Both recover above-chance predictive signal (AUC 0.52-0.60), but a 5-seed replication with paired significance testing finds no statistically detectable benefit from dose-conditioning (p = 0.895) or cross-layer attention (p = 0.635) at this scale, a properly tested null result rather than an unresolved limitation. We report these results transparently, situate them against the closest published models (iNcRD-HG; MHGTMDA) via a qualitative comparative-positioning table, and specify the real-data validation required before the architecture's specific contributions can be properly evaluated.

detail.title: Market Diffusion of Distributed Photovoltaics Incorporating Uncertainties and Behavioral Interactions
detail.abstract: Promoting the diffusion of distributed photovoltaics (DPV) is crucial for China’s low-carbon transition. Yet existing studies overlook the joint effects of multidimensional uncertainties, behavioral interactions, and agent heterogeneity on adoption dynamics. This study constructs a multi-agent evolutionary model coupled with social network analysis (SNA) to simulate DPV market adoption in China from 2026 to 2060. The model endogenizes the uncertainties of technological progress and climate change, and classifies potential adopters into four heterogeneous agent types: urban residential, public, industrial, and rural buildings. By embedding an SNA framework, the simulation captures behavioral interactions and dynamic state updates among these agents, revealing how multidimensional uncertainties shape micro-level diffusion processes. Results indicate that: (1) Multidimensional uncertainties reshape DPV trajectories asymmetrically. Under the baseline scenario, cumulative capacity reaches 2,440 GW by 2060. Climate risks suppress this to 1,457 GW (40% below baseline), exceeding the inhibitory effect of technological stagnation (1,634 GW, 33% below), as physical damage combined with network-propagated negative sentiment constrains adoption more than slow cost reduction. (2) Adoption behaviors exhibit profound structural heterogeneity. The urban-residential sector shows extreme risk-elasticity, with capacity plummeting by nearly 50% under climate risks. In contrast, industrial buildings demonstrate strong adoption rigidity, declining by only 10%. (3) Targeted interventions disrupt risk contagion effectively: insurance mechanisms enable the residential sector to recover nearly 80% of its climate-induced capacity loss, and synergistic policy incentives offset most hesitance from technological stagnation.

title: Intertemporal Return Contracts for Electricity Investment: A Feasibility Analysis Under Divergent Discount Rates

detail.title: Intertemporal Return Contracts for Electricity Investment: A Feasibility Analysis Under Divergent Discount Rates
detail.abstract:
In many electricity markets, private firms are expected to make investments that support public objectives such as decarbonization and security of supply. However, some projects with public value may not be investable under private actors’ required rates of return. Differences in public and private discount rates contribute to this gap because each actor values future outcomes differently. This paper proposes an intertemporal return contract that pairs upfront public support with future monetary value returned through electricity price reductions or repayments. A stylized project level feasibility model evaluates this contract for a private investor and a public actor. The model identifies combinations of upfront support and future price reductions that preserve private investability while keeping the public actor’s levelized cost below a benchmark electricity price.

Under the stylized assumptions, the proposed contract can satisfy both private and public feasibility conditions. The private actor places greater value on earlier support, while the public actor places relatively greater value on future price reductions under a lower discount rate. The modeling produces a feasible contract space, rather than just a single contract, showing which combinations satisfy both conditions. The feasible space is larger for the capital-intensive, long lifetime project than for the shorter lifetime project. Longer operating periods provide more years for future price reductions to return value to the public actor, while shorter lifetime projects have less room to offset upfront support. Ultimately, these contracts may be useful when public support is justified and policymakers want a mechanism for returning monetary value to consumers or public funding pools. An explicit return mechanism may also strengthen the policy case for support by making the public benefit direct and contractually bound.

title: Fiscal Multipliers during Natural Disasters
affiliations: , Catholic University of Milan and Banque de France

detail.title: Fiscal Multipliers during Natural Disasters
detail.abstract: Fiscal multipliers are larger during natural disasters. Using aggregate and state-level U.S. data, we show that the government-spending multiplier is significantly magnified when natural disasters occur. To rationalize this finding, we develop a New-Keynesian model augmented with disaster risk, in which higher public spending generates a larger output expansion through a strengthened investment channel. Two mechanisms are at work. First, by destroying productive capacity, a disaster raises the marginal productivity of capital, which further crowds in private investment. Second, wealth destruction leads households to draw down less of their savings in response to the fiscal shock, which boosts capital supply.

title: DECODEM: Data Extraction from Corporate Organizational Documents via Enhanced Methods
affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis - School of Law

detail.title: DECODEM: Data Extraction from Corporate Organizational Documents via Enhanced Methods
detail.abstract:
Much empirical legal research depends on translating unstructured text into structured variables. In corporate governance research as elsewhere, this translation has traditionally relied on human coding of documents such as charters and bylaws, a process that is costly, difficult to scale, and often opaque. This paper introduces DECODEM, a set of benchmark datasets for evaluating the automated extraction of corporate governance variables from organizational documents. The benchmarks pair randomly sampled corporate charters and bylaws with high-quality human annotations covering a range of governance provisions commonly studied in empirical work. 

Using these datasets, the paper evaluates several largelanguage-model extraction pipelines that vary in prompt design, task decomposition, and document handling. The underlying task consists of a set of document-level binary classification problems, one for each governance variable. The results show that automated extraction is feasible at a high level of accuracy for many provisions, with median performance near the upper bound across approaches. At the same time, performance varies systematically across variables, with a small number of provisions accounting for most of the remaining errors. More elaborate prompting strategies and cascading pipelines do not consistently improve performance for frontier models, but substantially narrow the gap between frontier and efficiency-oriented models in some settings, suggesting that pipeline design can partly substitute for model capability. 

 By providing a standardized benchmark and a systematic evaluation of extraction methods, the paper demonstrates that current frontier models can extract legally meaningful information from complex corporate documents with high accuracy and suggests an important future role for automated feature extraction in constructing corporate governance datasets.

title: From Rerum Novarum to Magnifica Humanitas: Antitrust Law and Catholic Social Teaching in the Era of Artificial Intelligence
affiliations: University at Buffalo School of Law and

detail.title: From Rerum Novarum to Magnifica Humanitas: Antitrust Law and Catholic Social Teaching in the Era of Artificial Intelligence
detail.abstract: This essay traces the historical links between U.S. antitrust law and modern Catholic social teaching, from their nineteenthcentury roots to the rise of artificial intelligence. It examines how both traditions arose out of threats to the social and economic order as industrialization rapidly expanded in the U.S. and parts of Europe in the late nineteenth century. The Sherman Act attacked cartelization of industry and the formation of monopolies; Rerum Novarum took a different tack, defending private ownership against utopian socialism while at the same time stressing the importance of voluntary associations in the relationship between employer and employee, capital and labor. The two traditions converged in postwar Germany in the form of the social market economy, only to diverge when U.S. antitrust shifted toward a strict focus on economic efficiency in the 1980s. We argue the rise of artificial intelligence is bringing these two traditions back together again. It is no exaggeration to call artificial intelligence the defining social challenge of our time. This is true for many of the same reasons that gave birth to the Sherman Act and modern Catholic social teaching: the threat of concentrated economic power, the potential for large-scale job displacement and degradation of human work, and the question whether government is up to the task of controlling private actors. Connecting Pope Leo XIV's 2026 encyclical Magnifica Humanitas with recent developments in antitrust theory and practice, we show how both traditions are relevant to the political dangers of concentrated economic power in the age of artificial intelligence. Ultimately, we suggest that strong antitrust enforcement is an essential check on AI market power, and Catholic social teaching on the dignity and value of human labor should inform the analysis.

title: The Effective Rate: Household Portfolio Returns and Monetary Policy Transmission
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Effective Rate: Household Portfolio Returns and Monetary Policy Transmission
detail.abstract: The New Keynesian IS curve measures the real interest rate using the federal funds rate, as if households save in a single risk-free bond. Over 40% of US household financial assets are now in equities, and this share has risen steadily since the 1980s. I derive an alternative IS curve input from a two-asset Euler equation: the "effective rate," a portfolio-weighted average of the policy rate and trailing equity returns, with weights given by the observed household equity share. The construction uses ex-ante fixed smoothing horizons grounded in the experienced-return literature, with no parameters estimated by optimisation. Estimated on US monthly data with highfrequency monetary policy surprises as instruments, the effective rate produces IS curve coefficients five to ten times larger than the federal funds rate when instruments are decomposed into conventional and unconventional channels. The advantage is concentrated during periods when the policy rate was fixed at zero but portfolio returns were not. A calibrated NK simulation using Survey of Professional Forecasters output gap projections demonstrates that the two rate measures imply opposite assessments of monetary policy stance in 36% of zero lower bound months, with the standard model accumulating 6.23 percentage-point-years of excess demand reading over 2009-2019. Crosscountry evidence from six economies confirms that the rate gap scales linearly with household equity exposure. The effective rate is a diagnostic, not a policy lever: its value is in providing a more accurate reading of the monetary stance as experienced by household balance sheets.

title: The Euro Adoption in Bulgaria Economic and Political Implications of Joining the Eurozone
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Euro Adoption in Bulgaria Economic and Political Implications of Joining the Eurozone
detail.abstract: Bulgaria is set to adopt the euro on January 1, 2026, becoming the 21st member of the eurozone and reaching a major milestone in its three-decade-long economic convergence with the rest of the European Union. This paper examines what that transition is likely to mean for Bulgaria's economy and politics, drawing on macroeconomic theory alongside data from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the National Statistical Institute (NSI), Alpha Research and European Commission public-opinion surveys, and the European Central Bank (ECB). The analysis combines a quantitative review of Bulgaria's compliance with the Maastricht convergence criteria, trade-effect estimates drawn from the existing "euro effect" literature, and a comparative look at how previous Central and Eastern European (CEE) adopters — chiefly Croatia — fared after joining. On the benefit side, the paper points to lower transaction costs (an estimated 0.1–0.5% of GDP in annual savings), a meaningful boost to foreign direct investment (FDI could add 0.5–1 percentage points to annual GDP growth in the years after adoption, or roughly 1–2% to the level of GDP cumulatively over five years), and stronger institutional credibility. On the cost side, it addresses the loss of independent monetary policy, a short-term inflation bump (historically 0.1–0.3% one-off in other adopters), and a genuinely divided public (49.2% support versus 45.8% opposition as of August 2025). Growth is projected at roughly 3% for 2025–2026, with inflation cooling toward the EU's own long-run targets, though credit overheating, energy-price shocks, and Bulgaria's fragile governing coalitions are flagged as the main downside risks. By setting Bulgaria's trajectory against Slovakia's, Estonia's, and non-adopter Romania's, the paper tries to isolate what actually determines whether euro adoption succeeds — and argues that fiscal discipline (a roughly 1%-of-GDP adjustment recommended for 2026), pension and energy-market reform, and stronger anticorruption governance will matter more to the outcome than the currency switch itself.

title: Institutional Shocks and GARCH Mis-specification: Evidence from China's 2016 Circuit Breaker Episode and AH Dual-Listed Pairs

detail.title: Institutional Shocks and GARCH Mis-specification: Evidence from China's 2016 Circuit Breaker Episode and AH Dual-Listed Pairs
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether standard GJR-GARCH volatility specifications remain structurally stable when subjected to abrupt institutional shocks, using China's January 2016 market-wide circuit breaker episode as a natural experiment. The circuit breaker mechanism was triggered twice within four trading days of its introduction and was abolished on January 8, 2016, producing a sharply defined exogenous policy shock within a market already characterized by ±10% daily price limits and T+1 settlement. Using a three-layer empirical design combining Bai-Perron structural break tests, a difference-indifferences comparison against Hong Kong equity benchmarks, and a novel GARCH Portability Index applied to 18 AH dual-listed pairs, the paper documents systematic mis-specification in baseline GJR-GARCH(1,1)-t models. Structural breaks cluster around the circuit breaker dates, leverage asymmetries diverge significantly (mean Portability Index 0.553, below the 0.80 threshold), and baseline models fail Kupiec coverage tests in all 16 sectors. Augmenting with institutional friction terms improves VaR pass rates from 0% to 44%.

title: When Growth Destroys Collateral: Technological Obsolescence and Macroprudential Risk in the AI Era
affiliations: University of Trento - Department of Economics and Management

detail.title: When Growth Destroys Collateral: Technological Obsolescence and Macroprudential Risk in the AI Era

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no conflicts of interest or competing financial interests associated with this research.

detail.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) are transforming not only production technologies but also the financial architecture supporting technological innovation. This paper argues that the growing reliance on private credit, asset-backed lending and structured finance has created a new channel through which technological shocks may propagate across the financial system. Unlike previous technology booms financed predominantly through equity markets, the current AI ecosystem increasingly depends on debt secured by technological assets whose value is highly sensitive to rapid innovation. The paper develops a conceptual framework in which technological progress simultaneously expands productive capacity and alters the informational and economic characteristics of collateral, thereby linking Schumpeterian creative destruction to financial fragility. Using the financing of frontier AI infrastructure as an illustrative case, it shows how GPU-backed lending, shadow banking and structured credit may amplify technological shocks through declining collateral values, fire-sale dynamics and institutional interconnectedness. The analysis suggests that macroprudential policy should move beyond its traditional focus on leverage and liquidity to incorporate the transparency, marketability and informational quality of technological collateral as essential components of financial stability in innovation-driven economies.

title: When Gold Fails: Asymmetric and Regime-Dependent Inflation Hedging Across Global Gold ETFs
affiliations: and Universiti Malaysia Terengganu (UMT)

detail.title: When Gold Fails: Asymmetric and Regime-Dependent Inflation Hedging Across Global Gold ETFs
detail.abstract: We examine the inflation hedging properties of 93 physically backed gold exchange-traded funds across 15 countries using NARDL, QARDL, and Panel Mean Group estimation with structural break decomposition. The panel-level long-run hedging coefficient is-0.242 (t =-2.234, p < 0.05), indicating that gold ETFs are, on average, negative inflation hedges. Only 3 of 15 countries (Japan, China, and Turkey) show positive hedging coefficients. The NARDL analysis reveals significant asymmetry in 2 countries, with positive and negative inflation shocks transmitting differently to gold ETF returns. The QARDL analysis uncovers distributional heterogeneity: Japan's hedging coefficient at the 5th quantile (L = 0.913, p < 0.01) is the strongest in the sample, but the effect vanishes at the median. Most critically, the 36-month rolling correlation between gold ETF returns and inflation turns sharply negative (-0.30) during the 2021-2023 inflation surge, precisely the period when hedging was most urgently needed. These findings challenge the conventional wisdom that gold ETFs serve as inflation hedges and have direct implications for portfolio construction during inflationary episodes.

title: Regret-Robust Newsvendor Model for a Trade Agent
affiliations: Dalian University of Technology, Department of Decisions, Operations and Technology, CUHK Business School, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Dalian University of Technology, Dongbei University of Finance and Economics and Dalian University of Technology

detail.title: Regret-Robust Newsvendor Model for a Trade Agent
detail.abstract:
Problem definition: In a newsvendor-type procurement problem, a trade agent bids for upstream supply under an all-or-nothing allocation mechanism to satisfy known downstream demand. The agent must determine the bid before observing the seller's private ask price and the realized supply yield. Because only limited historical data on ask prices and yields are available, their joint distribution cannot be reliably estimated. 

Methodology/results: We develop a data-driven minimax regret model to determine the bid that performs best against the worst plausible misspecification of the observed data. We derive finite-sample regret bounds and show that, under a uniqueness condition, the regret-optimal bid approaches the true optimum as more data become available. By exploiting the structure of the regret function, we obtain an exact, tractable reformulation and develop a finite-search algorithm to compute the optimal bid. 

Managerial implications: Numerical experiments show that the proposed minimax regret model delivers stable out-of-sample performance and strong average profits, particularly with small sample sizes and under ask-price shifts. This advantage diminishes under adverse yield shifts when the agent bears a larger share of supply risk. A regret-based policy supports more aggressive bidding when lost sales are costly and data are scarce, but recommends tempering that aggressiveness when the agent bears a large share of supply risk or expects yields to worsen.

title: Critical Notes on Marginal Abatement Cost and a Proposed Alternative Approach
affiliations: Ametis Institute, University of Glasgow, Ametis Institute, Ametis Institute, Ametis Institute and Ametis Institute

detail.title: Critical Notes on Marginal Abatement Cost and a Proposed Alternative Approach
detail.abstract: The marginal abatement cost (MAC) curve remains one of the most widely used instruments for assessing the economics of greenhouse gas mitigation, even though its weaknesses have been documented for more than three decades. This paper formalizes the construction of the MAC curve and develops three critical notes. First, the ranking produced by the curve is sensitive to the choice of baseline. Second, the cost effectiveness metric behaves incoherently for negative cost options, since at a constant cost the metric improves as emissions increase. Third, the curve ranks internal abatement options in isolation from the greenhouse gas offset market that decision makers actually face. As an alternative, the paper proposes a total cost approach built on a representation of mitigation alternatives as a set of discrete options, each characterized by a provision cost and an emission level that is valued at a greenhouse gas offset price. The solution concept rests on undominated options and on the climate neutrality solution set, which contains every option that minimizes total cost for at least one admissible offset price. The approach is shown to be independent of the baseline, coherent in the presence of negative abatement costs, and explicitly integrated with the offset market. The framework also clarifies the distinction between net zero and climate neutrality strategies, which appear as the two endpoints of a continuum indexed by the offset price. A comparative analysis positions the proposal relative to the Pareto based partial ranking and to other responses in the literature, and the limitations of the proposed approach are discussed.

title: From Bite to Burden: The Affordability Frontier of the Minimum Wage in India's Informal Firms
affiliations: Madras School of Economics and International Labour Organization (ILO)

detail.title: From Bite to Burden: The Affordability Frontier of the Minimum Wage in India's Informal Firms
detail.abstract: Nearly two-thirds of India's unincorporated-sector employers report average hired pay below a conservative, predetermined minimum-wage benchmark. Matching four rounds of the Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises, 2021-22 to 2025, to statutory floors and administrative enforcement returns, we distinguish statutory bite, wagesetting salience, and current-bundle accounting burden. Depending on the treatment of part-time exposure, the benchmark wage bill exceeds contemporaneous gross value added at the observed bundle for 5.1-6.5% of employers employing 12.0-13.3% of hired workers (11.5% under an all-full-time restriction). About four-fifths of measured noncompliers lie inside a 20% reserve frontier, so insufficient observed gross value added is not by itself sufficient to explain their shortfall. Statutory focality is weak: fewer than 5% pay within 1% of any skill-grade floor, nearby placebos attract at least as much mass, wages cluster on a Rs 500 grid, and threshold movement is a first-order source of measured reclassification; conditional wage estimates nevertheless admit modest responses. Recorded enforcement reach is sparse relative to a uniform sufficientdeterrence benchmark. A two-frontier model separates economic viability from statutory activation. Statutory bite, wage-setting influence, and accounting burden are distinct objects: compliance statistics conflate them, and the frontier separates them.

title: The Gwadar Port Nexus of Great Power Rivalry: A Trialogue of Marine Economics, Geostrategy, and Economic Impact Assessment in the Strait of Hormuz
affiliations: Al-Neelain University - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Gwadar Port Nexus of Great Power Rivalry: A Trialogue of Marine Economics, Geostrategy, and Economic Impact Assessment in the Strait of Hormuz

declarations.declarationOfInterest: As an economic strategist, I analyzed the marine trade routes.
declarations.ethicsApproval: I am the author of the paper
declarations.funderStatement: No funding

detail.abstract: Pakistan's Gwadar Port is increasingly at the center of heightened great power rivalry between the United States and China over the Strait of Hormuz, the world's premier tanker chokepoint. Chokepoint nations experience various conflicts and challenges associated with keeping the oil supply lines flowing. Greater US-China rivalry will have further implications on the Gwadar Port industry. Accordingly, the goal of this research is to: (1) identify and analyze the cost structure of the Gwadar port; (2) provide an evaluation of the port using the best vessel operating model in marine economics; (3) conduct a trade-creation versus trade diversion analysis of the Gwadar port using the CGE model and its corresponding indirect multiplier impact; and (4) assess the regional economic impact of the Gwadar port on Pakistan's GDP and regional job creation between 2024 and 2030. The findings of this research are as follows: (1) baseline values indicate that Gwadar offers a 14.5-17.2% cost advantage compared to Jebel Ali; (2) a full closure of the Strait of Hormuz would increase shipping costs to Gwadar by 189-240%; (3) the regional multiplier effect of the Gwadar port is 1.8-2.2 and could create 900,000 jobs between 2024 and 2030; and (4) the US Iranian confrontation is established to serve as an indirect tool to degrade the Gwadar port. Pursuing a cost-benefit analysis of alternate rail and maritime routes between the US and China, this paper argues that the US strategy to influence China is underlined with geostrategic considerations of building a "choke point leverage" and hence "entries" into the Persian gulf region. This strategy is incorporated in Gwadar port projects, together with the US-China agreement on trade-transport-late-kinematics, and the US interest in "busting" of the latter through competing activities at the Expanding Port of Duqm and the construction of the China Railway to Xinjiang. Three policy simulations are carried out to model the impact of a US blockade on the value of Gwadar port project, and test competitiveness of China Railway and Port of Duqm as "insurance" options. The simulations are based on empirical data from US-China trade flows, freight rates and port expandability, as well as historical data from the US-China trade war. The paper concludes that Gwadar is a critical asset in the US China rivalry, but its fate depends less on port infrastructure than on the stability of the Hormuz Strait and the evolution of Iran-US relations.

title: When Gradient Boosting Does Not Beat Momentum: A Significance-Tested, Walk-Forward Negative Result on Cross-Sectional Stock Selection in the Nifty 500

detail.title: When Gradient Boosting Does Not Beat Momentum: A Significance-Tested, Walk-Forward Negative Result on Cross-Sectional Stock Selection in the Nifty 500
detail.abstract: A large literature reports that machine-learning models improve cross-sectional equity return prediction, mostly on deep, liquid U.S. markets and mostly as positive results. We ask one narrow, falsifiable question on the Indian Nifty 500 (2018-2026): does a gradient-boosted crosssectional ranker, trained on standard point-in-time features, beat a plain 12-1 momentum baseline when both are evaluated through the identical walk-forward protocol, transaction-cost model, and selection machinery? The momentum baseline is numerically ahead on every metric (outof-sample Sharpe 1.73 vs. 1.55, CAGR 41.7% vs. 38.8%), but the honest finding is stronger and quieter than "momentum wins." A stationary block bootstrap and a Jobson-Korkie-Memmel test both show the Sharpe difference is statistically indistinguishable from zero (95% CI [-0.31, +0.69]; bootstrap p = 0.47; JKM p = 0.37), and the ranker's information coefficient-the rank correlation between its predicted scores and realised forward returns-is indistinguishable from zero across 51 rebalances (mean-0.004, t =-0.22). In other words, the pre-specified regressor demonstrates no cross-sectional ranking skill; its returns track the baseline (correlation 0.90) only because it is fed momentum features and ends up holding near-identical baskets, and it underperforms in later folds. A native learning-to-rank objective recovers marginal skill and matches the baseline's Sharpe, but only by trading 1.8× as much, so it too fails to beat it. The added complexity, turnover, and opacity buy no distinguishable benefit, so parsimony selects the incumbent. We interpret this not as "ML does not work," but as a worked instance of the evaluation discipline-significance testing included-that any candidate signal must survive before it is believed. Harness, features, and figure data are released.

title: Trade-First versus Technology-First Development Strategies in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Difference-in-Differences Framework with Staggered Adoption

detail.title: Trade-First versus Technology-First Development Strategies in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Difference-in-Differences Framework with Staggered Adoption
detail.abstract:
Since the foundational contributions of Lewis (1954) on structural transformation and
the subsequent literature on trade, growth, and development, two empirically distinguishable pathways to sustained prosperity have emerged. Strategy A—Trade → Investment → Technology (TIT)—characterised the export-led industrialisation of East Asia (Taiwan, South Korea, Hong Kong, and China). Strategy B— Technology →
Investment → Trade (TIT∗)—describes resource-extractive economies, particularly in Sub-Saharan Africa, that adopted imported technologies in primary sectors to generate tradeable surpluses, with investment channelled predominantly into large public or enclave projects. Building on a knowledge-augmented production framework grounded in endogenous growth theory (Romer, 1990; Lucas, 1988) and Schumpeterian innovation dynamics (Aghion and Howitt, 1992, 1998), this paper formalises and empirically operationalises both strategies within a unified augmented production function that incorporates artificial intelligence (AI) as a general-purpose technology (GPT) (Helpman, 1998; Comin and Hobijn, 2010). We employ a difference-in-differences (DiD)
design with staggered adoption (Callaway and Sant’Anna, 2021; Sun and Abraham, 2021; Goodman-Bacon, 2021; de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille, 2020) to estimate the differential causal effects of Strategy A versus Strategy B on real GDP per capita growth and the Human Development Index (HDI). The design accommodates hetero-
geneous treatment effects, institutional mediation, AI complementarity, and potential endogeneity of strategy choice via an instrumental-variables extension. Our theoretical framework predicts that Trade-first economies should enjoy larger growth dividends in an AI-intensive environment because of accumulated absorptive capacity, learning-by-exporting spillovers, and tighter domestic-innovation feedback loops. We derive a set of testable hypotheses, describe the required panel dataset, and discuss the identification strategy, with policy implications drawn for late-developing economies.

title: New Keynesian Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium Modelling of Jordan: Fixed Exchange-Rate Regime Versus Active Monetary Policy

detail.title: New Keynesian Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium Modelling of Jordan: Fixed Exchange-Rate Regime Versus Active Monetary Policy

keywords: Fixed Exchange Rate in the Middle East

detail.abstract:
This paper calibrates a small open-economy two-agent New Keynesian (TANK) DSGE model for Jordan with Ricardian and hand-to-mouth households, Calvo price stickiness with partial indexation, and oil as an intermediate input to production. Two monetary regimes are compared and evaluated: (i) the existing USD hard peg, implemented as an uncovered-interest-parity condition with a risk premium that effectively shadows the fed- eral funds rate; and (ii) a forward-looking Taylor rule that targets expected CPI inflation and the output gap with interest-rate smoothing. The model is calibrated to Jordanian macro ratios and nominal rigidities and is solved and simulated in Dynare. Shock ex- periments focus on two policy-relevant disturbances, a technology (TFP) innovation and a global oil-price increase. The comparison relies on impulse responses.

The findings show that under a positive TFP shock, the active inflation targeting stabilises domestic and CPI inflation and narrows the output-gap response relative to the peg, while tolerating larger short-run movements in real activity. Under a positive oil-price shock, the active rule increases rates, which tempers pass-through and cuts in- efficient gap dynamics. By contrast, the peg absorbs the disturbance mainly through larger and more persistent movements in the price level and inflation. Overall, for an energy-importing small open economy with nominal rigidities, an active forward-looking rule reduces inflation and output-gap fluctuations relative to a hard peg.

title: China's Policy Mix: Evidence from a DSGE Model
affiliations: University of Naples Parthenope, University of Naples Parthenope and

detail.title: China's Policy Mix: Evidence from a DSGE Model
detail.abstract: This paper develops a New Keynesian DSGE model for China with heterogeneous households, a housing sector, bank intermediation, and an explicit fiscal sector. The framework allows us to assess the macroeconomic implications of expansionary fiscal and monetary policies that are consistent with the policy orientation set out in the draft Fifteenth Five-Year Plan. It also examines the role of macroprudential policy in housing and credit markets, which are central to growth prospects, financial conditions, and debt sustainability in China. The main findings are threefold. First, fiscal and monetary expansions both stimulate output and inflation, but through different channels. The former raises aggregate demand and borrowers' income, whereas the latter reduces borrowing costs and increases the collateral value of housing. By contrast, macroprudential easing operates primarily through housing and credit markets, expanding borrowing without generating immediate inflationary pressure. Second, fiscal and monetary expansions reduce the consumption-based Gini index, while an increase in the loan-to-value ratio raises inequality. Third, the welfare analysis confirms and complements these results. Overall, the analysis sheds new light on the interaction among fiscal, monetary, and macroprudential policies in China and provides a useful basis for policy assessment in an environment of high debt, weak growth, and housing-market fragility.

title: A Fully Time-Varying Bayesian VAR with Stochastic Volatility and Narrative Restrictions: Monetary Policy, the Historic Pass-Through of Oil and the Dollar, and a Kaleckian Stock-Flow-Consistent Analysis of the United States
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Fully Time-Varying Bayesian VAR with Stochastic Volatility and Narrative Restrictions: Monetary Policy, the Historic Pass-Through of Oil and the Dollar, and a Kaleckian Stock-Flow-Consistent Analysis of the United States
detail.abstract: A single econometric framework, the time-varying-parameter Bayesian VAR with stochastic volatility (TVP-BVAR-SV) identified by sign and narrative restrictions, is used for all system-level inference on the United States. Two instances are estimated on fully balanced panels drawn from FRED and ALFRED: a macro-policy block for inflation, unemployment, and the federal funds rate (1959Q2 to 2026Q1, 268 quarters), identified with the Volcker narrative of 1980Q2, and an external-price block for the trade-weighted dollar, Brent crude, invoice-weighted import prices, headline CPI, and the trade balance (1987Q3 to 2026Q1, 155 quarters), identified with the Kuwait-invasion narrative of 1990Q3 and a dollar-invoicing magnitude bound. In each block the prior tightness and the coefficient-drift scale are selected at maxima of exact likelihood surfaces obtained by integrating the entire coefficient path out with the Kalman filter, and the volatility hyperparameters are estimated with full posteriors. All structural impulse responses are reported in cumulative form. The historic exchange-rate pass-through coefficient is traced quarter by quarter for all drivers: a ten percent dollar depreciation raises the import-price level by 4.5 percent and the CPI level by 0.4 percent at eight quarters, a ten percent Brent shock raises them by 1.2 and 0.3 percent, and the pass-through is not a fixed constant but rises with exchange-rate volatility, peaking near the 2008 crisis and easing thereafter. The econometric core is complemented by a Kaleckian stock-flow-consistent analysis of the full sectoral system: an eightpoint fall in the wage share since 1970, utilization-driven accumulation, a Kalecki-Levy profit decomposition, a specification-dependent Bhaduri-Marglin demand regime, and a five-sector accounting skeleton that closes exactly, with the complete transaction-flow matrix reported on a landscape page.

title: The Wrong Verb: Etiological Framing and the AI Psychosis Litigation

detail.title: The Wrong Verb: Etiological Framing and the AI Psychosis Litigation
detail.abstract: Seven product liability actions filed against OpenAI in California in November 2025 allege that a chatbot caused psychotic episodes in their users. The peer-reviewed clinical literature on which those claims must ultimately rest does not use that verb. Across research groups at UCSF, Aarhus, the Université de Montréal, and UCLA, investigators describe AI as inducing, triggering, amplifying, or exacerbating psychotic states in vulnerable users, and expressly decline the causal claim. The pleadings have committed to an etiological proposition their own evidentiary base rejects. This Article argues that the causal framing is a strategic error, and that the error is avoidable. It identifies four etiological relations implicit in the clinical literature, derivation, induction, triggering, and exacerbation, and shows that none is but-for causation and that none needs to be. Because specific causation evidence is admissible only after general causation is established, a complaint pitched at the individual level fails at the threshold rather than at trial. Because the eggshell plaintiff rule reaches aggravation and places the burden of apportionment on the defendant, the convergence of vulnerability and exposure is a defense the plaintiff can meet rather than one the plaintiff must avoid. And because the disability statutes turn on meaningful access rather than on the origin of the disability, they do not require the verb at all, subject to a circuit split on the availability of disparate impact under Section 504 that plaintiffs' counsel must plead around rather than through. The Article develops the fixity of the belief as the boundary condition of the whole account, distinguishing the cases these theories should reach from the cases they should not, and closes with a worked analysis of Brooks v. OpenAI, Inc., whose complaint pleads the one etiological relation its own alleged facts do not support.

title: Quantitative Easing, Quantitative Tightening, and House Prices: Beyond the Portfolio-Balance Channel in New Zealand

detail.title: Quantitative Easing, Quantitative Tightening, and House Prices: Beyond the Portfolio-Balance Channel in New Zealand
detail.abstract: Quantitative easing is understood to raise asset prices through several channels at once, particularly portfolio rebalancing, and its transmission to housing is hard to identify as these mechanisms operate together. This paper exploits New Zealand's 2020–2025 easing and tightening cycle as a natural experiment where the setting offers an unusually clean test. The Reserve Bank's operations were largely contained within the public sector, so the duration held by private bond holders changed little and the portfolio-balance channel was substantially muted. The two policy regimes are examined within a single cycle. Using local projections with event-time regime switches, randomisation inference and an error-correction adjustment for the tightening, We estimate how much of the rise and fall in house prices each regime produced. Easing raised house prices by roughly 19 per cent against counterfactual and 26 per cent above the pre-pandemic trend, and the tightening brought the correction forward, though with the unwind incomplete its eventual effect on price remains open. Large housing responses therefore need not require the portfolio-balance channel; the remaining channels, signalling and mortgage credit, are not separately identified. The findings foreground the distributional consequences of housing-sensitive monetary policy for central banks whose mandates exclude housing.

title: Architectural Optionality and the Option Overload Paradox: Organizational Antifragility in South Asian Food Services

detail.title: Architectural Optionality and the Option Overload Paradox: Organizational Antifragility in South Asian Food Services

detail.abstract: Purpose: This paper introduces Architectural Optionality (AO) as a theoretically precise construct explaining divergent crisis performance outcomes across South Asian food service organizations during COVID-19. It differentiates AO from Dynamic Capabilities, Strategic Flexibility, Real Options, and Resilience through a dedicated positioning table; justifies a multiplicative rather than additive dimensional specification; introduces and corrects an internal inconsistency in prior darkside formulations; and formally grounds Managerial Attention Capacity (MAC) as the moderating variable, anchored in attention-based theory. Design/methodology/approach: A theory-building comparative case study is employed using five organizational archetypes from India's food service sector during COVID-19. Cases were selected through theoretical sampling. Architectural scores were coded against 2019 pre-pandemic baseline data using an explicit three-tier rubric with observable decision criteria and documented source evidence. Findings: Eight propositions are derived. AO is specified as the multiplicative product of Option Volume, Option Diversity, and Option Activation Feasibility. Multiplication is justified over additive, geometric mean, and minimum-operator alternatives on grounds of dimensional complementarity. The AO-performance relationship is non-monotonic: moderate pre-embedded AO with selective activation outperforms both near-zero AO and reactive multi-domain construction under crisis conditions. MAC governs the overload threshold. South Asian institutional voids amplify the antifragility premium of pre-embedded optionality. Originality/value: The paper makes four novel contributions: a formal construct-positioning table distinguishing AO from six adjacent constructs; an explicit mathematical justification for the multiplicative specification; correction of the internal contradiction in prior dark-side formulations; and the first treatment of MAC as a formal moderator within the AO framework grounded in Ocasio (1997). Research limitations/implications: All propositions require large-sample quantitative testing. Panel data designs exploiting the COVID-19 natural experiment are recommended. Overload thresholds will vary by industry, firm size, and institutional context in ways the current framework does not yet specify. Practical implications: Firms should build redundancy that is commercially productive, calibrate AO to available MAC, and prefer sequential selective activation over simultaneous broad deployment. Platform architectures offer a resolution to the efficiency-redundancy double bind in South Asian markets. Social implications: Platform architectures that embed redundancy productively offer a mechanism for enterprise resilience in institutionally volatile South Asian environments, with implications for industrial policy and development finance in the region.

detail.abstract:
Background: For high-risk procedures such as esophagectomy, surgeons may increasingly encounter large language model (LLM) outputs that combine risk estimates with ranked clinical factors, categorical risk labels, and expressed confidence. The reliability of these accompanying representations is important for patient safety: prompt-dependent changes in stated risk factors or confidence could misrepresent the clinical basis of an assessment despite unchanged patient information.

Methods: In this retrospective cohort study, standardised outcome-blinded clinical vignettes were created for 299 patients undergoing curative-intent esophagectomy. Five LLMs evaluated each vignette under zero-shot, structured-reasoning, and simulated multidisciplinary-team prompts, producing 4485 assessments and 22 425 ranked factors. Factors were harmonised through automated outcome-blinded mapping into 24 clinical categories. We evaluated prompt-related factor shifts, within-model stability, intermodel agreement, associations between stated factors and LLM-assigned probabilities or prediction error, factor-based reconstruction of assigned probabilities, self-reported confidence, and agreement between categorical and numerical risk outputs.

Findings: All 10 within-model prompt comparisons showed significant changes in ranked factor distributions after Holm adjustment (all adjusted p<0·001). Mean rank-weighted Jaccard distance ranged from 0·262 to 0·611, while pairwise intermodel similarity ranged from 0·273 to 0·526. All five models selected the same highest-ranked factor for only 6·4–14·7% of assessments. Although 20 of 150 reasoning–prediction correlations remained significant after false-discovery-rate adjustment, only one involved prediction-error change; no pooled patient-clustered association remained significant. Eight of ten prompt-related confidence contrasts were significant, but the pooled confidence–error association was not (p=0·193). Numerical probabilities increased from low to intermediate to high categorical-risk labels in all 15 systems, although distributions overlapped.

Interpretation: Small changes in prompting can substantially alter the factors and confidence that LLMs present as the basis for surgical risk assessment. These outputs should be treated as model-reported risk representations, not verified clinical reasoning. Without validation of their stability and relation to patient outcomes, fluent explanations and high confidence could create misplaced trust and potentially unsafe AI-supported perioperative decisions.FundingNo specific funding.​

title: Nature of the Firm, Relations of Exchange, and Firm Dynamics: An inter-temporal study of micro-firms in West Bengal

detail.title: Nature of the Firm, Relations of Exchange, and Firm Dynamics: An inter-temporal study of micro-firms in West Bengal

detail.abstract: This paper examines inter-temporal changes in the nature of the firm, exchange relations, and firm dynamics of micro-firms in handloom weaving and forging-fabrication across four locations in West Bengal, using a primary panel dataset from 2017-19 and 2022-23. Our analysis shows that while the handloom sector continues to rely entirely on household labour, forging fabrication has become increasingly dependent on household labour owing to a decline in hired labour, while continuing to exhibit the absence of a conventional capitallabour dichotomy in the labour process. In relations of exchange, firms are increasingly relying on intermediaries, reflecting more stifled market access. Firm dynamics reveal heterogeneous transition pathways characterised by the coexistence of progression, persistence, and attrition. These trajectories are explained primarily by firm-level characteristics rather than sectoral differences or the effects of COVID. Drawing on case studies, we argue that firms that exited were already structurally disadvantaged and lacked expansionary motives, with COVID largely accelerating the exit of those already on the margin of viability. Taken together, our findings challenge the notion of a uniform and inclusive capitalistic transformation of informal firms and instead support the theoretical view that progression, persistence, and attrition coexist within India's informal sector.

title: Bowlby's Attachment Theory and Vivekananda's Vedānta
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Bowlby's Attachment Theory and Vivekananda's Vedānta
detail.abstract: Bowlby's attachment theory and Advaita Vedānta as presented by Vivekananda attach opposite valuations to one English word: attachment is the foundation of mental health in the first and the mechanism of bondage in the second. Most of that conflict is equivocation. What Vedānta condemns as āsakti is close to what Bowlby classified as insecure attachment, and both traditions make freedom of action rather than calm the criterion of health. What survives disambiguation is a disagreement not about clinging but about the ontology of the self and the terminal value of particular relationships. I give the two positions a common decision-theoretic frame. Let θ be the outcome an agent's security rides on and L the agent's loss. Anticipatory distress is the Jensen gap between expected loss and loss at the expected outcome, which to second order factors into the product of a curvature term, how much the self is staked, and a dispersion term, how uncertain the outcome is. Bowlby's secure base contracts the second factor. The Gītā's instruction at 2.47 annihilates the first. The two therefore produce the same behavioral signature by different means, which explains why measures of secure attachment and of nonattachment are positively rather than negatively associated, and it identifies the Vedāntic route as a robustness argument where Bowlby's is an average-case one. The frame also sharpens the central practical problem, that avoidant attachment mimics non-attachment, into a testable physiological prediction: suppressing the report of a stake is not the same operation as removing it, and the two should dissociate under measurement.

title: Why Profit Maximization Fails in Climate Stress-Testing: A Stochastic Control Perspective on Mitigation

detail.title: Why Profit Maximization Fails in Climate Stress-Testing: A Stochastic Control Perspective on Mitigation
detail.abstract: While current climate stress-testing frameworks increasingly seek to capture granular counterparty dynamics, they predominantly rely on exogenous mitigation pathways for credit risk assessment. This paper investigates whether classical profit maximization provides a viable endogenous representation of corporate mitigation under climate scenarios. We formalize the firm's strategic adjustment as a discrete-time stochastic control problem incorporating corporate cost dynamics, carbon tax pass-through, sector-level demand shocks, market share reallocations, and physical damage shocks. Using the dynamic programming principle and the framework of Bertsekas and Shreve (1978), we prove the existence and uniqueness of an optimal Markovian policy under mild regularity and economic viability conditions. We demonstrate that while this setup properly reflects the classical Pigouvian free-rider problem (Pigou 1920), rendering the firm's decarbonization policy invariant to its physical risk exposure, it exposes a fundamental mathematical pathology under pure profit maximization. Specifically, under economic viability conditions, the optimal policy systematically collapses into a corner solution, implying that the firm fully saturates its abatement capacity regardless of the carbon tax trajectory. This occurs because profit maximization treats carbon abatement as a free lunch rather than a capital-intensive adjustment under balance-sheet constraints. Ultimately, our findings reveal that corporate transition cannot be modeled merely as a profit-optimization problem, as it distorts credit risk assessment; instead, effective climate stress-testing requires framing mitigation as an endogenous cost-minimization and self-insurance problem under debt and capital constraints as in Ndiaye et al. (2026).

detail.abstract: We develop and apply a refined implementation of Robust Principal Component Analysis (ROBPCA) to 3,956 daily observations across nine assets spanning 2010-2025, covering equities, volatility, interest rates, and currency. Three financial adaptations are introduced: an extended iterative trimming loop that continues when dimension collapses reveal new outliers, MCD-based robust centering at each trimming iteration, and expanding-window z-score standardisation to eliminate look-ahead bias. Three principal components retained for economic interpretability capture 78.6% of total robust variance, revealing a market stress factor (PC1, 39.3%), an interest rate factor (PC2, 25.5%), and a residual factor (PC3, 13.8%). A systematic sensitivity analysis across nine parameter combinations confirms a robust core of 390-420 outlier days aligning with known stress episodes, independent of parameter choice. Distribution analysis of the resulting chi-distributed score distances reveals a lognormal body (∆AIC = 732 versus χ 2 k) with Pareto heavy tails (ξ ≈ 0.28), motivating a two-tier classification framework: a log-normal primary threshold and a Generalised Pareto Distribution (GPD) secondary threshold derived from the Pickands-Balkema-de Haan theorem. The GPD tier identifies four genuine systemic crisis days versus 341 produced by the standard chi-squared framework. A three-state Hidden Markov Model with Baum-Welch estimation is fitted on an expanding window of score distances, producing genuine one-step-ahead regime predictions. Validation on the COVID-19 crash and the September 2022 UK gilt market crisis demonstrates early-warning detection (Brier score 0.048) and correctly identifies an epistemic absorbing state at crisis peaks where no recovery data yet exists.

detail.abstract: Roodman (2025) challenges our findings in Summan, Nandi, and Bloom (2023) by arguing that the identifying variation in our analysis of India's Universal Immunization Programme derives primarily from the progression of survey time rather than the staggered rollout of the program and seeks to demonstrate this through a randomization exercise. In this response, we address these concerns directly. We acknowledge that our cross-sectional design, which relies on district-by-age fixed effects rather than a standard two-way fixed effects specification, leaves identification partially dependent on survey timing. We address this concern by adjusting outcomes for inflation, the most quantitatively important time-varying confounder during the 12-month survey window. The inflation-adjusted wage effect for the male subsample — the group with the strongest prior expectation of an effect given differential vaccination coverage and labor force participation — remains statistically significant at 0.125 log points (p = 0.007) using the International Monetary Fund Consumer Price Index, with similar results under the World Bank's Headline Consumer Price Index (0.127, p = 0.007). We acknowledge that the full-sample wage effect is only marginally significant after inflation adjustment (p = 0.071 with the International Monetary Fund Consumer Price Index; p = 0.067 with the Headline Consumer Price Index) and that the consumption expenditure result does not survive the revised specifications. We present additional randomization exercises that fully scramble treatment assignment as compared with Roodman's original exercise, yielding estimates centered on zero. The evidence supports a wage effect of Universal Immunization Programme exposure for males.

detail.title: Latent Welfare Equalization Under Constrained School Choice

detail.abstract: As affirmative action faces increasing legal and political scrutiny in school admission, this paper uncovers a latent welfare redistribution and equalization consequence of Constrained Preference Revelation (CPR) within the student-proposing Deferred Acceptance algorithm. We develop a simple matching model featuring a single dimension of asymmetry: "informed" students share correlated preferences with respect to school quality signals, while "uninformed" students form random preferences. To isolate the pure equalization effect of CPR, we analyze a theoretical baseline by suppressing strategic manipulation. CPR can act as a covert welfare equalization mechanism across the two student groups. Without CPR, informed students are systematically assigned to lower-quality (ranked) schools as safety nets due to fierce competition at high-quality schools. As CPR functions to sever these safety nets, informed students tend to be left unassigned to schools; in the large-market limit, informed students have a higher probability of being unassigned. Some of these vacated seats are then reassigned to uninformed students, who are more likely to capture them and improve welfare. That said, this equalization effect comes at a cost: welfare improvement of any student is strictly financed by the welfare loss of some others, meaning the mechanism achieves equity at the direct expense of Pareto-domination and stability, while also subjecting its intended beneficiaries to highly non-monotonic welfare trajectories (i.e., potential unassignment following improvements) as the constraint tightens.
