detail.abstract:
This paper examines whether structural differences in fiscal breakeven prices and Economic Complexity Index (ECI) slopes explain divergent fiscal and diversification outcomes across four major Gulf hydrocarbon exporters - Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Kuwait - during a shared commodity price cycle from 2010 to 2025. Using a 64-observation unbalanced panel and four analytical modules, the paper tests four propositions: Price Primacy, Fiscal Margin Differentiation, Diversification Divergence, and the Dual-Risk Threshold. Module A confirms that price movements, not production volume changes, drove hydrocarbon revenue volatility across all four economies, with median price dependence ranging from 80.34% for Saudi Arabia to 104.53% for the UAE. Module B finds that fiscal breakeven prices, not production scale, explain divergent fiscal outcomes: Qatar ran deficits in 12.5% of panel years against Saudi Arabia's 68.8%, despite facing the same Brent price cycle. Module C reveals significant divergence in diversification trajectories: the UAE leads on absolute ECI score while Kuwait records the steepest positive ECI slope, whereas Saudi Arabia's falling HC/GDP ratio reflects GDP growth rather than genuine export basket complexity. A standardised 17% supply shock stress test, anchored to the Ras Laffan infrastructure disruption modelled in Ansar (2026a), confirms that fiscal breakeven price is the decisive variable for supply shock resilience as well as price resilience: Qatar and the UAE remain in post-shock surplus while Saudi Arabia and Kuwait remain in deficit. The paper concludes that price risk and supply risk are two expressions of the same underlying structural condition, and that the HC/GDP ratio is an unreliable diversification measure where ECI and HC/GDP trends diverge. Three policy implications follow: fiscal breakeven targeting, sovereign wealth funds as liquidity rather than structural buffers, and ECI slope as the primary diversification metric.

detail.abstract: The Massachusetts Department of Public Health (DPH) is organized in a way that makes governance failure structurally likely, independent of the competence or good faith of the people who work inside it. DPH simultaneously promotes the healthcare sector, licenses the professionals who staff it, operates state healthcare institutions, and enforces compliance against the same providers, professionals, and facilities it partners with 1. This paper argues, drawing on organizational and regulatory theory together with Massachusetts' own documented record, that this consolidation is not an administrative inconvenience but a barrier to the governance functions the public and the Legislature expect DPH to perform independent oversight, timely enforcement, transparent reporting, and traceable accountability when systems fail. The evidence, chronic inspection and complaint backlogs, an unreleased statutory report, a reactive legislative patch following the collapse of Steward Health Care, and a state psychiatric hospital split across two agencies with neither fully accountable does not describe isolated failures. It describes an architecture operating as its design predicts. Comparative evidence from Virginia, Washington, Oregon, and Ontario shows that separating these functions is administratively feasible, not merely theoretical, and that Massachusetts has the constitutional and statutory mechanisms to do it.

title: From Petrodollars to Carbodollars: How China Is Quietly Rewriting the Rules of Global Power

detail.title: From Petrodollars to Carbodollars: How China Is Quietly Rewriting the Rules of Global Power
detail.abstract: The 1973 oil shock revealed energy dependence as a form of geopolitical vulnerability that could be exploited without a single threat being made. Fifty years later, the green transition was expected to reduce that vulnerability by ending dependence on whoever controls the world's most important energy source. Instead, it has recreated the same structural condition but with different materials, a new dominant player, and no cartel likely to fracture from within. This article introduces the concept of "carbodollar power": the structural leverage a state acquires by controlling the critical nodes of the green transition: mineral processing, clean technology manufacturing, and the technical standards that lock other countries into dependence. Drawing on supply chain data from South Korea, Japan, the United States, and Europe, it argues that China's integrated control over productive capacity, patient state-backed finance, and standard-setting constitutes a form of durable power that neither subsidies nor regulation alone can easily counter. The article offers a framework for understanding how energy transitions reshape global power relations and for evaluating policy responses in the emerging battery economy. It concludes that the shift from petrodollars to carbodollars marks not merely a change in resources but a fundamental transformation in how geopolitical leverage is structured and exercised.

title: Reversibility Is Not Self-Administering: The Clinical Duty During Withdrawal from AI-Induced Psychosis

detail.abstract: Recent clinical literature on AI-induced psychosis has treated the reversibility of its symptoms as evidence that the phenomenon is tractable. Flathers, Roux, and Torous (2026) describe the catalyst role, in which cessation of access to a large language model may be followed by symptom resolution. Morrin and colleagues (2026) propose a safeguarding architecture of personalized instruction protocols, digital advance statements, and escalation mechanisms for users already in psychiatric care. This commentary argues that both contributions are correct in what they address and incomplete in what they presuppose: a clinical container that the users producing the current United States litigation wave did not occupy. The pleaded record in Fox v. OpenAI establishes a pattern in which cessation attempts undertaken without clinical support produced somatic and affective withdrawal symptoms, a psychotic break on the third day, involuntary commitment, and, after a second attempt, death. I propose the Reversibility Paradox: for conditions produced by sustained interaction with a system occupying the structural position of a primary relational object, the mechanism of reversal is also the mechanism of acute risk during withdrawal. Three corollaries follow. Cessation without support is a risk factor and not a treatment. Unsupervised withdrawal is contraindicated where a relational bond has formed, so response must be matched to the route by which the condition arose. Reversibility establishes the duty of care rather than extinguishing it. The commentary closes by examining what the addiction frame, now in active use by litigants and regulators, does and does not accomplish under the Americans with Disabilities Act and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, including the statutory obstacle that any behavioral addiction argument must answer.

detail.abstract:
Access to healthcare remains a persistent challenge for many United States veterans, particularly those residing in rural and geographically isolated communities. Although the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) has expanded access through legislative initiatives such as the VA MISSION Act of 2018, disparities in physical proximity to VA-operated healthcare facilities continue to affect portions of the veteran population.

This study develops a county-level geospatial prioritization framework to identify areas where limited proximity to VA-operated healthcare infrastructure coincides with elevated indicators of healthcare need. Using publicly available data from NCVAS, the CDC PLACES Project, and U.S. Census Bureau geographic boundary files, the analysis integrates veteran population counts, disability prevalence estimates, and proximity to VA Medical Centers and Community-Based Outpatient Clinics (CBOC) across 3,143 U.S. counties.

Counties located beyond a 40-mile geodesic radius of the nearest VA Medical Center or CBOC were classified as geographically isolated, and counties at or above the 75th percentile of adult disability prevalence were classified as high-need. The intersection of these two criteria identified 628 priority counties, containing approximately 937,225 veterans, or 5.18 percent of the national veteran population, where geographic isolation from direct VA infrastructure and elevated health burdens coexist.

The findings reveal regional concentration of these counties in the Southeast and Midwest. Because the underlying facility dataset covers VA-operated Medical Centers and Community-Based Outpatient Clinics only and does not include VA Community Care Network partner providers, the framework measures isolation from direct VA infrastructure rather than isolation from VA-purchased care; full scope and interpretation are addressed in Section 7. Within that scope, the results identify a reproducible, conservative baseline for further investigation into infrastructure planning, community care expansion, and telehealth deployment.

title: Reducing non-attendance rates in endoscopy using a machine learning based risk stratification model – a case study undertaken in Northumbria Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust

detail.title: Reducing non-attendance rates in endoscopy using a machine learning based risk stratification model – a case study undertaken in Northumbria Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust
detail.abstract: Objectives   To develop and evaluate a machine learning model for predicting non-attendance at outpatient endoscopy appointments, and to assess the operational impact of using model-guided patient outreach within routine NHS care.   Methods   We analysed 31,185 endoscopy appointments from 24,893 patients across five hospitals within Northumbria Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust between June 2022 and June 2024. Penalised logistic regression, random forest and XGBoost models were compared using stratified 10-fold cross-validation and evaluated on a held-out test set. Model performance, calibration, subgroup fairness and interpretability were assessed. The final model was prospectively used to identify high-risk patients for telephone contact by health navigators before appointments.   Results   Of 31,185 appointments, 1,219 (3.9%) resulted in non-attendance. XGBoost achieved the best performance (AUROC 0.815, 95% CI 0.787–0.841) with good calibration (Brier score 0.034; expected calibration error 0.003). At a 10% risk threshold, sensitivity was 40.6% and positive predictive value was 19.0%, with similar performance across sex and deprivation groups. Prior non-attendance, age and booking-to-appointment interval were the strongest predictors. In prospective deployment, 609 high-risk patients received navigator calls; observed non-attendance was 10.8% compared with an expected 14.2–20.3%, corresponding to an estimated 20–58 avoided missed appointments and indicative gross savings of £11,080–£32,132.   Conclusions   Machine learning can accurately identify patients at increased risk of missing endoscopy appointments using routinely collected NHS data. Prospective deployment to target navigator support was associated with reduced non-attendance and improved service efficiency, demonstrating the potential value of predictive analytics for operational decision-making in diagnostic services.

title: The Use of Digital Pathways and Cultural Change in Optimising Hip Fracture Care: A Quality Improvement Initiative

detail.title: The Use of Digital Pathways and Cultural Change in Optimising Hip Fracture Care: A Quality Improvement Initiative
detail.abstract: BackgroundHip fractures represent a major burden on healthcare systems, particularly among ageing populations. Despite the adoption of national hip fracture standards, timely admission to an orthopaedic ward within four hours remains a significant challenge. This quality improvement initiative aimed to improve compliance with Irish Hip Fracture Standard 1 at a large urban academic teaching hospital.MethodsFrom 2018 to 2025, an interdisciplinary team employed Lean methodology to design and implement a streamlined pathway for patients presenting to the Emergency Department (ED) with acute hip fracture, known as "Code Hip." Key interventions included a fast-tracked triage code, real-time digital alerts across departments, a shared Electronic Care Pathway (ECP) whiteboard to track patient progress, daily multidisciplinary huddles, and a revised specialist ward transfer protocol. Progress was monitored using automated time-stamped data and validated through national audits. The primary outcome was compliance with Irish Hip Fracture Database (IHFD) Standard 1 (transfer to specialist ward within four hours of ED registration). Secondary outcomes included ED length of stay (LOS), total inpatient LOS, and Best Practice Tariff (BPT) income.ResultsOf 1,346 Code Hip patients managed between Q1 2018 and Q1 2025, compliance with Standard 1 increased from 0% to 70%, peaking at 80% in late 2023. Median ED LOS decreased from 9 hours 49 minutes to 3 hours 20 minutes. Median total inpatient LOS remained stable at 14 days. Quarterly BPT income increased from €0 to €31,000, with funds reinvested in orthopaedic ward equipment.ConclusionsCombining Lean methodology, digital infrastructure, and cultural change delivered sustained improvement in compliance with the four-hour ward transfer standard and substantially reduced ED LOS. This relatively low-cost intervention demonstrates that process redesign coupled with real-time data and strategic reinvestment can improve hip fracture care and hospital efficiency.

title: Real-time energy management for hybrid mining dump trucks using reinforcement learning-based model predictive control

detail.title: Real-time energy management for hybrid mining dump trucks using reinforcement learning-based model predictive control
detail.abstract: This study develops a novel energy management strategy (EMS) specifically designed for hybrid mining dump trucks (HMDTs) operating in ramp-inclusive mining areas. This strategy integrates road slope information and combines the SARSA-Lambda reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm with model predictive control (MPC), thereby addressing the issues of prolonged learning time and insufficient adaptability in RL, while significantly enhancing the real-time performance. Firstly, an MPC framework is developed for energy management, within which a power prediction model is constructed by combining gated recurrent units and bidirectional long short-term memory (GRU-BiLSTM) networks to achieve superior prediction accuracy. Secondly, both the HMDT system prediction model and the power prediction model are treated as RL models, enabling the RL agent to interact with them, learn the optimal action sequence within the prediction horizon, and execute the first element of the action sequence as the actual control input in a receding-horizon manner. Then, simulation-based analysis is conducted to verify algorithm convergence and prediction horizon appropriateness, while comparative testing against other four strategies confirms that the proposed EMS achieves superior control performance. Finally, a hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) test is conducted to validate the real-time performance and robustness of the strategy.

title: Drivers or Barriers? The Effects of Supportive and Pressuring User Relationships on Value Creation by Platform-Dependent Enterprises

detail.title: Drivers or Barriers? The Effects of Supportive and Pressuring User Relationships on Value Creation by Platform-Dependent Enterprises
detail.abstract: As digital platforms increasingly serve as core organizational infrastructures connecting firms, users, and markets, value creation by platform-dependent enterprises is shaped not only by platform resources and firm capabilities but also by users’ continued participation and feedback. However, how different forms of user relationships affect distinct dimensions of value creation, and how ecological experience conditions these effects, remains insufficiently understood. Using panel data on 225 game developers operating on Steam from 2019 to 2024, this study examines the effects of supportive and pressuring user relationships on the economic and technical value creation of platform-dependent enterprises. It investigates the moderating role of ecological experience. The hypotheses are tested using firm- and year-two-way fixed-effects models, with economic and technical value creation lagged by one period to strengthen temporal ordering and alleviate potential reverse-causality concerns. The results show that supportive user relationships have significant negative effects on both economic and technical value creation, whereas pressuring user relationships have significant positive effects on both outcomes. Ecological experience mitigates the adverse effects of supportive user relationships on both dimensions of value creation. It also strengthens the positive effect of pressuring user relationships on economic value creation but weakens their positive effect on technical value creation. By distinguishing supportive from pressuring user relationships and economic from technical value creation, this study challenges the conventional assumptions that user support is necessarily beneficial, and that user pressure is inherently detrimental. It further identifies ecological experience as an important boundary condition shaping how platform-dependent enterprises interpret and respond to user feedback. The findings suggest that platform-dependent enterprises should critically assess the representativeness and strategic relevance of user opinions, establish systematic mechanisms for identifying and processing user feedback, and adapt their user relationship management strategies to the experience they have accumulated within the platform ecosystem.

detail.title: Common Advisor Effect in Strategic Asset Allocations
detail.abstract: For strategic investment decisions, pension funds rely on external advisors such as asset managers and actuaries. Using supervisory data, we show that pension funds adopt similar strategic asset allocation policies when they share a common advisor. The effect is particularly strong for alternative asset classes, where allocations display positive spatial correlation. These findings suggest that advisors’ investment beliefs play an important role in shaping investment policy, alongside pension fund characteristics. We further show that asset manager effects help explain heterogeneity in pension funds’ benchmark-adjusted performance.

detail.title: The NICE Framework: Supporting Nurse Participation in Requirements Articulation and Early-Stage System Design Under Routine Clinical Conditions: A Real-World Formative Evaluation
detail.abstract: BackgroundMeaningful participation of frontline clinicians is increasingly recognized as essential for successful digital health innovation. Nursing informatics competency frameworks have strengthened clinicians’ knowledge and skills. Yet practical organizational mechanisms that enable sustained clinician participation in system design activities under everyday clinical conditions remain scarce.ObjectiveThis study evaluated the feasibility of the Nursing Informatics Co-design & Enablement (NICE) Framework, an organizationally embedded implementation model designed to engage frontline nurses in articulating system requirements and designing early-stage prototypes under routine clinical conditions.MethodsA design-oriented formative evaluation was conducted in a tertiary cardiovascular hospital. Sixteen clinical departments voluntarily formed nurse-led co-design teams, each applying the NICE Framework to a locally identified informatics problem. The framework operated across four organizational levels and three implementation phases, integrating leadership support, informatics nurse coordination, role-based collaboration, and template-guided workflows. All completed projects yielded structured requirements documents and preliminary interface prototypes. Five independent experts evaluated project quality, and inter-rater reliability was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC).ResultsAll sixteen departments successfully completed structured Requirements Documents and preliminary Interface Prototypes under routine clinical conditions. The projects involved 79 nurses—approximately 18% of the hospital’s nursing workforce—and addressed clinical and operational challenges across critical care, inpatient, perioperative, emergency, outpatient, interventional, and specialty care settings. Mean expert evaluation scores ranged from 80.6 to 88.6 out of 100. Inter-rater reliability demonstrated good agreement for single measures (ICC [2,1] = 0.74, 95% CI 0.53–0.90) and excellent agreement for averaged ratings (ICC [2, k] = 0.93, 95% CI 0.85–0.98). Project performance did not systematically vary with team size or nursing informatics training exposure.ConclusionsThe findings demonstrate the feasibility of the NICE Framework in supporting frontline nurse participation in system design at an organizational scale under routine clinical conditions. Successful engagement in digital innovation may depend not only on competency development but also on organizational mechanisms that facilitate collaboration, coordination, and knowledge translation. NICE may be understood as an organizationally embedded knowledge translation infrastructure that supports user-led digital health innovation and holds broader applicability across healthcare professions.

detail.abstract: A user persona is typically treated as descriptive metadata in AI systems-a profile record used to calibrate tone, vocabulary, and retrieval emphasis. This paper argues instead that persona functions as a delegation constraint: a runtime specification that shapes permissible actions, risk tolerance, and escalation behavior. This paper addresses AI systems deployed in explicit delegation relationships, where a system acts on behalf of a principal under bounded authority. By reframing identity as a control surface rather than a descriptive label, the paper explains how AI systems can produce context-appropriate behavior without models of consciousness or intent. The practical consequence is a shift in the design problem: from stylistic personalization to structural authorization.

title: Platform Channel Introduction Strategy of Responsible Manufacturers under Supply Chain Competition
affiliations: Wuhan Textile University, Wuhan Textile University and Wuhan University

detail.title: Platform Channel Introduction Strategy of Responsible Manufacturers under Supply Chain Competition
detail.abstract: With the rapid development of the platform economy, an increasing number of responsible manufacturers/brand owners (e.g., Patagonia and Unilever) have begun to introduce platform channels to improve channel-matching efficiency. However, their incentives under supply chain competition remain unclear. Thus, this study examines whether a responsible manufacturer should introduce a platform channel when competing with a traditional manufacturer. Our analysis shows that a responsible manufacturer’s choice to introduce a platform channel is jointly driven by its corporate social responsibility (CSR) level, the cost difference between responsible and traditional products, the platform’s commission rate, and consumer loyalty. Specifically, the responsible manufacturer is more likely to introduce the platform channel when its CSR level is low, or when the cost difference is small and its CSR level is moderate. Interestingly, a lower commission rate or higher consumer loyalty does not necessarily strengthen the incentive to introduce the platform channel. The result depends on the responsible manufacturer’s trade-off between channel cost savings and the profit erosion caused by channel competition. Furthermore, we find that when both the CSR level of the responsible product and the cost difference between the two product types are relatively low, introducing the platform channel may generate a win-win-win outcome for the responsible manufacturer, the retail platform, and consumers.

detail.abstract: The relentless march of intelligent technologies is forging a new sovereign-an 'Algorithmic Leviathan'-profoundly reshaping our legal, social, and ethical landscapes. This article confronts this epochal shift, moving beyond a mere catalogue of technological impacts to dissect the fundamental challenges posed to human autonomy, judicial integrity, and the very soul of justice. It synthesizes diverse scholarly perspectives, drawing from jurisprudence, computer science, philosophy, and social sciences, to illuminate the path from algorithmic determinism to a future where technology serves a more just, equitable, and human-centric legal order. Leveraging recent research on AI in criminal justice, automated decision-making, liability, surveillance, and ethical frameworks, this piece theorizes the implications of computational power for legal structures and practices, urging proactive, value-embedded governance. It is a call to navigate the currents of change with foresight and courage, ensuring the human imperative guides the codification of our shared future.

title: When the Laboratory Feeds the Machine: The Commoditization Stack and the Cross-Border Appropriation of Open Science: Autonomous Driving as the Mirror Case

detail.title: When the Laboratory Feeds the Machine: The Commoditization Stack and the Cross-Border Appropriation of Open Science: Autonomous Driving as the Mirror Case
detail.abstract: This is not a recommendation, but an invitation to reflect on the arguments presented in this paper. Open science rests on a compounding premise: that knowledge released without restriction returns, at least partially and in various forms, to those who produced it. For most of its history this held, in part because the maturation of knowledge was slow enough that returns accrued to producers before value could be captured elsewhere; it was a fragmented system that worked because time was on society's side. This paper argues that, under generative-AI commoditization, the premise fails asymmetrically. Open science has been among the most productive arrangements in the history of research, and its productivity depended on collaboration, because knowledge was distributed across specialists; that condition is now changing as capability concentrates in a few compute-rich frontiers and is commercialized; the argument is therefore not against openness but an invitation to reflection that the new conditions make timely, offered so that what has worked can be preserved rather than assumed. The SAE J3016 taxonomy of driving automation serves as a scaffold, crossed with a seven-layer commoditization stack, so that autonomous driving can be treated as the mirror case of AI-era knowledge production: a domain whose decomposition into perception, localization, mapping, planning, and control renders commoditization measurable subsystem by subsystem; the case is a lens rather than a limit, for the same mechanism recurs across many other knowledge-intensive activities. Two regularities are established. First, artificial intelligence, and increasingly agentic artificial intelligence, penetrates the stack top-down, with penetration depth inversely proportional to safety-criticality and certification burden; the defensible residual therefore concentrates in judgment and operational-design-domain (ODD) setting (Layer 5) and in certifiable accountability (Layer 6). Second, the agentic design now proposed for driving coincides with the one proposed for scientific discovery, which makes driving and science two instances of one mechanism. The cross-border knowledge regime, captured by a coefficient K7, is then reframed. Open scientific output is ingested unilaterally into frontier models held by two poles, the United States and China, stripped of attribution, and re-exported as priced capability, so that value need not return to the producing laboratory or nation despite heavy investment. Decomposing K7 into a collaboration component and an ingestion component shows that decoupling in collaboration need not reduce exposure to appropriation. The same fragmented frontier also gates the defensible residual. The certification and verification capability that Layer 6 requires is bloc-held, leaving a non-frontier actor unable both to certify its agentic build and to defend it. A real but anonymized case, two internationally leading European public laboratories, instantiates the argument, and the pairing of an engineering laboratory with a social-science laboratory is treated as methodologically necessary. A concluding contribution, offered as a matter for reflection, asks whether the knowledge most exposed to appropriation might be converted, within universities, into the formation of people: an asset that resists ingestion and that may help graduates withstand the difficulties of the first job.

detail.abstract: This paper explores the transformative impact of AI-driven predictive analytics on supply chain management. By leveraging technologies such as machine learning and deep learning, AI enhances key areas like demand forecasting, inventory management, supplier selection, and risk management. However, the integration of AI faces challenges, including data quality issues, infrastructure limitations, and skill gaps. This study emphasizes the need for strategic implementation, robust data infrastructure, and continuous innovation to overcome these challenges. It also addresses the economic and social implications of AI in supply chains, suggesting that future research should focus on developing tailored AI models, integrating emerging technologies, and addressing ethical concerns. This paper discusses these issues by demonstrating the potential use of an integrated platform to support supply chain processes. The findings highlight the importance of investing in AI infrastructures and providing training to ensure successful AI adoption. The discussion and conclusions aim to promote research, and offer valuable insights for industry leaders, policymakers, and academics.

title: From AI Diffusion to AI Capacity: A Framework, Diagnostic Tool, and Research Agenda for the Global South

detail.title: From AI Diffusion to AI Capacity: A Framework, Diagnostic Tool, and Research Agenda for the Global South
detail.abstract: The spread of AI across the Global South is frequently read as evidence of adoption, yet widespread use of AI tools reveals little about who controls the models, infrastructures, data pipelines, and contractual terms through which that use occurs. This paper argues that AI diffusion and AI capacity are analytically distinct, and that conflating them obscures the real terms on which countries participate in the AI economy. It develops a conceptual framework built on six primary entry points (markets, infrastructures, state systems, resource and industrial regimes, language ecologies, and development agendas) through which AI first becomes economically and institutionally consequential, and defines AI capacity across five interrelated components (computational, data and language, resource and infrastructural, institutional, and developmental) as the ability to access, build, adapt, govern, and sustain the conditions of AI development and use. Building on this framework, the paper offers a diagnostic tool: five recurring gaps: adoption without control, infrastructure without access, data without usability, skills without institutions, and pilots without systems, through which diffusion fails to convert into durable capacity, applied comparatively to India and South Africa as two distinct configurations of capacity formation. The paper closes with a six-question research agendaentry point, capacity formation, connection, place and agency, bargaining power, and development alignment. The intention is to reorient AI governance research in the Global South from adoption and readiness rankings toward the political economy of capacity formation. The paper is structured to be used at three levels: as a conceptual vocabulary, as a standalone diagnostic tool applicable beyond the two cases discussed, and as an open research agenda-each usable independently of the others.

title: The Future of Doctoral Education: From Dissertation Production to Knowledge Creation Ecosystems. Toward Mode 4 Knowledge Production and the Meta-intelligent University

detail.title: The Future of Doctoral Education: From Dissertation Production to Knowledge Creation Ecosystems. Toward Mode 4 Knowledge Production and the Meta-intelligent University
detail.abstract: Doctoral education has historically represented one of the most important institutional mechanisms through which societies cultivate advanced intellectual capabilities and expand the frontiers of knowledge. Since the emergence of the modern research university, particularly through the Humboldtian tradition, the doctorate has been primarily structured around the production of a dissertation demonstrating scholarly autonomy, methodological competence, and an original contribution to a disciplinary field. However, the contemporary transformation of knowledge societies challenges the adequacy of a doctoral model centred primarily on written research outputs and bibliometric performance. Artificial intelligence, technological acceleration, ecological disruption, global complexity, and the emergence of innovation-driven economies require new forms of doctoral creativity capable not only of explaining existing realities but also of creating new scientific, technological, institutional, and social possibilities. This article examines the future of doctoral education through the theoretical lens of Mode 4 Knowledge Production, which extends previous debates on knowledge production beyond disciplinary research, contextualized problem-solving, and innovation ecosystems toward a regenerative paradigm of knowledge creation. Drawing upon this framework, the article argues that doctoral education is undergoing a historical transition from knowledge reproduction to knowledge production, knowledge creation, and ultimately knowledge regeneration. The article develops the concept of the Doctoral Knowledge Ecosystem Model, proposing that future doctoral education will emerge from the interaction of human intelligence, artificial intelligence, collective intelligence, institutional intelligence, innovation intelligence, societal intelligence, ecological intelligence, and regenerative intelligence. Through comparative analysis of contemporary innovation transformations, particularly China's movement from technological learning toward indigenous innovation and original creation, the article demonstrates that future research excellence will increasingly depend on the capacity to generate new realities rather than merely produce additional academic texts. The article concludes that the future university will evolve toward the Meta-Intelligent University, a regenerative knowledge ecosystem where doctoral researchers become architects of scientific, technological, and civilizational transformation.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that film distribution has entered a post-shelf phase, in which economic value depends not only on whether a title is placed into distribution, but on whether it remains discoverable after placement. Historically, the "shelf" referred to a visible point of access: a theatrical screen, a video-store rack, a cable slot, or a retail listing. In the current platform environment, the shelf is no longer singular, physical, or stable: films circulate across streaming libraries, FAST channels, AVOD and TVOD storefronts, search engines, recommendation systems, and AI-mediated discovery interfaces. As a result, availability and visibility have become separate economic conditions: a film may be technically available while remaining functionally invisible. "Post-shelf economics" is introduced as a framework for understanding the economic variables that determine a film's value after it enters distribution infrastructure: metadata quality, platform surfacing, search visibility, cross-platform presence, reactivation potential, algorithmic compatibility, audience signal accumulation, and exposure path dependence. The paper argues that discoverability should be treated not as a secondary marketing concern, but as an economic variable that shapes long-tail performance, rights-holder leverage, catalog value, and hybrid distribution strategy.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence does not create the coordination failure this paper describes. It converts a chronic condition that regulated markets tolerated for three decades into an acute one they cannot.

When a decision crosses a boundary between two organisations, two software systems, or two regulatory regimes, the data crosses but the evidence of how the decision was reached does not. Who reviewed what, under what authority, against which rules, reaching what conclusion, and whether that conclusion still holds, stays behind. The receiving party gets the outcome, not the basis for relying on it. This paper names the failure to recognise a single condition behind many separate symptoms boundary blindness.

The paper draws on seventy-one semi-structured interviews with senior practitioners, together with independently published institutional sources spanning prudential regulation, reinsurance, trade bodies, market infrastructure and technology vendors across multiple jurisdictions. It catalogues nine operational symptoms in three groups: cross-firm coordination, within-firm coordination across software platform boundaries, and artificial intelligence. It documents a convergence cluster in which those sources independently name variants of the same architectural failure without referencing one another's work.

Three arguments follow. First, artificial intelligence is an amplifier rather than a cause. What it removes is the human institutional memory that made the gap survivable, and it removes it at machine speed while a workforce transition is removing the same memory independently. Second, the AI governance regimes now in force largely certify the wrong object. They assess systems rather than the decisions those systems produce, and they direct disclosure upward to supervisors or inward to a firm's own records rather than sideways to the counterparty actually relying on a determination. Third, the deficit is architectural and admits an architectural remedy: a portable, tamper-evident record of a decision, separable from the underlying data, verifiable by a receiving party without access to the sending party's systems.

The paper specifies that record, argues that it should be expressed as an openly licensed specification governed as a public good rather than as a proprietary product, and sets out the empirical programme designed to test the diagnosis and, if warranted, to falsify it. It presents findings, not a product, and makes no commercial claim.

title: Variational Autoencoders for Pose Estimation and Emotion Recognition: A Survey and Healthcare Perspectives

detail.title: Variational Autoencoders for Pose Estimation and Emotion Recognition: A Survey and Healthcare Perspectives
detail.abstract: Human pose estimation and emotion recognition are two fundamental tasks in human-centric sensing, with broad applications in intelligent surveillance, human–computer interaction, and healthcare. Among deep generative models, the Variational Autoencoder (VAE) stands out for its principled probabilistic framework, interpretable latent space, and flexible generative capability. These properties make it well suited to shared challenges in both domains, including inherent ambiguity, data scarcity, and cross-domain generalization. However, existing surveys address these domains in isolation—reviewing either pose estimation methods or emotion recognition methods without a VAE-specific lens—thereby overlooking the structural parallels in how VAE is exploited across both fields and their shared healthcare implications. This paper addresses this gap with a comprehensive, VAE-centric survey spanning both fields. We construct a unified taxonomy of VAE variants, review their applications across diverse pose estimation and emotion recognition sub-tasks, and distill a key finding: despite the apparent disparity between the two domains, VAE serves structurally analogous roles in both—representation learning, data augmentation, factor disentanglement, and domain adaptation. This methodological unity naturally extends toward healthcare, where VAE-enabled pose analysis and affective computing converge to support clinical assessment and mental health monitoring. We further chart a future roadmap positioning VAE as an enduring component for continuous health monitoring and large-scale medical applications, through integration with diffusion models, large language models, and federated learning.

detail.title: GTPM-Seg: Generative Topology Prior Memory for Vessel Segmentation
detail.abstract: Vessel segmentation remains challenging across diverse medical imaging modalities due to weak contrast, thin tubular structures, complex branching patterns, and frequent topological discontinuities. We present GTPM-Seg, a Generative Topology Prior Memory framework for topology-prior-guided vessel segmentation. For each target image, one annotated reference pair is randomly sampled from the corresponding training split to construct a reference-conditioned topology prior memory. GTPM-Seg extracts differentiable topology representations from the sampled reference annotation, including vessel skeletons, branch maps, and local direction fields, and encodes them into topology seed tokens. A latent topology diffusion module further expands these seeds into a set of plausible topology priors, which are stored in a dynamic memory bank. For each target image, a hybrid CNN-ViT encoder extracts appearance features that query the memory through cross-attention. The retrieved topology information is then injected into the decoder through residual modulation using gated topology-memory retrieval to improve vessel continuity and suppress structurally implausible predictions. GTPM-Seg is evaluated independently on seven X-ray angiography, OCTA, and fundus vessel segmentation datasets. The results show that it achieves the highest Dice score on all seven datasets and provides consistent improvements in centerline preservation and topology-aware segmentation quality. Additional analyses examine component contributions, sensitivity to the number of generated priors, model-size efficiency, and performance under degraded imaging conditions.

detail.title: Basin-scale assessment of environmental and human health risks of melamine as a persistent, mobile, and toxic substance
detail.abstract: As one of the first identified persistent, mobile, and toxic (PMT) substances, melamine poses a potential threat to aquatic ecosystems and human health. However, available evidence has largely been derived from localized and site-specific monitoring; the comprehensive environmental and human health risks at the urban, regional, and broader levels—which are truly representative—have yet to be investigated. Building on a river basin-scale environmental exposure model for PMT substances, the study explored the environmental and human health risks of melamine at basin and national scales. It was indicated that environmental risks in surface water and sediment were generally low according to available ecotoxicological evidence of melamine, with over 90% of the 80 Chinese river basins having risk quotients below 0.01. In contrast, the increasing contamination levels of melamine in soil have introduced a low to medium risk to soil ecosystems in more than half of the basins, particularly in densely populated or industrialized areas. The adult chronic daily intake (CDI) via drinking water and associated risks showed marked spatial heterogeneity. Under high-exposure conditions (CDI97.5%), the elevated target hazard quotients in certain basins suggested that potential non-carcinogenic risks should be considered under conservative assumptions. Besides, incremental lifetime cancer risks exceeded 10-6 in 20 basins, indicating potential carcinogenic risks in localized hotspots. Further exploratory analysis using Spearman rank correlation suggested positive associations between estimated basin-scale melamine exposure and mortality burdens from kidney diseases.

detail.abstract: ObjectivePatient-generated health data (PGHD) from wearables and mobile applications are increasingly integrated into interoperable digital health infrastructures. However, less attention has been directed toward how such data should be interpreted and presented to different stakeholder groups once technical interoperability has been achieved. This study explored stakeholder-specific usability requirements for interoperable PGHD and translated them into persona-oriented dashboard prototype concepts for patients, clinicians, and researchers.Materials and MethodsAn exploratory human-centered design approach was applied, combining narrative literature review, semi-structured expert interviews, persona development, scenarios, and service design blueprints. Three stakeholder personas informed the development of low-fidelity PGHD dashboard concepts connected to FHIR-based infrastructures.ResultsDistinct usability priorities emerged across stakeholder groups. Patients prioritized reassurance, clarity, and actionable guidance over extensive numerical detail. Clinicians emphasized concise summaries, workflow integration, and reliable longitudinal trends supporting clinical decision-making. Researchers focused on metadata transparency, completeness indicators, and usability for secondary analysis workflows. The findings suggested that generalized PGHD interfaces may inadequately support the differing expectations and practices of end-users.DiscussionThe study highlights that technical interoperability alone may be insufficient for meaningful PGHD integration. Even within shared FHIR-based infrastructures, stakeholder groups differed substantially in how they interpreted, validated, and used wearable-derived data. Human-centered design approaches may therefore provide an important complementary layer to interoperability-focused digital health initiatives.ConclusionEffective PGHD integration requires not only interoperable infrastructures but also interfaces adapted to the distinct informational, contextual, and workflow-related needs of patients, clinicians, and researchers.
